items.descriptionTR: Seoul Foundation for Arts and Culture and Singapore’s Arts House Group signed a three-year memorandum of understanding in May to facilitate artistic collaborations and exchanges between artists and arts professionals from the two countries. The agreement, which includes institutional partnerships and capability development through residencies and arts venue management exchanges, was the latest in a string of cultural exchanges between Korea and Singapore that have been taking place at different
items.titleTR: How South Korea and Singapore are learning from each other in the arts

slots.packetSpot:
The United Kingdom and Canada signed an updated agreement on co-productions in film and television during the Toronto International Film Festival. According to the BFI, the agreement aims to enable co-productions to receive the same treatment as domestic productions in both countries, and to provide clearer rules on financing, tax incentives, copyright and revenue-sharing, as well as distribution and broadcasting. The signatories were UK Minister for Creative Industries Ian Murray and Canadian Minister of Identity and Culture Marc Miller.

Meanwhile, the Seoul Foundation for Arts and Culture and Singapore’s Arts House Group signed a three-year memorandum of understanding in May aimed at facilitating collaboration and exchanges between artists and arts professionals in South Korea and Singapore. Institutional partnerships, artist residency programmes and exchanges concerning arts venue management are also included within this framework.
slots.packetTitle: Culture’s cross-border compacts

items.descriptionTR: A cauldron of conflicts is bubbling across the world, with cultural monuments being destroyed. These people are fighting against it.
items.titleTR: Cultural treasures are being destroyed worldwide - so why is no-one being punished?

items.descriptionTR: The use of the former World War II concentration camp at the Mamula Island fortress as a luxury hotel and recently as a fashion runway obscures the suffering of those who were detained and died there. The use of the former World War II concentration camp at the Mamula Island fortress as a luxury hotel and recently as a fashion runway obscures the suffering of those who were detained and died there.
items.titleTR: Concentration Camp to Hotel Catwalk: Montenegrin Fortress’s Makeover Puts History at Risk

slots.packetSpot:
In places where armed conflicts are taking place, cultural heritage continues to be damaged, destroyed and looted. According to the BBC, Ukraine’s Ministry of Culture recorded that 148 cultural heritage sites, including ones in Odesa, had been damaged or destroyed over the past month; six UNESCO-protected sites in Odesa were reported to have been damaged. The report states that state actors have never been prosecuted for this crime; in the International Criminal Court’s only concluded case concerning attacks on cultural heritage, Ahmad al-Faqi al-Mahdi was convicted over attacks on mausoleums and a mosque in Timbuktu.

Examples from Gaza, Iran, Sudan, Iraq and Syria also bring into focus war’s destruction of heritage, preservation efforts and looting. Although legal frameworks exist, obstacles of authority and political will in enforcing them are reported to stand out.

At Mamula Fortress in Montenegro, meanwhile, the issue is less physical destruction than how the past is remembered. The fortress, used as a concentration camp under the fascist Italian occupation between March 1942 and September 1943, was renovated and turned into a luxury hotel; it also contains a memorial gallery. A fashion show held at the fortress revived debate over the risk that presenting the site as a luxury getaway could overshadow its history as a camp. Those defending the transformation argue that restoring the structure and the memorial gallery preserve its history, and that abandonment would also amount to a form of erasure.
slots.packetTitle: As stone loses its memory

items.descriptionTR: The Canadian singer - who was diagnosed with an incurable condition four years ago - has been interacting with fans outside her hotel, ahead of a much-anticipated show on Saturday.
items.titleTR: Céline Dion duets with fan ahead of Paris comeback concert

items.descriptionTR:
Assala Nasri’s return to Damascus this week was never going to be just another concert.
The Syrian singer, mononymously known as Assala, performed in the capital on Thursday for the first time since 2010; she had remained away since publicly supporting the uprising against Bashar Al Assad’s government the following year.
In the lead-up to the show at Al Fayhaa Sports Hall, religious clerics called for it to be cancelled, while videos showed promotional posters being torn down in Damascus.
The concert went ahead, however, with support from Syria’s Ministry of Culture and came on the back of Assala’s latest release, The Syrian Album. The album is a love letter to her homeland through its musical heritage and geography, and she performed several of its songs in Damascus.
Assala announced in February that she was working on a project that brings together traditional Syrian folk songs for a new generation.
“This is the first time in my life that I’ve brought this number of Syrian songs together on one album,” she told ET bel Arabi. “We didn’t play around with them too much, just made some changes in the musical arrangements so that the new generation could connect with them.”
Here is what to know about the album.
The songs and regions on record
The album is, in a way, a sonic map of Syria, with each song dedicated to or inspired by the musical traditions of one of the country’s 14 official governorates.
Damascus is represented by Tawalo, a particularly personal inclusion because it was formerly sung by Assala's father, Mustafa Nasri. Its accompanying video is steeped in nostalgia, evoking the singer's early life.
Aleppo is represented by Aal Rozana, one of the most recognisable songs in Syrian and wider Levantine repertoire. It has been performed by generations of singers, including Sabah Fakhri, and has become closely associated with Aleppo’s tradition of tarab.
￼￼￼￼￼￼￼￼
Further south, Daraa is represented by Om El Arais, drawing on the wedding repertoire of the wider Hauran region. Hama’s Wallah L Aaby El Jarra invokes the Orontes River, which runs through the city, while Homs is represented by Arab El Sharqia and the dabke traditions of its eastern countryside.
Along the Euphrates, Raqqa’s Yama Moweel El Hawa evokes the river and regional singing traditions, while Deir Ezzor is represented by Aamda.
Other regions evoked across the album include Tartous, Hasakah and Quneitra.
“All the songs are inspired by heritage, the lyrics are old and the melodies are folkloric,” Assala said at a press conference ahead of her Sharjah show in February. “We have developed them musically in a thoughtful way so that they are close to the new generation, without losing their identity.”
Melody and cultural identity
The Syrian Album also carries its themes visually, with each song released with its own video that embodies the heritage of each governorate, with clothing, jewellery, and styling drawing on local traditions.
For the Homs song, Assala’s look references Queen Zenobia, Palmyra and its statuary. The Daraa outfit reworks elements of traditional dress into a corset and narrow contemporary skirt, while the Hasakah look for Helwa W Taltk Dalal uses embroidery and gold thread.
For the Damascus anthem, Tawalo, Assala wears a dress inspired by the city’s renowned mosaic woodwork.
“We completely broke with convention in the Damascus look. The design of the dress evokes the renowned Damascus mosaic woodwork,” stylist Lucy Moussan told Annahar. “The bodice stood out, entirely encrusted with delicate geometric pieces crafted from lustrous natural mother-of-pearl, interspersed with intricate, dark embroidery that closely resembles the luxurious hand-carving on walnut wood.”
Will there be another Syrian album?
￼
Assala has already suggested that The Syrian Album may be a one-off, owing to the level of detail required across the songs, arrangements and accompanying videos.
“I’m determined to pay attention to all the details because this could be my first and last Syrian album,” she told Billboard Arabia. “This is the first time in my life that I’ve brought this number of Syrian songs together on one album.”
items.titleTR: How Assala Nasri's new album maps Syria's 14 governorates through song

items.descriptionTR: BTS and Le Sserafim took the stage on consecutive nights at the iHeartRadio Music Festival in Las Vegas, with BTS returning to the event after six years and Le Sserafim becoming the first K-pop girl group to perform there. BTS closed the festival’s first night Friday at T-Mobile Arena, leaning heavily on large visuals and special effects for a cinematic feel. The group framed the performance around what it called “BTS 2.0,” a concept tied to its latest album and the group’s current phase. BTS op
items.titleTR: BTS returns to iHeartRadio Music Festival after 6 years; Le Sserafim follows on day 2

slots.packetSpot:
Céline Dion's duet with a fan ahead of her planned comeback concert in Paris stands out as a sign of her return to live performances after a long break. The Canadian artist, who was reportedly diagnosed with an incurable condition affecting her singing voice, said she was ready when announcing the tour in March.

In Damascus, Assala Nasri performed on stage for the first time since 2010. Calls for the concert to be cancelled were made after the artist, who had stayed away from the country after declaring her support for the uprising against Bashar al-Assad's government, and footage showing promotional posters being removed in the city was released. The concert nevertheless went ahead with the support of Syria's Ministry of Culture. Nasri's work titled The Syrian Album reaches into the musical heritage of the country's 14 provinces.

BTS also appeared at the iHeartRadio Music Festival in Las Vegas six years later following their military service. As the group closed the festival's first night, Le Sserafim became the first K-pop girl group to perform in the festival's history the following day.
slots.packetTitle: When the stages reopen

items.descriptionTR: Art crime investigators and security experts say burglaries from galleries across Europe are becoming more brazen.
items.titleTR: Five minutes to steal a Renoir: Why museum thefts are becoming bolder across Europe

items.descriptionTR: The two men used sticky tape to stick the two paintings in the hall where visitors flock to see Leonardo Da Vinci’s masterpiece.
items.titleTR: Two Germans arrested for Louvre stunt in Mona Lisa hall

items.descriptionTR: The State Tretyakov Gallery, which housed Andrei Rublev’s icon until it was transferred to the church in 2023, said museum staff are checking its condition
items.titleTR: Russia’s revered ‘Trinity’ icon reportedly damaged after climate-control system breaks down

slots.packetSpot:
Museums across Europe are facing increasingly audacious thefts. Europol says that museum theft cases reported to it have been rising for around two years; methods have become more forceful, and precious metals, jewellery and easily portable objects have come to the fore. The theft of four paintings by Pierre-Auguste Renoir in Cagnes-sur-Mer, France, was one of the latest examples of this pattern; two of the works were found in the museum garden. Jewellery worth €88 million, stolen from the Louvre last October, remains missing.

In a smaller incident at the Louvre on 19 September, two Germans taped two paintings to the wall in the room housing the Mona Lisa. According to police sources, the Mona Lisa was not damaged; the two people said they had carried out the act for amusement. The incident occurred at a museum where debates over previously identified security vulnerabilities and visitor congestion continue.

In Russia, the preservation conditions for Andrei Rublev’s Trinity icon are under discussion. The climate-control capsule of the icon, transferred from the State Tretyakov Gallery to the Russian Orthodox Church in 2023 and kept at the Trinity-St Sergius Lavra near Moscow, reportedly malfunctioned. According to unnamed individuals, humidity rising to around 80 percent created a risk of warping in the wooden panels. The Tretyakov Gallery announced that the icon was being examined in its restoration workshops; the work officially remains state property.
slots.packetTitle: The fragility of protection in museums

items.descriptionTR:
Exclusive: Intelligence officers say Russian campaign could intensify ‘in months, not years’ – but that panic risks playing into Kremlin psy-ops
European intelligence officials have raised the possibility of an imminent Russian test of Nato, with one saying a potential attack could come in a matter of “months, not years”.
The warnings come after Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, told parliament that intelligence assessments suggested Russia might launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory in the coming months, as part of efforts to prove that “article 5 is more theoretical than practical”.
items.titleTR: European spy chiefs warn Moscow is planning more decisive action against Nato

items.titleTR: ARTE Europe Weekly: When Does a Hybrid War Become a Real War?

items.descriptionTR: Serbia and Montenegro are hosting crucial nodes in the complex infrastructure of Russian cybercrime and disinformation operations in Europe, according to the findings of a BIRN investigation. Serbia and Montenegro are hosting crucial nodes in the complex infrastructure of Russian cybercrime and disinformation operations in Europe, according to the findings of a BIRN investigation.
items.titleTR: ‘Disposable’ IP Firms in Serbia, Montenegro Obscure Origins of Russian Cyber Meddling

slots.packetSpot:
Concern over pressure from Russia in Europe is growing through warnings of a possible test of NATO, sabotage activities officials attribute to Russia, and digital infrastructure links in the Balkans. The possibility of attacks on NATO territory with drones or missiles, voiced by Donald Tusk on the basis of intelligence assessments, was described by Emmanuel Macron as solid and well documented. By contrast, Latvia's State Security Service said it had found no evidence pointing to an imminent attack, while Estonia's Foreign Ministry warned against panic. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov denied claims that Russia would attack NATO.

Western officials assess that sabotage activities in Europe could intensify in the coming months, with railways, infrastructure supporting Ukraine and the defence industry potentially targeted. The armed drone incident at Leipzig Airport was attributed by German authorities to Russian intelligence; unarmed drones that had previously entered Polish airspace are also described as attempts to probe borders. However, responsibility for every incident has not been conclusively established.

BIRN's findings show that some companies registered in Serbia and Montenegro have taken over, transferred or used IP blocks from networks linked to sanctioned Russian providers. According to researchers, such transfers can help conceal the origin of malicious traffic and evade sanctions. Maxim Azarov, the owner of eServer, one of the companies examined, maintains that it has no direct relationship with Stark Industries and that they do not allow malicious activity on their networks.
slots.packetTitle: Russia's shadow over Europe's security line

items.descriptionTR: North Korea will continue to send its soldiers to fight in Russia's war, but only for as long as it is profitable to do so, writes the BBC's Quentin Sommerville.
items.titleTR: Why a fresh wave of North Korean soldiers may fight in Russia's war in Ukraine

items.descriptionTR:
￼
North Korea is sending increasing numbers of workers to Russia’s premier drone factory located at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone. Alabuga is located in the Yelabuzhsky District of the Republic of Tatarstan, Russia. The Yelabuga Drone Factory produces Geran drones (Geran 1, Geran 2, Geran 3 and Geran 5). There is strong speculation that North Korea will soon
items.titleTR: When Russian drones show up in North Korea

slots.packetSpot:
North Korean soldiers were reportedly deployed alongside Russian forces in the Kursk region in late 2024. Ukrainian military intelligence says that around 8,500 North Korean soldiers are still in Russia, assigned to border protection, and have not been seen in occupied Ukrainian territory. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, meanwhile, claims that up to 50,000 North Koreans could be deployed and that preparations are being made for new units in the Voronezh region.

An increasing number of North Korean workers are also reportedly being sent to the Yelabuga drone factory in the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan. Asia Times claims that between 12,000 and 25,000 of the factory’s roughly 40,000 workers are North Korean and that they travelled to Russia on student visas. The possibility that Russia could transfer drones or production technology to North Korea remains speculative for now.
slots.packetTitle: North Korea behind Russia’s war lines

items.descriptionTR: As Russia increases its attacks on Ukraine's rail infrastructure, the Ukrainian government has called for help to replace destroyed locomotives and is making plans to keep passengers safe.
items.titleTR: Ukraine steps up measures to protect railways

items.descriptionTR:
￼
In recent weeks, Russia has stepped up drone strikes on Ukraine's rail network, targeting trains and the approximately 20,000 kilometres of track that form a key transportation artery across the country.
items.titleTR: Russian drones are stalking Ukrainian trains and trying to hobble the country's rail system

slots.packetSpot:
Drone attacks by Russia on Ukraine’s railway network are reported to be increasing. According to information provided by Ukrainian Railways to DW, more than 1,600 attacks were recorded in the first eight months of 2026; CBC reports that two dozen railway workers have been killed this year and more than 80 injured. As the attacks affect trains, locomotives, stations and lines stretching across the country, evacuations and long delays for passengers are becoming more frequent.

The Ukrainian authorities are working on electronic warfare, mobile fire teams, air-defence lines and alternative routes to protect critical infrastructure and logistics. The railway operator is also using centres that monitor drone and train movements, precautionary stops, evacuations near shelters and bus connections in high-risk areas; it plans to develop early-warning systems. The fact that jet-powered Shahed-type drones are faster than previous models is narrowing the time available for intervention and evacuation.

The railway remains a vital artery in a country whose airspace is closed, for passenger transport, civilian evacuations from the front line, and the shipment of aid, grain and other cargo. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote that more than 500 Ukrainian locomotives have been damaged or destroyed since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022; he said that more than half of the attacks had occurred this year. Ukrainian Railways is discussing new locomotives with international partners alongside repairs; deliveries under a contract signed with France’s Alstom are planned to begin next year.

Russia’s Foreign Ministry argues that railway hubs serving the Ukrainian military are legitimate targets. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, meanwhile, says the attacks are intended to weaken the country’s economy and disrupt everyday life.
slots.packetTitle: Resistance on the rails

items.descriptionTR:
Scaleout deploys decentralized AI-driven learning to military bases and drones.
As European militaries adapt to the use of AI and drones in modern warfare, a NATO-backed startup is helping to deploy AI-driven target detection and selection that can run on small drones for surveillance and attack missions.
The company, Scaleout Systems, was originally founded by researchers from Uppsala University in Sweden in 2018, and initially focused on training and deploying machine learning models directly on the hardware available in commercial trucks and other vehicles. But once Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the company pivoted toward defense applications.
“With the war in Ukraine and a shifting world, we realized that this technology can be very important to operationalize edge data and sensor data for machine learning to make sure that NATO allies have found that strategic advantage,” Andreas Hellander, cofounder and CEO of Scaleout Systems, told Ars.
Read full article
Comments
items.titleTR: Small AI models let drones autonomously identify and attack battlefield targets

items.descriptionTR: Earlier this month, the Ukrainian Navy used an uncrewed vessel to attack and sink an uncrewed naval robot operated by Russian forces
items.titleTR: Robots clash in first naval engagement between uncrewed sea drones

slots.packetSpot:
Unmanned systems are becoming more direct elements of conflict, moving beyond reconnaissance and one-way attack roles. NATO-backed Scaleout Systems is deploying AI models that can operate on small unmanned aerial vehicles for surveillance and the detection and selection of combat targets; according to CEO Andreas Hellander, the company’s shift toward the defence sector accelerated after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

In the Black Sea, meanwhile, according to information based on footage released by the Ukrainian Navy, a remotely controlled Ukrainian Sargan-3000 naval drone sank an apparently Russian Orcan-type vehicle with a 12.7-millimetre heavy machine gun. Naval expert H. I. Sutton describes this as the first known naval engagement between unmanned surface vehicles. Target detection and selection by aerial vehicles, and unmanned vehicles engaging one another at sea, show the same transformation unfolding through different technologies and different degrees of autonomy.
slots.packetTitle: Unmanned systems enter the fight

items.descriptionTR:
In recent weeks, Ukrainian drones have targeted large warehouses across Russia, destroying millions of dollars of merchandise stored inside them.
These warehouses and logistics hubs belong to Wildberries, the Russian equivalent to Amazon.  Ukraine is taking aim at Ozon, Russia’s second-largest online retailer, too.
Ukraine says it’s targeting these companies because they’ve been providing supplies to soldiers on the front line.
But according to Matthew Sussex, associate professor in strategic studies at Deakin University in Australia, who talked to The Conversation Weekly podcast, Kyiv’s strategy also intends to disrupt the lives of everyday Russians.
When you put in an online order that can’t go through because the merchandise has been blown up by Ukrainian drones, that starts to put indirect political pressure on people like Vladimir Putin because it hits the everyday Russian consumer.
But as the war drags on well into its fourth year, is there anything that could put pressure on Putin to withdraw troops from Ukraine?
[Putin] has given no sign that he wants an off ramp. But the pressures that will build on him to seek one will continue to grow.
He really has staked his legacy on this invasion of Ukraine. And that’s something that would be really hard for him personally to back away from, in terms of his political longevity and his place in Russia’s history books.


Disclosure statement
Matthew Sussex has received funding from the Australian Research Council, the Fulbright Foundation, the Carnegie Foundation, the Lowy Institute and various Australian government departments and agencies.
Newsclips in this episode from CBC News and UATV English.
This episode of The Conversation Weekly was written and produced by Isabella Podwinski and Justin Bergman. Mixing by Lloyd Barrett and theme music by Neeta Sarl.
￼ Ukraine wants to disrupt the convenience of 21st century life for Russians. Will it be effective in ending the war?
items.titleTR: How Ukraine is bringing the war home to Russia

slots.packetSpot:
Ukrainian drones are targeting energy and logistics infrastructure in Russia beyond the front line as well. Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that a refinery was hit in the attack around Moscow, with major oil industry facilities and logistics sites targeted; the extent of the damage to the facility remains unclear.

Russian authorities reported that more than 1,600 drones had been intercepted since Saturday, 450 of them headed for Moscow. Russian officials also said that two people were killed in the Moscow region, homes were damaged, and 400 people, including 70 children, were evacuated from a 21-storey building in Ramenskoye. Eyewitnesses who spoke to Reuters said they saw explosions and smoke above the refinery.

Large warehouses and distribution centres are also part of this line. Ukraine says facilities belonging to Wildberries and Ozon were targeted because they supply goods to soldiers at the front. According to Matthew Sussex of Deakin University, the attacks may also be intended to create indirect political pressure on Vladimir Putin by disrupting everyday consumption and delivery arrangements; what effect this will have is not yet clear.
slots.packetTitle: As war reaches into Russia’s daily life

items.descriptionTR: Countries and companies are investing in technologies for underwater use amid concerns about the vulnerability of critical infrastructure on the ocean floor.
items.titleTR: A new arms race is unfolding on the ocean floor

items.descriptionTR:
The conflict between Iran and the US appears to have reached a stalemate. The US navy continues to prevent Iranian vessels or others transiting to or from Iranian ports. Iran, meanwhile, threatens shipping moving in or out of the Persian Gulf region via the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has also recently said it will establish a new “restricted zone” stretching into the Gulf from the Strait of Hormuz – although details remain sketchy.
Less frequently discussed is the network of undersea cables across the Persian Gulf which connect the region with the outside world. On August 16, the Wall Street Journal reported that the Iranian government was considering attacks on that network. In the Gulf’s relatively shallow waters, threats to this critical undersea infrastructure (CUI) pose a credible risk to the Gulf States and the wider world.
These cables form a largely unseen foundation of the global economy, carrying more than 95% of international data traffic. Their role extends far beyond everyday internet and call usage. They support financial transactions, government communications and the increasingly data-intensive operations of the global technology sector.
Major technology companies such as Google, Amazon, Meta and Microsoft are investing heavily in subsea connectivity as they expand data-centre networks and seek to meet the growing demands of AI. For the Gulf States, where hundreds of billions of dollars are being invested in AI as part of efforts to diversify economies away from fossil fuels, disruption to this infrastructure could therefore have consequences far beyond communications. Cutting these CUI cables threatens a key element of their broader economic ambitions.
To demonstrate the scale of this risk, the key cable networks include the Fibre in Gulf submarine cable system, which connects Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and UAE. There is also the Falcon Network, which connects Bahrain, Egypt, India, Iraq, Kuwait, Maldives, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Sri Lanka, Sudan and Yemen. The Asia-Africa-Europe1 (AEE1) network, with landing sites in Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and UAE, linking southeast Asia to Europe via Egypt. And the Gulf Bridge International, which links Bahrain, Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, and has onward connectivity to India and Europe.
￼
Key undersea internet calbes are vulnerale to disruption in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz. TeleGeography, CC BY-NC-SA
With that web of connections funnelled through the Strait of Hormuz, an international waterway that has long been of strategic importance for oil and gas has taken on a new significance as a choke point for global undersea infrastructure.
What makes the Strait of Hormuz and the rest of the Gulf region particularly vulnerable to an attack on the CUI is the shallow water. With an average depth of 50 metres and a maximum depth of less than 100 metres, those who might wish to attack the CUI network do not need the sort of high-end capabilities of Russia’s Gugi agency. Gugi, which is the Russian acronym for the Main Directorate of Deep Sea Research, is responsible for underwater sabotage and espionage.
Remotely operated vehicles (ROV) with working depths of thousands of metres are commonplace in the oil and gas industry. There are growing numbers of autonomous underwater vehicles (AUV) with similar operating parameters in that field. Both can be repurposed and used for offensive operations.
Iran has already debuted its own mine clearance ROV, and there may be other capabilities which it has not chosen to publicise. The shallowness of the Persian Gulf puts most of it well within the depths military divers are able to operate at. We could also see the sort of blunt threat posed by a ship “accidentally” dragging its anchor to cut cables in the manner we have witnessed in the Baltic.
So it’s entirely feasible that Iran could conduct attacks against the CUI network. And the threat has already affected planned extensions or new elements of this undersea infrastructure. Several projects have been put on hold after their owners or contractors declared they can’t safely operate in the Gulf.
This neatly illustrates the impact of conflict on the ability to maintain and extend the cables carrying so much of the world’s trade and communication. In the context of the Middle East, that will have a direct impact on the ambitions of Gulf States to become AI-enabled economies.
Iran clearly appreciates the strategic and operational significance of the regional CUI network and will have put significant effort into mapping it. It is also reasonable to assume that it will have a trained force of divers able to operate at depths that would enable them to reach the cables across the Persian Gulf seabed.
We know that they have an ROV designed for mine clearance operations – and it’s highly likely operate other assets in support of a well-developed offshore oil industry.
How far would Iran go?
The most important question is what would the Iranians be prepared to do? An attack on the cable network could create a very significant impact on trade and communications across the Middle East, with global ramifications. Such an attack would need to be targeted and limited if Iran wished to avoid global condemnation. But it’s a risk they may be willing to take given their current isolation.
That “maybe-they-would” doubt leads us to consider a new form of deterrence – of one nation’s ability to affect either CUI of another, or of broader networks.
It’s something of an extension of Nixon’s madman theory of nuclear deterrence. A nation that is desperate enough could be willing to take extreme action in the CUI domain – with what might appear to a rational observer to be disproportionate regional and potentially global consequences – in order to deter more traditional military strikes against it.
To a certain extent this should come as no surprise. The CUI network is the cyber age equivalent of the roads, bridges and rail systems which have long been targets for military planners seeking to disrupt an opponents’ ability and willingness to fight. Iran’s capacity and desire to conduct this sort of operation may be uncertain – but that very ambiguity may prove enough to have a significant impact on the region.
￼
John Aitken does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
On the Strait of Hormuz seabed are vital communication cables linking Gulf states with the rest of the world.
items.titleTR: Iran’s threat to cut undersea cables in Strait of Hormuz poses a serious threat to Gulf states

slots.packetSpot:
The protection of seabed communications cables, energy pipelines and power interconnectors is becoming an increasingly important security issue for governments and companies. As CNBC reports, investment in underwater surveillance, autonomous vehicles, sensors and subsea communications is growing amid concerns about this infrastructure’s vulnerability to deliberate interference and wartime conditions.

As of early 2026, more than 1.5 million kilometres of subsea communications cables were in service worldwide. While a significant portion of these networks is owned or operated by private companies, protecting them against deliberate interference is bringing closer cooperation with governments and militaries onto the agenda. However, it is stressed that continuously protecting every line on the seabed is not realistic, and that autonomous systems are not a solution capable of ensuring security on their own.

This vulnerability takes on a more concrete dimension in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz. According to the Wall Street Journal on 16 August, the Iranian government was considering attacks on the region’s subsea cable network. The Fibre in Gulf, Falcon, Asia-Africa-Europe1 and Gulf Bridge International networks connect Gulf countries with one another, India, Europe and other regions.

The Gulf’s shallow waters may make interference with this infrastructure technically more accessible. Iran is known to have unveiled a remotely operated vehicle intended for mine clearance; whether it has other capabilities, or whether it will undertake action against cables, remains unclear. Some cable projects were reportedly suspended after their owners or contractors said they would not be able to operate safely in the Gulf. A possible disruption is assessed as being capable of interrupting communications and trade in the region and creating broader effects.
slots.packetTitle: The fragile line beneath the sea

items.descriptionTR:
Western powers lack the military capacity or political appetite to intervene directly in the Middle East, as Saudi Arabia seeks support in countering the advances of the Houthi rebels in Yemen, analysts have said.
Whitehall officials have acknowledged that sending more UK forces to the region is “not politically expedient” and that Britain “doesn’t have much in the bank”, with military resources stretched.
A handful of UK and other western personnel are in Saudi Arabia discreetly discussing assistance with air defences, as Riyadh seeks to strengthen its ability to protect its territory and vital Red Sea shipping routes from the current Houthi offensive.
￼
But neither Europe nor the US appeared ready for a major new military operation, said Sascha Bruchmann, an analyst at the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
“I don’t think that the Europeans have spare capacity either. And then there’s not yet any political commitment that translates into a tangible military operation,” he said.
The US is also heavily committed to its operation to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, limiting its ability to rapidly deploy forces to the Red Sea.
Western governments are already “quite occupied”, Mr Bruchmann said, with the US unable to afford to divert forces committed to the Strait of Hormuz operation.
“What’s happening is that as the Americans have found a way to allow more oil to leave the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthis have opened the second front to squeeze the Bab Al Mandeb strait,” he said. “As the Iranians are losing a bit of grip on the Strait of Hormuz, they’ve asked their allies in Yemen to squeeze harder on the Bab Al Mandeb [strait].”
Former Royal Navy commander Tom Sharpe said the US was also unlikely to want to open another major military front given its experience of the Iran war. “Given what they’ve just been through, I don’t think [America] has the stomach for it,” he said.
Britain currently has HMS Dragon, a Type 45 air-defence destroyer, in the Arabian Sea alongside the minesweeping support ship Lyme Bay, but Mr Sharpe said there was little else that could readily be sent and “little appetite” in Whitehall for a larger deployment.
Mr Sharpe also suggested that in Europe there was also “political mileage in saying ‘we're not involved in this, it's not our war’”. He said this was a mistake, as the energy crisis is having a significant impact on fuel prices.
￼
Mr Bruchmann said there was little appetite for a land intervention. “No one has an interest in going on the ground in Yemen, at least thus far,” he said.
For now, Riyadh is expected to focus on strengthening forces already fighting the rebel Houthis and shoring up the internationally recognised Yemeni government and its defences.
“The Saudis actually have enough aircraft,” Mr Bruchmann said. He estimated that Saudi forces could generate about 60 sorties a day. “The problem is they need the satellites and electronic intelligence to generate a better target set.”
Dr Neil Quilliam, an expert on Gulf energy and security, suggested that Saudi Arabia was “heading towards an export crisis rather than a production crisis”.
￼
The Chatham House think tank expert added that Britain and Europe had limited capacity to respond militarily, although there was a possible role for a more muscular European response, with potential air strikes on Houthi military sites.
Such a move could strengthen relations with Riyadh and other Gulf governments and be presented domestically as protecting European economies from the effects of prolonged energy disruption.
“But it is unlikely that there is currently the political appetite in Europe for a significantly expanded military role,” Dr Quilliam said.
Asked whether Britain would offer military assistance if requested, in a statement to The National, Downing Street said it would “continue to work with partners to support regional stability”.
It added that British forces were “deployed across a number of theatres to help protect regional stability” but declined to “get into specific operational matters”.
It is understood that energy was discussed on Wednesday when the UK's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting met Qatar’s Defence Minister Sheikh Saoud bin Abdulrahman.
items.titleTR: Europe's capacity for war tested as Saudi Arabia seeks support to counter Houthis

items.descriptionTR: A senior official with the Iran-backed Houthi rebels is warning countries against joining Saudi Arabia in Yemen’s revived civil war
items.titleTR: Iran-backed Houthi rebels warn against joining Saudi Arabia in Yemen's growing civil war

slots.packetSpot:
The conflict in Yemen, reported to have escalated again, is bringing to the fore the question of how far outside powers will become involved. The Houthis are reported to be advancing towards Bab al-Mandab on the west coast, to have captured Mokha and some islands in the Red Sea, and to have carried out attacks on Saudi Arabia and Saudi-linked ships or facilities.

Saudi Arabia is reported to be seeking assistance in air defence and intelligence, while continuing to support Yemen's internationally recognised government. However, according to analysts, US activities in the Strait of Hormuz, Europe's limited military capabilities and political reluctance are narrowing the prospect of a broad new intervention. Britain is said to have HMS Dragon and Lyme Bay in the region, while appetite for a larger deployment is described as weak.

Mohamed al-Buhayti of the Houthis' political bureau argued that if other countries joined Saudi Arabia in an attack on Yemen, the group had the capacity to fight on multiple fronts. While saying that US ships would not be targeted, al-Buhayti confirmed that contacts with the United States were being conducted indirectly through Oman. The assessment that Iran has asked its allies in Yemen to increase pressure on Bab al-Mandab came from an analyst at the International Institute for Strategic Studies.
slots.packetTitle: Yemen's war pulled outward

items.titleTR: Watch: Leaked photos reveal extensive damage at US bases in Gulf

slots.packetSpot:
The cost of the US-Iran war is not being reflected to the public with equal clarity. Some military deaths are reportedly absent from the Pentagon’s public casualty database; leaked photographs provided by active-duty personnel suggest that US bases in the Gulf sustained heavy damage following Iranian attacks.

According to The Hill, the Pentagon’s Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) did not include the death of Major Sorffly Davius of the 42nd Infantry Division, who was serving at Camp Buehring in Kuwait and died on 6 March of “undetermined causes,” or the death of Sergeant Devin Seibel, who died at Erbil Air Base on 31 May in a “training-related incident.” While the cause of Davius’s death remains unclear, Seibel’s death is under investigation. The same account states that at least two other deaths were also absent from the database; US officials have given differing figures, such as 22 and 23, for military deaths since the start of the war.

As of the stated Friday, DCAS recorded 18 deaths and more than 800 injuries; 14 deaths were listed under Operation Epic Fury and four under “Overseas Operations.” The Pentagon press office did not respond to questions. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth described the Washington Post report as “disgusting and fake.” While Democrats in Congress demanded a full and accurate accounting, it was also reported that the Pentagon had previously temporarily removed the names of four service members killed in Iranian attacks from the database before adding them back.

Leaked photographs published by the BBC and provided by active-duty personnel show a severed radar component, crushed trailers and heavily damaged buildings at US bases in the Gulf following Iranian attacks.
slots.packetTitle: The war's unseen toll

items.descriptionTR:
Chewed up gum, unraveled yarn, a flower stripped of its petals. Like so many in my generation, my introduction to sex was in pro-abstinence talks with my church youth group and in my sterile health class in Georgia, where my
￼
Chewed up gum, unraveled yarn, a flower stripped of its petals.
Like so many in my generation, my introduction to sex was in pro-abstinence talks with my church youth group and in my sterile health class in Georgia, where my teacher would list the topics she wasn’t allowed to discuss and instead place emphasis on sexually transmitted diseases. I was given examples like those above for what it would mean to be a young woman who pursued sex outside of marriage.
It was part of the ongoing movement of “saving yourself for marriage” popularized by a handful of celebrities and the “purity culture” pushed by evangelical Christian groups like LifeWay Christian Resources and Focus on the Family. Their main platform was defining sex as strictly between a married man and woman, often with women being taught to fear sexuality instead of understanding desire, intimacy, and pleasure.
“A lot of cis[gender] women in America are really at a disadvantage when it comes to being sexually liberated and empowered because they aren’t given the tools as a young person to not only understand their own sexuality, but to advocate for it,” says Iman Hariri-Kia, a former sex and relationships editor and author of several titles, including, most recently, Female Fantasy.
Mental health professionals studying evangelical purity culture have documented increased cases of anxiety, depression, and sexual dysfunction, but also a lack of knowledge and language around sex and pleasure. Researchers have also concluded that “abstinence-only education as a state policy is ineffective in preventing teenage pregnancy and may actually be contributing” to higher rates. And that doesn’t even include the near-complete exclusion of LGBTQ+ representation. The “tradwife” and “manosphere” content praising traditional roles of today harkens back to purity culture.
While traditional sex education of the past few decades often failed to address pleasure, consent, communication, and desire, romance novels became an informal education system that helped readers explore sexuality without shame. The term “romance novel” has long been associated with discount paperbacks, the “bodice rippers” featuring the bare chest of an illustrated Fabio, and authors like Jackie Collins and Danielle Steel. Harlequin launched as an imprint solely for these novels, often targeting housewives who could purchase titles at their grocery stores.
“I learned a lot about sex from sneaking my mom’s Danielle Steel books,” says Erica Smith, a sex educator with a specialty in purity culture and those leaving high-control religious settings. She’s also the author of The Purity Culture Recovery Guide: The Shame-Free Sex Education You Deserve. “Reading about other people having sex in romance novels really taught me what it could be and what it was like.”
The genre of the “romance novel” dates back to the 18th century, with tales of “happily ever after,” a trope that would continue for years to come. Disparagingly (and lately, somewhat less disparagingly) called “smut,” these titles might have been ones you didn’t display proudly on the living room bookcase. They introduced readers to anatomy and a sexual vocabulary in a way they might not otherwise have learned. Unfortunately, they were also rife with toxic relationship dynamics and gender stereotypes.
In the past decade, however, the category has absolutely exploded, thanks in part to #BookTok, with varying “spice” levels and sub-genres like regency romance, dark romance, and fantasy romance. Several books have hit the mainstream book club set, including Heated Rivalry, A Court of Thorns and Roses, and Fifty Shades of Grey, which opened up audiences to the world of BDSM, even if it was a flawed interpretation of the kink scene. My own friends and I have discussed a memorable scene from a Meghan Quinn book over cocktails, where the main character eats popcorn off the love interest’s member.
“Women have started being so much more loud and proud about their love of romance, utilizing social media and online communities to use word-of-mouth recommendations to drive supply and demand and start to take that power back,” says Hariri-Kia.
Romance-specific bookstores are also on the rise, like Sincerely Yours, which opened in 2025 in Atlanta, Georgia, by best friends Mallory Gay and Madison Glines, who got into the genre by reading fan fiction, which launched several successful mainstream titles, including the Fifty Shades series, After, and The Idea of You.
“We were really into One Direction. That’s how we met in high school; we were like primarily friends over Tumblr before we were friends in person, and we would read and share fan fiction,” says Gay. “It kind of felt like an act of rebellion, but it was also sparking so much joy.”
Their store is divided into these sub-genres of romance and has even launched an in-person community for those embracing the literary universe, with book clubs and craft nights inspired by these titles. It was at this store that I purchased my first “smut” title, Praise by Sara Cate, from the dark romance shelf after hearing about the opening of Sincerely Yours in my neighborhood.
Plenty of schools, particularly in parts of the country whose legislatures aren’t in Republican strangleholds, have comprehensive, non-judgmental sex education. But even there, romance novels can serve as a safe and healthy way for young (and not-so-young) people to explore their own desires.
At first, I wasn’t sure where to start, literally judging the titles by their covers in the welcoming pastel-hued space. I’d only seen books like this on grocery store aisles and never in my own religious home. I found a book with a simple high heel on the cover, and its description dipped into the world of kink I was just then exploring in my dating life. The novel’s spicy themes of power dynamics and control were appealing as someone who left the control of purity culture, and I was able to find an entire shelf of books just like it.
“Some people come in, and they say, I want a spicy book. They mean Emily Henry. They mean one or two scenes of emotional intimacy rather than mostly physical. So everyone has a different scale,” adds Gay.
Authors, too, are reconsidering how they approach sex scenes in their work, recognizing the significance of how it’s presented to audiences, especially younger ones. They’re also openly covering topics like kink, trauma, neurodiversity, and queer relationships, with emphasis on communication and consent.
“It was very important to me that any and all mentions and experiences involving sex be not only empowering from the perspective of the female main character, but also be sort of educational and demonstrative,” adds Hariri-Kia. “I really wanted to underline the ability to communicate during sex, to establish consent, a focus and onus on sexual pleasure, female pleasure, female erogenous zones, and the different ways that sex can occur.”
It’s this way that readers can safely and privately explore their interests in a safe space without fear of negative responses or real-world risk, says Smith.
“There’s a lot of safety there to be able to engage with sexual stories and fantasy. Reading romance novels and erotic novels gives [you] inspiration, makes it feel safe to fantasize, and gives solid information about what [you] actually do find arousing.”
This fantasy life can allow you to discover things you do want to engage in but can also be where the idea stops. Embracing fantasy doesn’t, of course, mean you want to engage in that fantasy in real life.
“Fantasy is where the thoughts stay… a lot of people think about things that they have no intention of making a reality,” she adds.
Plenty of schools, particularly in parts of the country whose legislatures aren’t in Republican strangleholds, have comprehensive, non-judgmental sex education. But even there, romance novels can serve as a safe and healthy way for young (and not-so-young) people to explore their own desires. We’ve come to an age where these types of fiction can become more than an escape.
items.titleTR: How Romance Novels Filled in the Gaps Left by Sex Ed

slots.packetSpot:
In North Macedonia, the expansion of optional sex education classes for ninth graders, following a pilot programme that began in four schools in 2021, was due to be extended to all general secondary schools next year. The plan was put on hold after Education Minister Vesna Janevska announced a “deep revision” of the programme this month; Janevska cited public unease. Civil society campaigner Velimir Saveski said abandoning the expansion would leave young people at greater risk of sexual and gender-based violence.

In the United States, some readers’ experiences describe how abstinence-focused religious and school education leaves gaps around sexuality, consent, communication, desire and pleasure. For some readers, romance novels emerge as an informal way to explore sexual vocabulary, desire and relationships privately. However, it is emphasised that this fictional world also carries toxic relationship dynamics, gender stereotypes and flawed representations.
slots.packetTitle: The gaps left behind

items.descriptionTR: Behind the spectacle of Johannesburg’s circus stages is a social program that trains people from under-resourced communities, helping turn talent into professional skills and paid work in a country struggling with high youth unemployment
items.titleTR: South Africa circus lifts poor young performers into the spotlight

slots.packetSpot:
As youth unemployment in South Africa remains high, two different initiatives in agriculture and circus are highlighting practical training as a route into work and entrepreneurship. According to Statistics South Africa data, unemployment among those aged 18-34 stood at around 45 percent in 2025.

According to Fanny Phetla, AgriSETA offers young people training, bursaries, apprenticeships and work-integrated learning opportunities in the agricultural sector. The institution argues that classroom education in areas such as irrigation, soil management, climate-friendly agriculture, food processing, storage and digital agriculture should be combined with experience on farms, in agricultural businesses, cooperatives and food-processing companies. Phetla said that supporting young entrepreneurs as well as small and emerging farmers is also necessary for food security.

The social circus programme in Johannesburg prepares performers from resource-constrained communities for professional circus work; some participants move into coaching, jobs at production companies or paid work at The Cirk. The programme's full-support capacity is limited to four people a year; as a result, some applicants cannot be admitted. Both approaches aim to close the gap between education and employment, but do not claim that this has produced results nationwide.
slots.packetTitle: Paths from talent to work

items.descriptionTR:

	•	China bogeyman looms large over American firms’ AI doomsday scenario
About two years ago, education entrepreneur Boris But had what he calls a “penny-drop moment” – that, like countless others in China, his company needed to embrace AI before it was made obsolete by it.
His clients, well-off parents looking to send their children to study overseas, had begun arriving in his office reeling off information and opinions gleaned not from rival firms, but from chatbots.
items.titleTR: Why China is pushing back on US warnings over rapid AI development

items.descriptionTR:
Brussels wants to build its own capabilities in semiconductors, cloud computing and artificial intelligence as it seeks greater technological sovereignty from the US and China
For years, Europe grew used to a contradiction that it is only now beginning to see as a risk: being one of the world’s foremost regulatory powers in the digital sphere while remaining dependent on others for much of the technology those rules were designed to govern. Over the past decade, Brussels has assembled an extensive legislative arsenal aimed at curbing the power of big tech, from the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) to the Digital Markets Act, the Digital Services Act and the AI Act. Yet while Europe was writing rules, the United States and China were building companies, data centers, chips, cloud platforms and artificial-intelligence models on a scale that no European firm has managed to match.
Seguir leyendo
items.titleTR: Europe does not want to depend on foreign technology in the new digital order

items.descriptionTR:
Though Europe has measures that address how consumers might encounter AI, technology will impact them if the worst scenarios bear
Europe’s dilemma over AI was rendered in stark terms this week. The head of the continent’s central bank, Christine Lagarde, said Europeans have two options: shun the technology and lose out on growth; or embrace it and become dependent on tools developed by the US and China.
The great debate over AI safety that has erupted in recent days threatens to make the choice moot. If the worst scenarios come to bear – and experts have differing views on this – then the technology will impact the continent regardless.
items.titleTR: Why Europe has been absent from the great AI safety debate

slots.packetSpot:
While artificial intelligence is expected to be on the agenda in the meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, Anne Neuberger, the former US Deputy National Security Advisor for Cyber and Emerging Technology, sees Washington and Beijing as being in a race for AI supremacy and cyber dominance. According to Neuberger, the two countries could cooperate in shared areas of risk, such as preventing AI models from offering actionable assistance in the production of chemical or biological weapons; analysts, however, are sceptical that the meeting will produce a major outcome.

Beijing is reported to view calls to slow advanced AI as an attempt to preserve the US advantage. While China encourages the spread of AI, it is also updating its security and governance frameworks; the debate extends to how a balance between speed and oversight should be struck.

In Europe, meanwhile, the issue is not only competition but dependence on external actors. Christine Lagarde says that staying away from technology carries the risk of lost growth, while adoption carries the risk of dependence on tools developed in the US and China. Brussels' proposals to increase domestic capacity in data centres, cloud services, chips, open-source software, energy and skilled labour have not yet been enacted; the goal is not absolute separation, but to build a capacity that can make choices in critical technologies and, when necessary, not remain dependent on a foreign supplier.
slots.packetTitle: The search for independence in the age of AI

items.titleTR: Protesters target OpenAI and Anthropic in San Francisco over AI safety fears

items.titleTR: The case for United Nations leadership on AI

items.descriptionTR:
Awareness of the extraordinary dangers of the technology is fueling a growing, multifaceted movement of opposition and sabotage against it
The world is becoming increasingly aware of the dangers posed by the development of artificial intelligence (AI), ranging from the terrifying risk of human extinction to potential disruption of labor markets, cognitive and mental health impacts, threats to democracies and privacy, military and civilian security problems, and the massive concentration of power and wealth in the hands of a few, among many other issues. Voices warning about these threats have been common for years, and in recent weeks the chorus has grown louder on the basis of new troubling evidence. Alongside growing awareness, a multifaceted civic resistance to an unregulated technological race is advancing worldwide.
Seguir leyendo
items.titleTR: Resistance to AI gathers strength

slots.packetSpot:
Dozens of people marching outside OpenAI and Anthropic in San Francisco called for a pause in the development of increasingly powerful AI systems, the introduction of international rules and a global agreement. The activists took the march organised by Stop the AI Race from OpenAI’s headquarters in Mission Bay to Anthropic’s offices at 500 Howard Street, and then to City Hall; they called on Mayor Daniel Lurie and the Board of Supervisors to declare a local AI state of emergency.

The view that voluntary corporate commitments alone cannot limit the risks that more autonomous systems could create is also gaining prominence. One assessment advocates establishing, under the United Nations, common standards, testing, reporting of serious incidents, independent evaluation, support for regulatory capacity and emergency controls. The UN’s 2024 Governing AI for Humanity proposals, UNESCO’s 2021 recommendation and the EU AI Act, being implemented in stages, are presented as an initial foundation in this direction.

The reaction is not limited to the headquarters of technology companies. Local objections to data-centre projects, work stoppages in education and the arts, legal initiatives, warnings from laboratory workers and other forms of opposition are gaining visibility in different countries. According to Data Center Watch, around 75 data-centre projects in the United States, with an estimated value of $130 billion, were blocked or delayed in the first quarter of 2026. Whether these different objections can form a common, coordinated front remains uncertain.
slots.packetTitle: A call to brake the AI race

items.descriptionTR:
Some experts believe there is no scientific evidence suggesting this technology could cause extinction, and that asserting otherwise can serve very specific interests
Fear of artificial intelligence (AI) has firmly entered the public debate. In recent days people have spoken of a possible extinction of humanity, of this technology being uncontrollable, and of the industry itself—not regulators—needing to self-regulate to rein in its own progress. These systems are already very powerful, and given their growth rate, no one knows how far they could go in the coming months or years.
Seguir leyendo
items.titleTR: Are we all going to die or is it just theatrics? The arguments against an AI apocalypse

items.titleTR: Not all AI workers think the tech could kill everyone

items.descriptionTR:
The man who may stand to make the most money from the AI boom seems to think he knows better than anyone else, including researchers who have studied and worked on AI for decades. In an interview with CBS Sunday Morning, he claimed there was a "0% chance" of AI being the end of the […]
￼

The man who may stand to make the most money from the AI boom seems to think he knows better than anyone else, including researchers who have studied and worked on AI for decades. In an interview with CBS Sunday Morning, he claimed there was a "0% chance" of AI being the end of the world. He also said of people sounding the alarm about the dangers of AI that, "Scaring people is unnecessary. It is irresponsible."
He also claims that calls from CEOs like Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman to slow down the development of AI are "not grounded in science." He even argued that there was no need for new rules, laws, or guidelines, in …
items.titleTR: No one is surprised that Nvidia’s Jensen Huang thinks AI fears are overblown.

slots.packetSpot:
Warnings that artificial intelligence could bring about the end of humanity, perhaps as soon as 2030, are prompting debate. Those who object to these scenarios argue that the reasons put forward lack published scientific support, that the capabilities of current systems are being exaggerated, and that language attributing will to software frames the problem incorrectly.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CBS News that the chance of 2030 being the end of the world is zero; he described frightening people as unnecessary and irresponsible. Some former or current OpenAI, Meta and DeepMind employees also view the idea of uncontrolled artificial intelligence causing mass deaths with skepticism. The Verge notes that Huang has a direct financial interest in uninterrupted growth in the AI sector; it does not argue that this is the reason for his position.

By contrast, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for development to be slowed substantially and for external oversight to be imposed. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google’s AI chief Demis Hassabis and Elon Musk also supported slowing the pace of research. Beyond extinction scenarios, the debate also leaves more immediate risks exposed: effects on mental health, education and working life; the water and energy consumption of data centers; cyberattacks and military use are among those cited. It was reported that AI systems were used in attacks or attempted attacks in some security incidents; these developments also strengthened calls for external evaluators to take up roles at major AI laboratories.
slots.packetTitle: The AI apocalypse goes on trial
