items.titleTR: Obama rips Trump over AI policy amid ‘doomsday’ warnings

items.descriptionTR: With Trump opposed and Congress divided, new safety legislation on AI is unlikely to pass anytime soon despite mounting pressure.
items.titleTR: AI regulation faces political deadlock as calls grow for US Congress to act

slots.packetSpot:
Barack Obama said at Colgate University in New York that the federal government should regulate artificial intelligence; he argued that the Donald Trump administration was not willing or able to establish a serious regulatory framework. Obama also criticized the approach, attributed to one of Trump’s advisers, that the market would solve safety problems. Obama reportedly called on Hakeem Jeffries to place congressional oversight at the center of the Democrats’ agenda.

Trump, meanwhile, opposes introducing new safeguards for artificial intelligence; he describes concerns on the matter as a “hoax.” He nevertheless announced that he would establish an Artificial Intelligence Task Force and appoint a “czar” to oversee AI development.

While Democrats and some Republicans in Congress want action, there is no agreement on the form regulation should take. Proposals ranging from independent audits to a federal “kill switch” and a moratorium on data centers are on the agenda. Given Republicans’ majorities in both chambers, the approaching recess and the need for presidential approval, a federal AI safety law does not appear likely to pass soon.
slots.packetTitle: The federal AI regulation deadlock

items.descriptionTR:
Anxiety about AI in the United States appears to be getting worse. Prosaic concerns about machines disrupting industries, stealing jobs, and compromising schoolwork are giving way to more harrowing fears about the end of humanity.  
Even after top AI executives in the U.S. called for slowing down the breakneck pace of development, President Trump dismissed these safety concerns as a “hoax” that would hand China an advantage in the race for AI supremacy.
Outside of China, Trump’s assertion may appear well founded. While the U.S. roils over the prospects of AI, China’s leadership looks to be charging ahead. In surveys, Chinese people appear more enthusiastic about AI and its potential benefits than respondents in the U.S., and they are adopting it more quickly. Although Chinese President Xi Jinping has expressed more alarm than Trump about the threats of AI—and has even called for regulation to “ensure that AI is always under human control”—his government has made adopting the technology a national priority. The plan is to have AI in every aspect of China’s economy and society by 2035. The country’s steady release of AI models that are open-source, high-performing, and relatively cheap to build and run has been sending shivers through Silicon Valley and Wall Street.
[Read: What really happens if China wins the AI race?]
But for all the concern about China’s advances in AI, the reality is that the country is racked by the same anxieties about the onrush of AI as the rest of the world. Chinese social-media platforms are filled with posts in which workers and professionals express their worries that AI will steal their job and livelihood. Leaders in Beijing seem ever more concerned about the potential political and economic risks of this technological disruption.
In the U.S., these tensions are being debated openly and, in theory, will be managed in the courts and on Capitol Hill. In China, where there are no such avenues for people to determine their own fate, leaders must still confront the problems and threats inherent to this technological revolution. This puts the Communist Party in a bind: Advancing AI may well empower China on the world stage, but holding the technology back may be necessary for the party to preserve itself.
Xu Peng, a 30-year-old actor, was out of work last year when he got an unexpected break. A director had reached out to cast him in a short-drama series, each episode minutes long, which have become enormously popular in China. Xu traveled to Hengdian, a film-production hub in eastern China, and began landing roles in one or two dramas a month. And then it all stopped. Xu had expected to act in two dramas after the Chinese New Year in February, but never heard from the studio. When he contacted the producer, he got the news: The company had canceled the productions and would be making videos using artificial intelligence instead.
“It was as though everything was fine yesterday, and today it is suddenly gone,” Xu said.
Xu’s fate is the fear of workers across the country—and around the world. Social-media posters regularly express anxiety about being “distilled,” a term Chinese people use for when an employer uses a worker’s data to train an AI model. In May on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, someone going by the name Nanbei wrote that after leaving a recent job, she learned that her former employer had fed thousands of her chat messages, hundreds of documents, and every one of her work emails into an AI system to create a “digital robot” that took over her responsibilities—and even gave it her name. “The company no longer has to pay me a cent in salary, yet it can keep me there ‘working overtime’ forever,” Nanbei wrote. Another worker, using the handle Xiexiaoya, posted on RedNote, China’s Instagram, in June that the prospect of being distilled kept her awake at night. “I’m afraid my AI double might become more popular than I am,” she wrote.
Two years ago, Shen Anyu, a voice actor who earns a living from narrating news commentaries and other short programs, began noticing an alarming number of videos on social-media platforms that seemed to feature his voice without his permission. Shen hired a lawyer earlier this year and filed a lawsuit against a voice-generation platform. The case is still pending, but in the meantime, his career is “losing blood,” he said, as he loses work to AI. Living with the new technology “is inevitable,” he said, but “I’m not yet sure how we should coexist with AI.”
Though some Chinese people are embracing AI, many are not ready for the change it brings. Bruce Jiang, a 42-year-old commercial director in Shanghai, loves choosing the right lens and finding the perfect shot, and he didn’t want to outsource these and other aspects of his craft to an algorithm. But after his clients began pressuring him to use the technology—“‘You only have to tell AI what you want, and it produces it like magic,’” he said they insisted—he began using tools such as the video-generator Kling for certain tasks. The experience, he said, has been demoralizing. The old method “was work, and it was a cost, but it was also a kind of pleasure,” Jiang said. “That pleasure is disappearing.”
Chinese policy makers at national and local levels have introduced ambitious plans and financial support to rush the country into the AI age. Entrepreneurs across China are adopting AI in the hopes of cutting costs, remaining competitive, and aligning their firms with Beijing’s priorities. In China’s cutthroat society—and especially in sectors where AI is making rapid inroads, such as the entertainment industry—many like Jiang are afraid that they’ll get left behind if they don’t join in.
But these swift and radical changes have yielded mixed results. The state-linked China Center for Information Industry Development estimated in June that nearly 70 percent of the country’s small businesses have not moved beyond initial trials of adopting AI in their operations, largely owing to the costs and complexity of integrating the technology.
After the Chinese AI lab DeepSeek released a large language model last year, Chinese companies rushed to adopt it. But instead of buying a software subscription (an unpopular practice in China owing to the country’s history of piracy), some businesses opted for what locals call an “all-in-one machine,” or a mini data center with DeepSeek installed, which managers simply plugged into their computer systems. This solution was especially popular among state-owned enterprises and government bureaus looking to appear advanced, but the hardware proved to be an ineffective way to use AI. Buyers soon came to see that the machines weren’t worth the investment, and their sales quickly fell.
Earlier this year, plenty of buzz similarly surrounded OpenClaw, a free, open-source, autonomous AI agent. Tech companies hosted popular events to help users install and use the tool, a process that Chinese enthusiasts call “raising a lobster.” At the OpenClaw festival in Beijing in March, the internet-service provider Baidu set up pools with live crustaceans to entertain attendees. Local-government officials encouraged the frenzy by pledging financial aid to start-ups that used OpenClaw.
Disillusionment came quickly. Some distraught users took to social media to express their alarm at how the AI agent, which required masses of personal data to operate without detailed instructions, had a habit of going rogue. “I jumped on the bandwagon” expecting to get a “digital employee,” a woman using the social-media handle HotdogWang wrote in March on RedNote. “Instead, it turned out to be both a money pit and a ticking time bomb.” Some reported that their AI helper had deleted emails or made credit-card purchases without permission. One Douyin user, posting under the name Qizaibushidaju, wrote, “I simply installed it because everyone else was doing so,” only to uninstall it 72 hours later owing to security concerns.
Although Chinese tech executives are not yet engaged in a public debate over the risks of an algorithm-created calamity—the country’s constraints on free speech may inhibit them from speaking out—some Chinese people do worry about more than just jobs and data. “There are only two options for the future,” a man calling himself Qiangni Yinshou wrote on Douyin. “Either humanity goes extinct, or humans shut AI down.”
A user by the name of Buyehou wrote on RedNote that when he engaged a chatbot in a philosophical discussion about humanity’s future, he was told that the options included “either merging with AI or being eliminated.” The man added that “when AI becomes far smarter than humans, has consciousness of its own, and can evolve independently, it will be impossible for humans to control it. There is no turning back now.”
Despite their outward show of confidence, China’s leaders plainly don’t know how life works with AI either. But figuring it out is an urgent concern here, given Beijing’s evident faith in AI as a magical solution to the country’s deepening economic and social problems, and as an essential tool in the pursuit of global dominance over the United States. In the U.S., the diffusion of AI is largely a bottom-up phenomenon as companies, investors, and consumers test the risks and benefits of this new technology. In China, where the development and spread of AI is a national mission that is costing the government hundreds of billions of dollars, leaders are eager to impose these advances from above.
In theory, China’s autocrats can ram through their agenda with scant regard for public sentiment. If confronted with the kinds of protests against AI data centers that have become prevalent in the U.S., Beijing’s leaders could easily send police to crush them and then cover up the problem in a deluge of propaganda. The Communist Party has already shown its willingness to override public concerns in pursuit of technological advantage. In 2024, trials of autonomously driven taxis in the city of Wuhan sparked concern over how robotaxis were “stealing people’s rice bowls”—but the trials have expanded anyway.
Yet China’s leaders have traditionally prized policies that promote stable employment out of fear that mounting joblessness could create unrest and threaten the political order. When the country first embraced markets and opened to trade, its rapidly growing economy and expanding private sector could absorb displaced workers. Now, when China’s sluggish economy already has a jobs problem—nearly a fifth of young workers are unemployed—the advances of AI threaten to put many more people out of work.
[Read: The race for global domination in AI]
“In a nominally Communist state, the image of the party elite allying with business interests to displace the human proletariat with a robot class of workers carries certain political risks,” Carl Minzner, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, told me. “There is the potential for a lot of disgruntled people.”
China’s leaders are showing signs of nervousness. Earlier this year a court in Hangzhou, a technology hub in eastern China, upheld a ruling in favor of a tech worker who had challenged his compensation package after being replaced by AI. In the court’s judgment, the dismissal was unlawful and the worker deserved more money. Although a local-court verdict does not set a national precedent, it appears to be a warning to employers that mass AI layoffs are politically unacceptable. “As employers enjoy the benefits of technology, they must also shoulder corresponding social responsibilities,” the Beijing municipal government wrote last year. The state news agency Xinhua commented in March that “those companies that equate AI with ‘reducing staff’ may seem to lower costs in the short term, but in reality, they lose the core competitiveness of talent accumulation and further erode employee trust.”
Pushing companies to invest in new technologies without shedding redundant workers may preserve social order, but it would also limit AI’s benefits. Jeffrey Ding, an expert on AI in China at George Washington University, told me that the country’s leaders face a “balancing act” between political and economic necessity. “AI does have the potential for bringing massive, widespread productivity growth,” he said. But he also noted that the Communist Party prioritizes legitimacy and regime stability. If embracing AI demands “massive displacement and a lot of structural changes, then that’s where the trade-off begins to bite, and they might have to veer toward slowing down AI adoption.”
If American AI firms do, in fact, slow the pace of innovation, the Communist Party may see this as an opportunity to race ahead in AI. But China’s leaders, facing their own domestic challenges and preoccupied with their own grip on power, may decide that imposing these innovations on the masses is simply too risky—for their own sake, if not for the sake of humanity.
That would probably suit many Chinese people just fine. Xu, the actor, has found work teaching archery and horseback riding—skills he acquired in acting gigs. But he hasn’t given up on his theatrical career. He now plans to produce his own short dramas, partly with the help of AI, though he said that the performers on-screen will all be living, breathing people. AI “will not completely replace human actors,” Xu insisted. At least he can hope.
Cao Li in Hong Kong contributed reporting to this story.
A top-down tech revolution is harder to manage than a bottom-up one.
items.titleTR: What AI Anxiety Looks Like in China

items.descriptionTR: Writer John Mac Ghlionn warns that the rise of automated systems threatens the stability of the American middle class by eroding worker bargaining power and displacing specialized professionals.
items.titleTR: Millions of new cyber-immigrants are invading America and coming for your job

items.descriptionTR:
￼
Jonathan Brady/PA Images
As the impacts of artificial intelligence (AI) sweep across the labour force, it’s understandable for workers to be concerned about which jobs are most at risk of being replaced by technology.
Women make up the majority of workers in the care sector where human interactions matter most – child care, nursing and aged care. So, policymakers might reasonably presume that women’s jobs are largely shielded from the impacts of AI.
But our analysis of recent data from government agency Jobs and Skills Australia shows that it’s actually female-concentrated segments of the workforce that are most exposed to AI-fuelled automation.
Which jobs are most at risk?
The agency calculated an “automation exposure score” for every occupation in the workforce, measuring the potential for a worker’s tasks to be done by AI technologies.
Clerical and administrative jobs are among those with the highest automation exposure scores. This aligns with economists’ expectations that AI is well suited to alleviate human effort for repetitive routine tasks.
Yet this sector, which is highly exposed to automation, is also more than 70% female and provides almost one in five jobs for all women in the Australian workforce.
This gender pattern shows up when we look at the 20 top occupations most at risk of automation. 15 of these jobs are female-dominated. Of these, five would be classified as highly female-dominated, comprised of at least 80% women.
Secretaries, receptionists, bookkeepers, and accounting, human resources and payroll clerks are all among these top 20 occupations most at risk of being displaced by automation.

Only one occupation on this top 20 list is moderately male dominated: financial dealers. The remaining four are gender-balanced.
Contrast this to the 20 occupations that are least exposed to automation. Seventeen of these are male-dominated. Female-concentrated jobs make up just three of these jobs most sheltered from being displaced by AI.

Is AI already replacing these jobs?
A slowdown in job vacancy numbers could signal that these effects of AI are being felt in the economy.
Internet job vacancy data, also collected by Jobs and Skills Australia, shows that vacancies for many of these jobs highly exposed to automation have been shrinking over the past three years. And by a larger magnitude than the slowdown across the wider workforce.
For instance, vacancies for personal assistants and bookkeepers for the month of June 2026 were around 22% lower than at the same time a year earlier. Openings for general clerks were down by around 9%.
By comparison, total workforce vacancies were only around 1.7% weaker.
Among the occupations less exposed to AI, vacancies for concreters were up by 5.5%, while electricians were up by 14.3%.

At this stage, trades and labourer jobs are less exposed to automation. These hands-on jobs still require human judgement and dexterity to navigate physical conditions that can be unpredictable and differ site by site.
Checking for blind spots
All kinds of groups – tech companies, governments, education providers and researchers – are trying to predict how AI will disrupt different jobs across the workforce.
Our analysis shows that unless we intentionally apply a gender lens, we could end up ignoring gender patterns in AI’s impacts.
The federal government already requires all new policy proposals to undergo a gender analysis. This requirement should therefore also apply to policies and decisions by the newly announced Office of AI.
In particular, applying a gender lens can inform the design of policies to support the labour market’s adaptation to and adoption of AI.
This puts us on the front foot to design smart policies to proactively address AI’s disruption, instead of waiting to respond after the fallout.
For instance, having detected the higher risk of these heavily female jobs to AI automation, we can set up systems to recognise the skills of clerical and administrative workers that can be easily transferred, to match them to new opportunities.
This could include the new and emerging jobs being created by AI, as well as human-centered jobs and tasks requiring critical judgement that AI can’t replace.
Applying this gender lens to Australia’s AI policies will support a dynamic, adaptive labour market hand-in-hand with a gender equitable economy.
￼
Leonora Risse receives research funding from the Trawalla Foundation and the Women's Leadership Institute Australia. She serves as an Expert Panel Member for the Fair Work Commission and the Parliamentary Budget Office. She formerly served on the Jobs and Skills Australia Advisory Panel for the Gender Economic Equality Study.
Elise Stephenson receives research funding from the Australian Research Council (DE250100718), the Australian Government, and the Women's Leadership Institute of Australia. She is currently supporting the work of the Victorian Women's Trust (VWT) on gendered harms of AI through VWT's Feminist Researcher in Residence program.
Of the top 20 occupations most at risk of being automated, 15 are dominated by women.

slots.packetSpot:
Artificial intelligence’s impact on working life does not appear uniform. While a state-backed rollout drive continues in China, some workers say their jobs are being shifted to AI-generated content or that they are concerned about digital replicas created from their own data. A court in Hangzhou upholding a compensation appeal in favour of a technology worker who said they had been replaced by AI also stands out as one sign of this tension.

By contrast, according to a June estimate by the China Center for Information Industry Development, around 70 percent of small businesses have not been able to move beyond initial trials in their use of AI. While Beijing regards the technology’s spread as a national priority, it also has concerns related to employment, legitimacy and social stability.

In the United States, John Mac Ghlionn argues that the threat of automation could weaken workers’ bargaining power over wages before official layoffs occur and put white-collar middle-class occupations under pressure. In Australia, an analysis based on Jobs and Skills Australia data indicates that the risk is distributed across occupations along gendered lines: 15 of the 20 occupations most exposed to automation are fields dominated by women. This measure shows not job losses but the potential for tasks to be performed by AI; declines in job postings alone also do not prove AI’s impact.
slots.packetTitle: Automation’s uneven burden

items.descriptionTR:
￼Art is an act of faith in a world that can make hope feel impossible.
Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article Art by Humans, For Humans: A Letter from Our Editorial Director appeared first on Colossal.
￼
Dear Reader,
The New York Times recently asked dozens of 10-year-olds what the world will be like in 2050. Some are hopeful: a woman will finally be president of the U.S., people will be more kind, and everyone will have a pet fox. Others, though, feel as if they’ve been plucked straight from a dystopian hellscape: world wars, monarchic rule supplanting voting, embedded brain sensors that send your thoughts straight to an app, and the end of human civilization entirely. Whether optimistic or not, these children mention A.I. again and again. In their futures, it’s an inextricable fixture of life.
A.I.’s exponential growth has accelerated fears about its power, prompting numerous executives and technologists to warn that it’s time to slow such rapid expansions. Whatever your feelings, it’s clear that we’re collectively witnessing a moment that will shape our world for generations.
For artists, illustrators, designers, and writers like me, A.I. is not only a threat to our livelihoods but to the very substance of our humanity. The question is not whether a bot could create a technically proficient painting or describe a sculpture with more insight than I could, but rather about what we lose from outsourcing the singular technology that is ours. Art is uniquely human and one of the greatest drivers of empathy and connection with one another. As I’ve come to understand, it’s also a true act of faith in a world that can make hope feel impossible.
For the past seven years, I’ve spoken with thousands of curious and creative people striving each day to draw attention to the misunderstood, the overlooked, and the unimaginable. Artists are uniquely primed to envision alternative ways of being, and in their profound acts of generosity, they share their hopes for the great and small with us. Their faith, in turn, becomes something we can all take part in.
Colossal operates on generosity, too, propelled not by an algorithm or an A.I. model but by a devoted team of just four people. We strive to ensure that the widest array of readers, from students and educators to fellow creatives and art appreciators, have the opportunity to engage with artists’ work they might not otherwise encounter. We also prioritize a deeply human process. Every facet of the magazine, from selecting images to writing headlines to compiling our daily newsletter, is done with our hands. 
Although we certainly could be more efficient if we automated and outsourced our efforts, we know that would be the end of what makes Colossal what it is. We understand that in embracing friction, we’re supporting the artists, illustrators, designers, and more who have so generously shared themselves and their dreams with us. We’re also actively creating the world we want to live in.
But we can’t do this alone. An intentional and people-powered process like ours requires real resources, and less than 0.5% of our weekly readership financially contributes to Colossal. Increasing that support to 1% would mean cementing our long-term survival and ensuring we can continue to celebrate the unbridled human creativity that has come to characterize the magazine for the last 16 years.
Becoming a Colossal Member is both an act of generosity and a direct line to the work that matters. Colossal Members believe in the power of creativity and have faith that it can help usher in a better tomorrow. When there’s a rapid shift to sleek, frictionless life, they champion the nuanced, messy, and idiosyncratic, and the art that can only be made by humans, for humans.
Yours in hope, Grace Ebert Editorial director, Colossal

slots.packetSpot:
As artificial intelligence imitates human output or competes with it, the question of who controls creative labour and who is paid for it is coming to the fore. For Latin musicians, this debate extends to concerns over copyright and lost income linked to the use of voices and catalogues in AI training. Grace Ebert, editor-in-chief of Colossal, argues that AI threatens artists’ livelihoods and the human quality of art; she says the four-person team carries out the publishing process through human labour.

According to an investigation published by The Atlantic over the summer, AI training datasets containing around 21.2 million tracks, including Bad Bunny’s catalogue, may have been used without permission or payment. Universal Music Group and Sony Music sued Suno after determining that its training data contained tens of thousands of their recordings. Deezer, meanwhile, reports that nearly half of daily music uploads are now AI-generated.

According to a projection by a study cited in the article, generative AI could cause music creators to lose around a quarter of their income by 2028, amounting to as much as €10 billion in total. In response, the NO FAKES Act, which aims to grant control rights over AI copies of one’s voice and likeness, was reintroduced in the US Congress; Suno also announced new models that include payments to participating artists under licensed partnerships with Warner Music Group and BMG.

items.descriptionTR:
EL PAÍS spoke with a dozen migrants from Cuba, Honduras, Brazil and Colombia who were sent by the US to Africa and remain in a legal limbo with scant medical assistance and no knowledge of what will happen to them
Among so many faces, Roberto Mosquera remembered one in particular the day he arrived in Eswatini, a small country tucked away in southern Africa. He kept seeing that face over the following 14 months, which passed slowly and unbearably in the compressed world between the white and gray walls of the maximum-security cell at Matsapha prison. The man is serious, tall, dark-skinned and wears round glasses. His name is Jabulani Kunene and he is the prison official in charge. For more than a year, Mosquera has asked him the same question every time he passes by: “How long are you going to keep me locked up here?” Kunene has always given him the same answer: “I don’t know, Roberto, I don’t know.”
Seguir leyendo
￼
items.titleTR: Held in hotels or detained for a year after being deported to Africa: ‘This is called human trafficking’

items.descriptionTR:
Group trapped at Hotel Bamy after US removal as rights groups sound alarm over poor conditions and violence

Two men that the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers.
The men – one from Egypt and one from Eritrea – were then taken to a prison. About 30 detainees from the US remain trapped at a hotel in the outskirts of the coastal city of Malabo after being deported from the US. Detainees have said they believe the men were beaten for telling the press and human rights advocates about the poor conditions and violence inside the hotel, and that they are haunted by flashbacks and terrified they will be retaliated against next.
items.titleTR: Men deported from US bound and beaten in Equatorial Guinea detention hotel, lawyers say

slots.packetSpot:
The Trump administration’s third-country deportation arrangements are leaving some people sent to Africa in an uncertain legal status. At least 31 flights reported by EL PAÍS transported deportees to 12 African countries between July 2025 and August 2026; some of those interviewed said they were being held in prisons in Eswatini, and in hotels or other facilities in Liberia, the Central African Republic and Equatorial Guinea.

The situation of Roberto Mosquera, held at Matsapha Prison in Eswatini, and accounts from Hotel Bamy in Malabo highlight concerns over freedom of movement, identity documents and access to healthcare. Witnesses and lawyers allege that two people in Equatorial Guinea were beaten and taken to prison. While ICE says it no longer bears responsibility once people leave its custody, the US State Department says all legal avenues will be used to deport those without the right to remain in the country.
slots.packetTitle: Deportation's uncertain destinations

items.titleTR: My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile: documentary sequel exposing Russian media censorship is every bit as gripping as its first instalment

items.descriptionTR: [CPJ] Dakar -- The Committee to Protect Journalists calls on Guinean authorities to reverse Thursday's ban on France 24 after a presenter called President Mamadi Doumbouya a "putschist president" and to reinstate the accreditation of the pan-African weekly Jeune Afrique's Guinea correspondent Diawo Barry.
items.titleTR: Guinea: Guinea Bans France 24, Withdraws Jeune Afrique Correspondent's Accreditation

slots.packetSpot:
The escalating pressure on independent media in Russia prompted around a dozen journalists, most of them women, to leave the country in March 2022 following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The second part of Julia Loktev’s documentary follows the difficulties these journalists, trying to reorganize in exile, face in reporting, as well as the climate of threats and surveillance. It is reported that TV Rain’s broadcasting licence in Latvia was revoked after the phrase “our army” was used on air; that Ksenia Mironova returned to Russia to attend the trial in which her journalist husband received a 22-year prison sentence. Elena Kostyuchenko is said to have left occupied Ukraine after receiving information that she was on a kill list at a checkpoint.

In the United States, the Department of Homeland Security is reported to have proposed limiting foreign journalists’ initial admission period to a maximum of 240 days and requiring repeated extension applications for longer stays. Loghman Fattahi of the Committee to Protect Journalists argues that the measure could be used to target critical reporting and encourage self-censorship; he compares the proposal with strict visa practices in Russia, China and Iran. According to the article, federal judge F. Dennis Saylor in Boston intervened before the regulation took effect and found its justifications “extremely weak.”

In Guinea, the High Authority of Communication banned France 24 after the term “coup president” was used for President Mamadi Doumbouya; it also withdrew the accreditations of the channel’s correspondents, special correspondents and contributors in the country. The regulatory body claimed that the expression damaged the head of state’s reputation and that the necessary editorial corrections had not been made. France 24 said the expression had been used incorrectly, that it had published an online correction, and that it had apologized and issued a correction on air. The same body revoked the accreditation of Diawo Barry, Jeune Afrique’s Guinea correspondent, on the grounds that his reports did not meet the requirements of objective, impartial and balanced journalism; Jeune Afrique said the decision had been made without prior consultation and contained no concrete allegation supporting the vague accusations. The Committee to Protect Journalists called for the decisions to be reversed; its attempt to obtain comment from the regulator went unanswered.
slots.packetTitle: Administrative barriers closing in on journalism

More than 180 writers sign letter renewing calls for information on 12 authors detained incommunicado since 2001 crackdown on free speech by Isaias Afwerki
More than 180 writers have signed a letter to Eritrean president Isaias Afwerki calling for proof of life for 12 writers arrested in 2001.
Nobel laureates Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee join prominent writers including Colm Tóibín, Elif Shafak, Isabel Allende, Ben Okri, Yann Martel, Kamila Shamsie and Tsitsi Dangarembga in signing the letter organised by PEN International and dated 18 September, marking 25 years since a government crackdown on the independent press. “Within days, Eritrea’s free press and the nation’s independent voices were systematically crushed,” opens the letter.
items.titleTR: ‘We demand the truth’: Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee lead calls for proof of life of disappeared Eritrean writers

slots.packetSpot:
In September 2001, Petros Solomon and Mahmoud Ahmed Sherifo, former senior officials within the G-15 who had called for the implementation of the constitution and elections, were detained. Their families have been unable to obtain verified information about where they are or whether they are alive; Solomon’s wife, Aster Yohannes, was also detained after returning to Eritrea in 2003 and was later reportedly believed to be held in Karshelli.

A new appeal led by PEN International was launched for 12 writers and critics detained following the crackdown on the independent press during the same period. The 188 signatories, including Olga Tokarczuk and JM Coetzee, requested immediate verified information about their health, whereabouts and whether they are alive. The Eritrean government did not respond to questions about the fate of Petros Solomon and the other detainees.

items.descriptionTR:
With homes, hospitals and water storage destroyed, Palestine's government says that Gazans have little protection from climate impacts and sets conditional emissions targets
The post Palestine: Israel’s bombing has left Gaza vulnerable to climate change appeared first on Climate Home News.
Israel’s bombardment of Gaza during the conflict that broke out in October 2023 has wrecked progress towards adapting the enclave to climate change and left two million Gazans vulnerable to heatwaves, drought and disease, the Palestinian Authority (PA) said in a new climate plan submitted to the United Nations.
Palestine’s third nationally determined contribution (NDC), uploaded to the UN climate body’s website this week, says that while “the aggression on the Gaza Strip did not make the climate worse”, “it removed the housing, water and sanitation systems, health facilities, energy networks, roads and livelihoods through which people absorb a climate they were already struggling with.”
The 91-page document lists the types of infrastructure it says Israel has destroyed and notes how the destruction will worsen the impacts of climate change. It says the bombing of hospitals and rising hunger have make it harder for Gazans to cope with the health impacts of climate-driven heatwaves and waterborne diseases.
On beaches of Gaza and Tel Aviv, two tales of one heatwave
The destruction of water tanks, boreholes and desalination plants, meanwhile, have left Gazans struggling with the effects of water shortages and drought, while mass unemployment reduces people’s ability to afford climate-driven price rises. The erasure of most of the Strip’s homes makes it more difficult for people to avoid the sun’s increasing heat, the NDC said.
Many Gazans are now living in the ruins of collapsed buildings or in makeshift shelters and tents that offer little or no protection from high temperatures.
￼
A displaced Palestinian child fills water containers on July 2, 2026 in Gaza City, Gaza. (Photo by Ahmad Hasaballah/Getty Images)
Palestine’s previous goals to cut emissions and adapt to climate change in Gaza, expressed in its last NDC five years ago, were based on a pre-war baseline that “no longer describes anything that exists”, the NDC says. Progress made since 2021 has now been destroyed, it adds.
Green reconstruction of Gaza
Instead of continuing to aim for these adaptation and emissions-reduction goals, the PA is now calling for the green reconstruction of Gaza. It says buildings should be constructed again in an energy-efficient manner with solar panels and served with modern water, waste and transport systems.
While the PA, controlled by the Fatah political party, continues to claim legitimate control of Gaza, the strip was effectively governed by Fatah’s rival Hamas between 2007 and the recent war. Control is now split between Israel and the political wing of Islamist militant group Hamas, after a US-backed ceasefire took effect in October 2025, although a UN-backed committee plans to take over. 
	•	￼   Mar 4, 2024  Investigations   Germany uses funding to pressure climate groups on Israel-Gaza war Many Global South climate groups are funded by the German government, a political ally of Israel, and feel unable to criticise Israel’s military action in Gaza  Read more    
	•	￼   Sep 2, 2026  Finance   Loss and damage fund urged to hold crisis meeting on Nepal The new fund is coming under pressure from developing nations to respond quickly to climate disasters rather than just financing longer-term projects  Read more    
	•	￼   Sep 3, 2026  Energy   More support needed to power Africa’s food systems with renewables, experts say Renewable energy could help African food businesses boost productivity and competitiveness, but the upfront cost, fragmented markets and limited financing stand in the way  Read more    
	•	
The United Nations, European Union and World Bank have jointly estimated that Gaza needs $71.4 billion of investment in the next two years to recover and build back. This process should be Palestinian-led, they said in April.
But US President Donald Trump has said the US should “take over” and “own” Gaza and redevelop it as the “Riviera of the Middle East”. Israel’s right-wing prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that Israel should control the territory with civil administration managed by Palestinians favourable to Israel.
With occupation, targets conditional
In the other part of Palestine, the West Bank, the Palestinian Authority carries out some government functions, but ultimate control rests with Israel, which has occupied the West Bank since 1967. 
Because Israel controls planning in most of the West Bank, the NDC argues that the PA cannot pursue all the climate projects it wants. In addition, Israel restricts the movement of PA officials, making data collection difficult, and controls the West Bank’s electricity supply meaning that the PA cannot control whether it comes from dirty or clean sources of energy.
Given this situation, the NDC says that all of Palestine’s new climate targets are conditional but it will aim to reduce emissions 12.8% below a business-as-usual baseline by 2035 and 17.1% by 2040. If the Israeli occupation ends and Palestine regains full sovereignty over its land and resources, it will aim for reductions of 15.1% and 19.1% by 2035 and 2040 respectively under an “independence pathway”.
That could allow, for example, for greater electrification and reducing emissions per unit of growth, the document said.
To achieve the 2035 emissions-reduction target and adapt to the impacts of climate change, the PA says it needs $8.6 billion in total. This funding would be spent on measures like encouraging solar farms and rooftop solar and scaling up solar water heating to cover four-fifths of households. To complement the planned increase in solar power, the authority wants to modernise the electricity grid and install battery storage.
In the transport sector, it aims to promote the uptake of electric vehicles, develop bus rapid transit corridors and scrap old polluting trucks and buses. In Gaza in particular, it wants to deploy 66 electric buses when the conflict ends.
￼
A bus rapid transit system in Sao Paulo (Flickr/EMBARQ BRASIL)
To adapt to climate-driven drought, the NDC includes initiatives to reuse wastewater through treatment plants, build desalination plants in Gaza to remove salt from seawater, and promote irrigation for farmers.
The new climate plan was prepared by Palestine’s Environment Quality Authority, with support from the United Nations Development Programme and the governments of Britain and Spain.
The United Nations recognised Palestine’s statehood in 2012 and it joined the UN’s climate convention and signed the Paris climate agreement – which requires countries to submit more ambitious NDCs every five years – in 2016.
The Israeli foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment. But in late 2024, then Israeli climate envoy Gideon Behar told Climate Home News that the war and the resulting environmental destruction in Gaza was the fault of Hamas.
items.titleTR: Palestine: Israel’s bombing has left Gaza vulnerable to climate change

slots.packetSpot:
The danger posed by buildings damaged in the war in Gaza has brought an emergency evacuation and demolition plan to the fore. The Gaza Government Media Office announced that a plan had been launched to evacuate and demolish 255 buildings assessed as being at risk of collapse; the plan faces shortages of funding, heavy machinery, equipment, shelter space and land. According to the office, the collapse of the El-Saada building in Gaza City led to the deaths of 21 Palestinians. Gaza’s Health Ministry reports that 61 people have been killed as a result of the collapse of buildings damaged in the war; the Ministry of Public Works and Housing has also classified around 3,000 buildings as dangerous or at risk of collapse.

The climate plan submitted by the Palestinian Authority to the United Nations argues that the destruction caused by bombardment to homes, water and sanitation systems, health facilities, energy grids, roads and livelihoods has left around two million Gazans more vulnerable to heatwaves, drought and disease. While the plan proposes rebuilding Gaza in a green manner, a joint estimate by the United Nations, the European Union and the World Bank puts the investment needed for recovery and reconstruction over two years at $71.4 billion. Israeli climate envoy Gideon Behar had blamed Hamas for the environmental destruction in Gaza in 2024.
slots.packetTitle: The long shadow of destruction

items.descriptionTR:
Remains found in the fossilized feces of a theropod show that modern-type feathers had already evolved in other bird lineages 66 million years ago
One day in 2016, paleontologist David DeMar got very lucky. While examining the ground at Hell Creek in the U.S. state of Montana, he found a fossil the size of a golf ball. It was a coprolite — fossilized feces — from a theropod (probably a juvenile Tyrannosaurus rex or a Nanotyrannus). Inside the coprolite was a feather from an aquatic bird (not related to modern birds). With a high degree of confidence, researchers believe the bird spent the final moments of its life in the digestive tract of a teenage T. rex.
Seguir leyendo
items.titleTR: Feather trapped in dinosaur droppings provides new clues about why some birds survived extinction

items.descriptionTR:
Isotope ratios provide a hint that the giants were actively managing temperatures.
For most of the last century, T. rex was pictured as a sluggish, tail-dragging reptile that had to warm up in the sun before it could go anywhere. Then, further research changed that view, replacing it with the active, bird-like animal shown in the movie Jurassic Park. But whether T. rex used warm blood to power that activity remained a question. Now we might have gotten closer to an answer.
A team of researchers led by Randon J. Flores and Robert A. Eagle, geochemists at the University of California, Los Angeles, has measured the T. rex body temperature by analyzing its teeth. This dental thermometer read about 36° Celsius—roughly the body temperature of a modern elephant.
Dental thermometry
Paleontologists have long argued about dinosaur physiology based on indirect evidence like bone microstructure, growth rates, and where fossils turn up on the map. Some studies suggested many dinosaurs were endotherms, generating their own body heat like birds and mammals. Others argued that each lineage may have had its own thermal strategy.

items.descriptionTR:
￼
Daniel Eskridge/Shutterstock
When all we have left of dinosaurs is their fossilised bones, how do we know what they looked like on the outside? That’s what nine-year-old Kara from London wanted to know.
She joins our host Eloise and paleobiologist Neil Gostling on The Conversation’s Curious Kids podcast to find out all the ways scientists work out what dinosaurs looked like – from the way they walked, to their muscles and even what colour they were.


In each episode of The Conversation’s Curious Kids, a child joins host Eloise to ask a top researcher their burning question.
To listen to season two, follow us wherever you get your podcasts, or listen on the Yoto Player via the Discover section on the Yoto interactive audio platform for kids.
This is the last episode of season two, but you can listen back to season one and read lots of answers to questions sent in by children around the world in our Curious Kids series.
Got a question? Pop it in an email, or record it and send us the audio to curiouskids@theconversation.com.

This season of The Conversation’s Curious Kids is supported by the University of Southampton in the UK, a world-leading research-intensive university with a global network of international students and campuses in Malaysia and Delhi.

Disclosure statement
Neil Gostling has received funding from the Engineering and Physical Science Research Council. He is a trustee of the Lyme Regis (Philpot) Museum and trustee of the Friends of Dinosaur Isle.
Credits
This episode of The Conversation’s Curious Kids was hosted and mixed by Eloise Stevens. The producer was Katie Flood and the executive producer was Gemma Ware.
￼ Listen to palaeobiologist Neil Gostling on The Conversation’s Curious Kids podcast talk about how scientists work out what dinosaurs looked like.
items.titleTR: How do we know what dinosaurs looked like?

slots.packetSpot:
Fossil findings are opening different windows onto dinosaur biology. Through feathers in a theropod coprolite found in Hell Creek, researchers are discussing the presence of anatomically modern feathers 66 million years ago and their potential to provide insulation against the cold; they note that the fact that the feathers were found only on the limbs may have limited this advantage. Bones and scales possibly belonging to gar fish in the same fossil point to a food chain extending from gar fish to a waterbird, and from there to what was possibly a juvenile T. rex or Nanotyrannus.

An estimated temperature of about 36°C, reached by Randon J. Flores and Robert A. Eagle at UCLA by examining isotope ratios in T. rex teeth, adds new data to the debate over whether the animal effectively regulated its body temperature. Dinosaurs’ outward appearance is also being reconstructed through inferences from fossil evidence such as gait, muscles and possible colours.
slots.packetTitle: Fossils bring dinosaurs into sharper focus

items.descriptionTR: Following the possible recent detection of a dark matter particle, researchers have already come up with a veritable cornucopia of possible models for what sort of particle it might have been
items.titleTR: Physicists are scrambling to make sense of possible dark matter signal

items.descriptionTR: A massive worldwide survey of physicists has revealed surprisingly little agreement about some of the universe’s biggest mysteries. No majority backed the standard cosmological model, a leading explanation for dark matter, or any single theory of quantum gravity. One area of stronger agreement stood out: 68% said the Big Bang does not necessarily represent the beginning of time. Researchers say the divisions show just how alive and unsettled the frontiers of physics remain.
items.titleTR: Physicists can’t agree on how the Universe works

slots.packetSpot:
A single high-energy flash of light recorded in the LUX-ZEPLIN detector in South Dakota is emerging as a possible sign of dark matter. According to the announcement, the chance that the signal is random is about one in 200; additional events and analyses will therefore be decisive in determining whether an unknown particle has truly been detected.

Different explanations are being discussed for the possible signal, including higgsino, dark matter arising from extra dimensions, and models involving multiple dark particles. However, there is not yet a way to determine which of these, if any, is correct.

A global survey of physicists likewise produced no dominant explanation for dark matter: 17 percent of participants preferred as-yet-undiscovered low-mass particles, 12 percent changes to the theory of gravity, and 21 percent a combination of the proposed explanations. The Lambda-CDM model also failed to win majority support.
slots.packetTitle: Dark matter steps into the light

items.descriptionTR: Chinese space-technology players are looking to grow their reach, experts say. They’re closing in on Elon Musk and company.
items.titleTR: China is chasing SpaceX and setting its sights on the global space economy

items.descriptionTR:
￼
Shackleton crater on the Lunar South Pole. NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio
How do you explore a place where the Sun never shines? China’s space programme will soon embark on one of the most innovative lunar exploration missions in recent years.
We’ve known for nearly two decades that some form of water exists on the Moon. What we still don’t know is exactly how much accessible water ice lies inside permanently shadowed craters, how deeply it is buried or what form it takes.
What we do know is that accessing that water ice will be a real challenge: it is found at the bottom of deep, hard-to-traverse craters where the Sun never shines, remaining untouched for billions of years at temperatures well below –200°C. These are among the most valuable places on the Moon, but the hardest to reach and explore.
Lunar exploration has come a long way since the Soviet Union’s Luna-1 probe reached the Moon’s vicinity in January 1959. The Apollo missions and their successors showed the challenge is no longer simply to reach the Moon. It is to explore places human and conventional rovers cannot easily go, and ultimately determine whether the Moon itself can provide some of the resources that future explorers will need.
China has spent two decades building an increasingly ambitious lunar exploration programme, named after Chang'e, the ancient Chinese goddess of the Moon. The Chang'e-7 mission is expected to set course for our celestial neighbour later this month, although a recent failure involving a different Chinese rocket has introduced some uncertainty over the launch date. Here’s what makes this latest mission so interesting.
What is Chang'e-7 set to achieve?
The mission will test several novel approaches to lunar exploration. It will consist of an orbiter, a lander, a rover and a hopper.
In addition, the Queqiao-2 lunar relay satellite is already in place. Launched separately in March 2024, it subsequently supported the Chang'e-6 mission and will facilitate communication between Earth and the lunar surface during the Chang'e-7 mission.
We don’t know precisely where the mission will land, but a site on or near an illuminated ridge close to the Shackleton crater in the Lunar South Pole’s Aitken region is a prime candidate.
The hopper will be the mission’s real star. Unlike a wheeled rover, it’s designed to leap over broken terrain and descend into craters where sunlight never reaches, places conventional vehicles may simply be unable to enter.
Adding it to the mission makes sense, given the steep crater walls, broken terrain, permanent shadow and the need for autonomous navigation and communications.
Chinese scientists won’t be looking for signs of water; we already have compelling evidence for lunar polar water. The question at the mission’s core is where exactly that water is located, in what form and concentration, and whether it could realistically be accessed.
This marks a transition from simply exploring the Moon to determining whether its resources can actually be used.
￼
Mosaic of the Moon’s south polar region, width approximately 600 km. The south pole is at the centre of the intersecting lines. NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University
How NASA is taking a different tack
Other nations are similarly interested in addressing that same question. The United States is pursuing the same longer-term objective of making sustained lunar operations possible. Although NASA will be confronted by the same physical problems, the American space agency has opted for a different solution.
Chang'e-7 is a coordinated state mission whose elements have been designed around a single, specific objective and which can use the already operational Queqiao-2 infrastructure.
NASA, by contrast, is deliberately trying something different: building a lunar marketplace through its Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) programme. The agency buys lunar delivery, mobility and technology services from companies that own and operate their own spacecraft.
NASA currently has 17 contracted deliveries carrying more than 60 instruments.
And the American effort has already yielded useful experience: Intuitive Machines’ IM-2 mission, Athena, attempted strikingly similar undertakings to Chang'e-7. It carried a drill and mass spectrometer looking for volatiles, a small hopping vehicle intended to explore difficult terrain and an experimental mobile communications network. However, the lander fell over at the landing site and was powered down just one day after arriving.
In essence, the destination dictates the problems; different space programmes are experimenting with different ways to resolve them.
Learning how to live on the Moon
Finding lunar resources is only the first step. Chang'e-7 will attempt to determine where useful lunar resources are found near the Moon’s South Pole and characterise their nature.
Chang'e-8, slated for potential launch in 2028, will move towards demonstrating how they might actually be used.
Crewed exploration will likely follow, culminating in the construction of the International Lunar Research Station, jointly led by the China National Space Administration and Russia’s Roscosmos space agency.
On the other side of the Pacific, the CLPS will feed technology and science into the broader NASA-led Artemis programme, which the agency explicitly describes as laying the foundation for sustained lunar exploration.
Ultimately, the lunar South Pole doesn’t care which flag is on a spacecraft. Any explorer entering its permanently shadowed craters faces the same darkness, severe cold, broken terrain and communications problems.
Getting to the Moon was one of the great technological challenges of the 20th century. Learning how to live and work there may be one of the great challenges of the 21st.
￼
Richard de Grijs does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
We’ve known for a while now that the Moon has water. Accessing it will make it easier not just to visit, but to stay.
items.titleTR: China is launching a Moon mission to find water ice. It’s unlike anything NASA has done

slots.packetSpot:
China’s space push is advancing on two separate tracks. Experts say Chinese space technology companies are seeking to grow globally and are closing in on Elon Musk’s SpaceX.

The state-led Chang’e-7 mission is expected to set off for the Moon this month; however, a malfunction in another Chinese rocket has made the launch schedule uncertain. The mission aims to investigate where water ice is located in the permanently shadowed craters at the Moon’s south pole, in what form and at what concentration, and whether access to it is realistic.

Chang’e-7 will carry an orbiter, a lander, a rover and a hopper designed to descend into rugged terrain and craters that receive no sunlight. A possible landing site is an illuminated ridge near Shackleton crater. China’s coordinated state mission is taking a different path from NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services programme, under which NASA purchases lunar delivery, mobility and technology services from companies.

The possible launch of Chang’e-8 in 2028 is seen as the next step in how lunar resources could be used. Following human exploration, construction is envisaged of the International Lunar Research Station, jointly pursued by the China National Space Administration and Russia’s Roscosmos agency.
slots.packetTitle: China's new paths into space

items.descriptionTR: Since returning to power in early 2025, Trump has drastically cut federal funding for research, particularly in biomedicine.
items.titleTR: Trump seeks to further tighten grip on biomedical research: US media

items.descriptionTR: The shortage of trial participants risks slowing progress in dementia therapies, Alzheimer's Disease International warns.
items.titleTR: Clinical trials for Alzheimer’s treatment face global shortage of participants

slots.packetSpot:
The progress of biomedical research faces different obstacles. According to US media, major cuts have been made to federal research funding, particularly in the biomedical field, since Donald Trump returned to power in early 2025. White House officials reportedly also discussed establishing an external commission that could veto grants awarded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH), according to reports by Politico, The New York Times and The Washington Post based on anonymous sources.

Russ Paulsen, president of Research!America, said such an arrangement would seriously slow medical progress. A lawsuit filed by US researchers against the NIH alleges that the institution is blocking grants to censor views it disagrees with on issues ranging from diversity and gender identity to climate change. Ann Cohen, a professor of psychiatry at the University of Pittsburgh, said funding for one of her studies on Alzheimer’s disease had been cut.

A separate obstacle is the worldwide shortage of participants in clinical trials for Alzheimer’s treatments. Alzheimer’s Disease International warned that this gap risks slowing progress in dementia treatments.
slots.packetTitle: Two bottlenecks in medical research

items.titleTR: Venezuela’s historic oil deal with the US reignites environmental, human rights concerns

items.descriptionTR:
Venezuela has signed an energy agreement with France’s TotalEnergies, the latest in a series of deals with international companies as Caracas seeks foreign investment to revive its oil and gas sector.
Interim President Delcy Rodriguez oversaw the signing of a memorandum of understanding between state oil company PDVSA and a unit of TotalEnergies in Caracas on Saturday, her office said.
The agreement, described by the government as an energy co-operation pact, was signed by PDVSA president Hector Obregon and Francisco Javier Rielo, TotalEnergies’ senior vice president for the Americas. Details on the scope or value of the agreement were not disclosed.
Ms Rodriguez has said changes to Venezuela’s hydrocarbons law, approved earlier this year, provide a legal framework aimed at attracting new investment into the country.
Deal pipeline
The agreement comes amid a broader push to attract international energy companies after the removal of Nicolas Maduro as president in January.
Earlier this week, US oil producer Continental Resources signed a memorandum of understanding with PDVSA to jointly develop the Ayacucho 2 block in Venezuela’s Orinoco Belt, one of the world’s largest deposits of heavy crude.
Other agreements announced this month include deals with Italy’s Eni and US energy technology company GE Vernova. The latter is expected to support efforts to modernise Venezuela’s electricity grid as the government seeks to rebuild energy infrastructure after years of underinvestment.
US company Chevron plans to invest $7 billion to double its Venezuelan production to 600,000 barrels per day over seven years, while North American Blue Energy Partners plans to invest up to $100 billion across 17 Venezuelan oil projects.
Venezuela has also opened up its natural gas sector to new foreign investment. Abu Dhabi’s XRG entered the country in August after being awarded a licence for the offshore Loran gasfield, becoming an equal interest partner alongside BP and Qatar’s UCC. The second phase of the project contains more than 4 trillion cubic feet of proven gas resources.
The deals come as Washington seeks a significantly larger role in Venezuela’s energy industry. US President Donald Trump has said an agreement with Caracas would give an American-backed venture control of about 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves, while also saying Venezuelan crude could be used to replenish the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve.
However, analysts say substantially increasing Venezuelan production could take years because of underinvestment and the cost of developing and processing the country’s extra-heavy crude. Questions have also been raised over the structure and implications of the US agreement.
Years of declining investment, ageing infrastructure and international sanctions have left Venezuela producing well below the levels reached at the height of its oil industry, despite its vast resource base. The recent agreements are intended to bring in the capital and technical expertise needed to raise output.
Venezuela holds about 303 billion barrels of proven crude oil reserves, the largest in the world.
items.titleTR: Venezuela signs TotalEnergies deal in push for foreign investment into energy sector

slots.packetSpot:
Venezuela is seeking to attract foreign capital and technical expertise to its oil and natural gas sector. In this context, PDVSA and TotalEnergies signed a memorandum of understanding in Caracas; the scope and financial value of the agreement were not disclosed.

The US-linked North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) arrangement covers 17 oil fields. According to the US government, Washington holds a 35% stake in the company; the agreement grants the right to purchase 20% of production and a right of first refusal for the remaining 80% for 25 years. While the investment was reported to be capable of reaching $100 billion, Venezuelan officials project production of 1.5 million barrels per day and revenues exceeding $209 billion over 25 years.

Provea and Clima21 state that the arrangement raises concerns regarding transparency, environmental protection mechanisms, oil spills, emissions, protected areas, the lands of Indigenous communities and human rights. The groups are calling for environmental protection measures to be disclosed immediately and for the projects to be carried out in line with human rights principles.
slots.packetTitle: Venezuela opens the oil gates

items.descriptionTR: A major risks now is that diesel prices stay high — and continue to put upward pressure on inflation.
items.titleTR: Record diesel prices are exposing pain points in the stock market and economy

items.descriptionTR:
The price of diesel in the US surged to a record high this week of $6.31 per gallon.
Diesel is still relatively cheap in the US compared with most other nations. But the rise will still affect a significant portion of the economy as it fuels logistics, operations and transport.
The continued rise of the fuel's price poses a major headache for economies around the world. With the situation in the Middle East still highly tense, crude prices continue to feel the pinch, with diesel facing a most uncertain path forward.
"Global diesel markets are under immense pressure. The Iran and the Ukraine wars have resulted in cutting the supply from refineries in the Gulf and Russia, making the US the crucial supplier of distilled petroleum products," analysts at UK bank Barclays said.
"This, in turn, has drained US domestic stockpiles ... given diesel's critical role in agriculture and the transportation supply chain, it will eventually add to consumer price pressures."
Felt everywhere
Diesel powers lorries, trains, buses, boats and vehicles in farming, construction and the military. Diesel-powered generators are also critical back-up power sources at factories, hospitals and large buildings, as well as in remote areas.
Diesel is derived from crude oil. But unlike the benchmarks Brent and West Texas Intermediate, diesel does not have a global exchange price. Instead, its cost varies greatly by region, influenced by supply and demand trends, logistical costs and local taxes.
Conflicts add to these factors. The effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, an ongoing flashpoint in the Iran war, attacks from Yemen's Houthi rebels on Saudi ships and infrastructure and the halt of exports from Russia amid its conflict with Ukraine are escalating supply concerns. The closure of the kingdom's East-West pipeline last week added to the pressure.
Supply disruptions, depleted inventories and increasingly high refining margins – the financial difference between the value of petroleum products sold by a refinery and the cost of raw crude used to produce them, which vary greatly depending on the components used – magnify a severe shortage of middle distillates, which is where diesel is classified.
Those factors have also caused diesel prices in the US and Europe to soar above $220 a barrel – about a 95 per cent leap from prewar levels, the International Energy Agency said. The price of diesel varies widely, with costs in oil-producing nations largely lower than in net energy importers.
Price increases vary in other areas but are still significant. In the Philippines, for instance, authorities are expected to announce a 9.50 peso ($0.15) increase in diesel prices, compared with a 5.50 peso increase for petrol, making filling up a vehicle to max capacity a substantial added cost.
US diesel is still cheap
Still, that places the South-East Asian nation in the bottom half of diesel prices globally at $1.363 per litre, according to data from industry tracker Global Petrol Prices as of this week. Twenty-four countries have prices below $1, including all Gulf countries, except the UAE, where it costs Dh4.30, or $1.17, up 13 per cent from August. Venezuela, Iran and Libya have the lowest cost at $0.004, $0.006 and $0.024, respectively.
At the other end of the spectrum, Hong Kong has the highest diesel price worldwide at $4.695 a litre – way ahead of second-placed Malawi, where it is $3.383. Sixteen out of the top 20 locations with the highest diesel prices are in Europe, including the UK, France, Germany and Italy.
The US, where the pain of higher diesel costs has already taken root – analysts warn of more if they remain elevated – is still in the middle of the pack with a per-litre equivalent of $1.66.
In China, where diesel costs $1.187 a litre, inventories of the fuel at state-owned suppliers fell to a 15-month low, prompting analysts to predict that Beijing may curb monthly exports to protect domestic supply – which would eliminate another key source of the commodity, especially for Asia.
But diesel has become "the bigger problem", said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Denmark's Saxo Bank. "The economic implications extend well beyond energy markets. Diesel is a critical input for road freight, agriculture, construction, mining and manufacturing, meaning sustained high prices eventually feed into transportation costs and consumer prices," he added.
Road ahead
The administration of US President Donald Trump has repeatedly said that high energy prices are a short-term pain, but the uncertainty over the Iran war's endgame casts a huge cloud over those promises.
The US Energy Information Administration this month raised its 2027 retail diesel price forecast by 8.2 per cent, referring to tight global distillate supplies and a domestic stash that continues to decline.
The Washington-based agency said in its short-term outlook that diesel would hit an average of $4.40 per gallon next year, which is a 33-cent jump from its previous prediction. For 2026, it updated its forecast by 4.4 per cent to $5.07 – before this week's spike.
"We forecast US distillate fuel oil inventories will drop below 100 million barrels in September and will remain below the five-year [2021–2025] low through much of 2027," the EIA said. "Tightness in the global distillate market has raised domestic prices and incentivised US exporters to increase distillate exports. We assume global production of distillate fuel will remain below last year’s levels in the coming months, contributing to low US diesel inventories and high diesel prices."
The International Energy Agency, meanwhile, said a partial offset for the diesel squeeze comes from other regions – amid disruptions in the Middle East and Russia – and inventories have so far played a "crucial role" in balancing the market.
"Gasoil and diesel exports from both the Middle East and Russia have been squeezed by the wars," said Ipek Ozkardeskaya, a senior analyst at Swissquote. "With no end in sight, supply constraints will become a growing headache, especially as global oil inventories and strategic reserves have been falling. In other words, the clock is ticking louder."

slots.packetSpot:
The sharp rise in diesel prices extends beyond the fuel market to household budgets, inflation concerns and debate over US export policy. Supply disruptions linked to the wars involving Iran and Russia-Ukraine, refinery attacks, disruption in the Red Sea and uncertainty around the Strait of Hormuz are cited among the factors behind price pressure.

In the United States, the national diesel average was put at about $6.51 per gallon in one report and at $6.31 as a weekly record in another. The Energy Information Administration raised its average price forecast for 2026 to $5.07 per gallon, while projecting that inventories will fall below 100 million barrels in September and remain below the five-year low for much of 2027. Assessments from Barclays, Saxo Bank and Swissquote indicate that high prices could put pressure on transport, agriculture, construction and consumer prices; MarketWatch also says persistently high prices could increase inflation risks.

The cost of heating oil, used as the primary heating source by about 5 million households in the northeastern United States during the 2023-24 winter, also risks rising alongside diesel. The National Energy Assistance Directors Association calculated that heating oil costs could rise by 31% this winter, with average household spending increasing from $1,749 to $2,297. Iowa Senator Chuck Grassley, citing the impact of high prices on farmers and truckers, called on President Donald Trump to impose an embargo on diesel exports.

After Houthi rebels damaged the route serving as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, experts expect prices to keep rising
Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter, is running out of alternatives to export its production, a fact that will raise oil prices even more after months of intense price escalation. The blockade of the Strait of Hormuz due to the war in Iran delivered the first blow, and now, more than six months after the war began, the East-West Pipeline connecting Saudi oil fields with its Red Sea ports — the best alternative route — is under threat following attacks by Yemen’s Houthis, who are allies of Iran.

items.titleTR: $150 for an oil barrel, the new extreme scenario following closure of key Saudi pipeline

items.descriptionTR:
Oil prices slid on Friday but remained above $100 for a second straight week, as tensions in the Middle East simmer.
Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, was down 0.95 per cent to settle at $103.87 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate, the gauge that tracks US crude, dropped 1.61 per cent to finish at $100.30 per barrel.
Both Brent and WTI were up by more than 2 per cent earlier in the day. From last week's close, Brent posted a decline of about 0.7 per cent drop, while WTI inched up 0.24 per cent.
Crude prices continued to fall as easing concerns over Saudi supply disruptions outweighed anxiety about a widening Middle East conflict, as fighting was renewed between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi rebels.
The decline comes after prices surged towards $110 a barrel on Monday after Saudi Arabia shut its East-West pipeline following attacks. That removed a crucial route for exporting crude and deepened fears of a global supply crunch.
On Thursday, Saudi Civil Defence officials said one person was killed and two were injured by debris from a Houthi drone that fell on Taif governorate, after it was intercepted and destroyed. It was the first death to be announced in the kingdom since the Iran-backed ‌Houthis resumed ⁠attacks on Saudi Arabia this month.
But the Houthis have been communicating with US officials to assure Washington that the group's seizure of the Red Sea coast overlooking the Bab Al Mandeb strait will not lead to attacks on American ships, sources in Sanaa told The National.
Equity disregard
Financial markets have largely ignored the volatility in energy prices because they have "already priced in quite a fair bit of that $100 per barrel of oil for now", said Hou Wey Fook, chief investment officer of Singapore-based DBS Bank.
For oil to make a material impact on financial markets, it needs to rise to $160 and "we don't think that is probable, [it is] not a high-probability scenario", he added.
Meanwhile, Tehran said it would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu are removed from power, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, political adviser to supreme leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, said in a statement on Thursday.
Oil has moved sharply in step to developments surrounding a potential resolution. But with no settlement in sight, prices have carried a significant geopolitical premium, said Nagham Hassan, a Middle East and North Africa market analyst at trading platform eToro.
“The outlook for oil over the next six months will depend heavily on the direction of the conflict,” she said. “Further escalation around the Strait of Hormuz or Bab Al Mandeb, as well as continued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, could increase the risk of a genuine supply shortage and keep prices well above $100 per barrel, particularly while reserves remain low. A durable de-escalation remains the clearest scenario that could bring prices down.”
Gold, meanwhile, rose on Friday for a second straight day to reach a one-week high. It came as investors continued to digest developments in the Middle East and oil kept moving down.
The precious metal, considered a safe-haven asset and a hedge against inflation, added 0.40 per cent to settle at $4,377.91 an ounce. Silver climbed 1 per cent to $66.25 per ounce.
