items.descriptionTR: North Korean state media remained silent early Monday morning on the country's latest missile launches. The Korean Central News Agency made no mention of Sunday's launch of two short-range ballistic missiles toward the East Sea, fired hours apart. North Korea has typically reported its missile tests the following day, though that pattern has grown inconsistent in recent months. Three missile launches last month were not reported at all, while a Sept. 12 launch, which came a day after South Korea
items.titleTR: N. Korea stays quiet on Sunday's missile launches

slots.packetSpot:
South Korea said that North Korea fired two short-range ballistic missiles toward the East Sea on Sunday. Seoul reported that the first missile was launched from Wonsan at around 3 p.m. and travelled 450 kilometres, while the second was fired at around 5:50 p.m. and flew more than 600 kilometres. It was reported that South Korea and the United States were conducting a joint analysis of the missiles; Seoul raised its security alert and shared information with the United States and Japan.

South Korea's presidential office held an emergency meeting following the development and called on Pyongyang to halt ballistic missile launches prohibited under United Nations Security Council resolutions. Japan's Ministry of Defense also announced that it had detected a suspected North Korean missile, but that the missile had not fallen into Japanese territorial waters.

North Korea's state media did not announce the launches as usual. The tests came two days after Pyongyang said it would strengthen its nuclear deterrence capability in response to what it described as U.S. hostility.

items.descriptionTR:
Colts WR Alec Pierce was taken to the locker room with a left heel injury. He is questionable to return
KANSAS CITY, Mo. — The Colts offense might have lost a critical piece of the passing attack.
Alec Pierce, the deep threat who signed a four-year, $114 million contract this offseason because of his ability to take the top off defenses, was carted off the field after suffering an apparent injury to his left heel.
The Colts declared Pierce out for the game shortly after taking him to the locker room.
Pierce has been listed with a heel injury on the team's injury report for the last two weeks, an injury that was apparently related to his recovery from offseason ankle surgery to repair a bone issue causing pain in his left ankle.
The Colts' deep threat has acknowledged that he was initially told the surgery would take roughly six months for a full recovery. Indianapolis general manager Chris Ballard initally said Pierce would be back on the field one to two weeks into training camp, but he did not return until two weeks before the start of the regular season.
Pierce played only 32 snaps in the season opener as he tried to manage the injury; he said the team's goal was to give him more snaps against Kansas City this week.
Pierce was running a route on the Colts’ third drive, planted with his left leg and drove off to the sideline, but as he got close to the sideline he pulled up and started hopping, his left leg in the air. The wide receiver was helped off by trainers, unable to put weight on the left leg.
Buy Colts tickets
Colts doctors immediately took Pierce to the blue tent that the team uses to diagnose injuries.
The examination was lengthy. Pierce spent the rest of the Indianapolis drive and the entire Kansas City offensive series in the tent, and when he emerged, he sat in the front seat of a cart and was driven off the field.
Losing Pierce for any amount of time would be a crippling blow to the Indianapolis offense.
Joel A. Erickson and Nathan Brown cover the Colts all season. Get more coverage on IndyStarTV and with the Colts Insider newsletter.

According to ESPN, X-ray results showed no negative findings; further evaluation on Monday is expected.

The player, who saw limited time in the season opener, had been expected to remain on the field more against Kansas City.

items.descriptionTR:
Can a country change continents? Canada seems set to try.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has announced an intention to seek some novel form of associate membership in the European Union. It’s no mere flight of fancy, either, as Ursula von der Leyen, president of the EU Commission, has already endorsed the idea.
It’s a proposal that manages to be both absurd and eminently logical, depending on how you frame it. Geographically, Canada remains firmly affixed to North America, sharing a border with its increasingly unpredictable neighbour to the south, the United States.
In other important ways, however, Canada clearly has much more in common in recent months with European countries than the unstable U.S. That’s because in the space of a year, America has gone from Canada’s most important friend and ally on the world stage to the clearest threat to Canadian sovereignty.
By deepening links with other European democracies, Carney clearly hopes to buy Canada a degree of insurance against continuing American intervention and hostility from U.S. President Donald Trump. There’s a logic to the argument.

Read more: Trump’s geopolitical aims, not economics, are behind his trade hostility towards Canada

Middle powers coming together
In fact, in many ways this proposal is very much in keeping with Canada’s multilateral approach to international politics since the Cold War era. This is a history Carney clearly invoked when he spoke about the need for middle powers to forge their own path together in his landmark speech to Davos earlier in the year.
Canada, then as now, is not a match for the greatest powers in the world. But working with other like-minded states, it can find ways to defend itself and amplify its power. The difference, of course, is that now the U.S. is no longer one of those allies but, instead, Canada’s biggest threat.
That threat cannot be underestimated, either. While observers like myself have been warning of the danger ever since Justin Trudeau’s ill-fated mission of supplication to Mar-A-Lago prompted Trump’s 51st state joke, the scale and severity of the problem has become impossible to ignore.

Read more: Canada’s fight with Trump isn’t just economic, it’s existential

The latest trade negotiations have made that clear. From ugly jokes and offensive maps, the Trump administration has proceeded to make more concrete demands of fealty.
Even before taking office, Trump was inventing border drug-trafficking problems for Canada to solve — a grievance the president continues to return to.
More recent trade negotiations included demands that amounted to the surrender of Canadian sovereignty. They included a veto over who Canada trades with internationally, an entrenched dependency on the U.S. for defence procurement and security provision and, incredibly, even an attempt to interfere with official Canadian bilingualism.

Read more: Caught between culture and commerce: Canada’s high-stakes trade clash with the United States

Looking for help elsewhere
Along the way, Canada has watched figures close to Trump pumping up the idea of Alberta’s secession and the U.S. ambassador treating Canadians with utter contempt. Worst of all, Canada has had precious little in the way of support even from Americans who are sympathetic.
The message is clear: Americans have been cowed by a bullying administration with no respect for Canada or Canadians. If Canada wishes to defend its sovereignty, it must look for help elsewhere. No country is more vulnerable than the one without allies.
That brings us back to a more European-allied Canada.
The European Union is the world’s foremost club of democracies and economic force in the world. When European states can co-operate politically — not always a given — they are a force to rival the other great powers of the world.
Canada also has long ties to Europe, not only cultural connections in the form of a shared heritage for many — though far from all — Canadians, but through diplomatic and defence collaboration in numerous international institutions. Those organizations include NATO, the United Nations, the G7, la Francophonie and many others.
As democracies that are facing shared vulnerabilities from increasingly assertive authoritarian regimes, Canada and EU member states have a mutual interest in protecting one another and collaborating to defend democratic values and institutions.
Potential risks, drawbacks
There are many unanswered questions about Canada becoming an associate member of the EU, and some real risks associated with the idea as well. European Union membership is not without its drawbacks, as Brexit clearly demonstrated just a decade ago.

Read more: The lesson Canada’s prime minister learned from Brexit is helping in its trade rift with US

The United Kingdom voted to leave the European Union, and while that was an economically problematic decision, it was not without its logical arguments in favour. EU membership remains controversial because pooling sovereignty requires sacrifice: nations trade away unilateral control in exchange for shared, broader gains.
This is not a minor point. The loss of control over decision-making is, in no small measure, what Canada is objecting to in trade negotiations with the U.S. While it’s far too early to know what goes into associate membership, Carney will need to be careful to ensure steps are taken to prevent Canadian populists from finding a new distant target in Brussels.
Harmonizing policy with European allies would also likely become a further barrier to trade with the U.S. While it’s clear Canada can no longer rely on a trusting relationship with its southern neighbour, the two countries will remained joined at the hip, and the U.S. will likely remain Canada’s biggest trading partner as a function not only of geography, but decades of investment and policy.
As much as Canada needs friends, it’s important for the country to proceed in a way that does not blow up its relationship with the U.S.
Asian trade
Finally, Canada must be careful not to lose sight of the fact that millions of Canadians trace their heritage to places far beyond Europe.
The Pacific Rim remains Canada’s largest source of trade outside the U.S., and the democracies of the region are in many ways caught in a situation more analogous to Canada’s own than the countries of the EU.
Japan, South Korea, Australia and Taiwan are, like Canada, caught between U.S. and Chinese influence and must find a way to walk that line. Accordingly, in its search for friends, Canada cannot be too narrow-minded or historically oriented. Europe is Canada’s past, but the Pacific Rim looms large in its future.
One thing is clear, however. Canada’s prime minister understands that the world has changed; the old normal is not coming back. Canada is in a fight for its existence and is acting accordingly.
￼
Stewart Prest does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
Canada has spent the last century defending European democracies. Now it’s asking them to return the favour.

The US president threatened to impose 'very heavy tariffs' on the EU if its offer to Canada was made with 'bad intentions'.  Donald Trump's comments came after the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said she wanted to open the door to Canada becoming the EU's first 'associate member', and the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, said Ottawa was seeking a 'unique alliance' with the bloc
	•	Trump calls EU offer to Canada of associate membership ‘laughable’, while threatening tariffs

items.titleTR: Trump calls EU's offer of associate membership to Canada 'laughable' – video

slots.packetSpot:
Canada’s search for a closer relationship with the European Union is taking shape amid escalating trade tensions with the United States. While Mark Carney said they wanted a “unique alliance” with the EU, Ursula von der Leyen expressed an intention to pave the way for Canada to become the first “associate member.”

The rapprochement on the agenda is being presented as a search for diversification that could extend to areas such as trade, energy, digital technology, raw materials and defence procurement. However, the existing ties between Canada and the EU rest on CETA; the United States retains a decisive position in Canada’s trade. For this reason, a complete break with Washington does not appear realistic.

Trump called the associate membership proposal “ridiculous” and said he could impose very heavy tariffs on the EU if it were made in bad faith. Associate membership or a broader alliance still stands only as a proposal and a subject for negotiation.
slots.packetTitle: Canada moves closer to Europe in Washington’s shadow

items.descriptionTR:
Anti-ICE protests break out in push for transparency as unnamed man is in serious but stable condition at hospital
A US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer shot and wounded a man on Sunday afternoon in Texas’s capital of Austin, local authorities said, and anti-ICE protesters quickly gathered at the scene.
The unnamed man was in serious but stable condition at a hospital after being shot once in the torso on the city’s north side, Austin’s police chief, Lisa Davis, said at a news conference with the mayor and other city officials.
items.titleTR: ICE agent shoots and wounds man at traffic stop in Austin, Texas, officials say

slots.packetSpot: Authorities said an ICE officer shot 28-year-old Venezuelan Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez during a traffic stop in Austin. Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said Pérez, who was shot once in the torso, was taken to hospital in serious but stable condition; he was later taken into custody. About 100 people gathered in the area after the incident, while Mayor Kirk Watson and House member Greg Casar called for transparency in the investigation. The Department of Homeland Security said it was conducting the investigation with FBI support; Watson, meanwhile, said Austin police should also be involved in the process.
slots.packetTitle: Austin's ICE flashpoint

He posted that his administration "will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows!"
In the rambling post, Trump said that data centers were "wealthy and prestigious" and claimed without evidence that they raised salaries, lowered taxes, and made for safer streets in the communities in which they were …
items.titleTR: Trump now says he wants to form an ‘AI Force’

slots.packetSpot:
President Donald Trump announced that he plans to establish an “Artificial Intelligence Force” to steer and oversee the development of AI in the United States, as well as appoint an AI czar. In a lengthy post on Truth Social, Trump described concerns over inadequate federal AI safeguards as a “hoax”; he wrote that he would not allow the technology to be “destroyed,” particularly as US-based industry leaders continue to compete with China.

Trump compared his proposed structure to the Space Force he established during his first presidential term; however, it remained unclear how the institution would operate or what duties it would undertake. He said only people with “high IQs” should apply for the new czar role. Venture capitalist David Sacks, who had previously served as Trump’s AI and cryptocurrency czar, left his post earlier this year.

AI researchers, technology company executives and world leaders are calling for safety measures as increasingly powerful systems are developed. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has called for a global slowdown, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Elon Musk of SpaceX, SpaceXAI and Tesla have joined that view. Trump, however, argues that new federal restrictions could jeopardize the United States’ global position in the AI race; his administration prioritizes accelerating the technology’s development while using guidelines for potential problems.
slots.packetTitle: A new force in the AI race

In his first major decision as Fed chair, Kevin Warsh raises interest rates by a quarter point and signals another increase before year-end
Kevin Warsh has been chair of the Federal Reserve for just four months, but this Wednesday will be remembered as the day he showed that he and his fellow governors, not outside forces, are the ones truly steering U.S. monetary policy. The Fed has done exactly what U.S. President Donald Trump did not want it to do under any circumstances: raise interest rates just six weeks before the midterm elections, in which Republicans risk losing control of Congress.

items.titleTR: The Federal Reserve defies Trump with a unanimous rate hike six weeks before the midterms

items.descriptionTR:

From mortgages to auto loans to credit cards, borrowing is set to get even pricier. But the Federal Reserve’s decision on September 16, 2026, to hike its baseline interest rate also highlighted an increasingly confounding dilemma: It can raise the price of money across the economy, but it can’t determine which sectors are most affected.

items.titleTR: Gold Steadies as Traders Weigh Inflation and Fed Path for Rates

slots.packetSpot:
The Federal Reserve’s unanimous quarter-point rate increase on September 16 lifted the target range to 3.75%–4%. The Fed, chaired by Kevin Warsh, said inflation remained elevated and that the decision would support a more timely return to the 2% annual target; it also pointed to strong economic activity, productivity, investment and domestic spending.

Donald Trump argued that rates should be at 1% or lower, criticized other members of the Fed’s Board of Governors and said he trusted Warsh to cut rates. By contrast, the named Republican senators argued that the Fed was acting within the framework of its mandate to keep inflation under control and its independence.

Warsh’s description of the increase as “withdrawing a dose of support” rather than tightening monetary policy intensified debate over the scope of further increases. Markets were pricing the probability of an increase in October at about 58%, up from 42% a week earlier; Goldman Sachs and Bank of America also highlighted expectations of an October increase. Futures indicated that the federal funds rate could reach 4.635% toward the end of 2027.

Uncertainty persists over the extent of the impact higher rates will have on mortgages, home equity lines of credit, auto loans, credit cards, small businesses and public borrowing. Analytical assessments suggest that areas such as the more interest-rate-sensitive housing market could face greater pressure, while artificial intelligence investment could be affected more modestly because of high expected returns. Gold also remained flat as investors weighed the risk of persistent inflation and the Fed’s rate path.
slots.packetTitle: The Fed in the shadow of higher rates

items.descriptionTR:
On the eve of the derby, Diego Simeone described this as a special week in Madrid, a “tremendous energy about the city”, and it closed the way he wanted. He had enjoyed the Formula One, he said, and he had enjoyed seeing Shakira in concert, but he enjoyed this even more. At least he did by the time the last of many, many blows on the referee’s whistle brought it to an end, sprinting up the tunnel punching the air. Having been 2-0 up against 10 men through goals from Álex Grimaldo and Jonathan David, seemingly in control, a late header from Antonio Rüdiger awoke old ghosts and brought tension, but they did it.
José Mourinho’s first derby back at Real Madrid ended in defeat and recriminations: he turned up in the press conference with a picture of two moments in which he claimed that Lee Kang-in and Cristian Romero should have been sent off and insisted the story was there. And yet there are other questions: over the way Dean Huijsen gave away the penalty and got the red card that tilted the game against them, and how his team played, how little they did.
items.titleTR: Jonathan David earns Atlético precious win over 10-man Real Madrid in fractious derby

slots.packetSpot:
Atlético Madrid beat 10-man Real Madrid 2-1 in the Madrid derby. Dean Huijsen was shown a red card following a VAR review after bringing down Giuliano Simeone in the penalty area, earning Atlético a penalty; Álex Grimaldo converted the opportunity, and Jonathan David doubled the lead. Antonio Rüdiger's late goal did not change the result.

José Mourinho argued that Atlético players should have been shown red cards in first-half incidents involving Cristian Romero and Jude Bellingham, and Lee Kang-in and Federico Valverde; he described the refereeing decisions as mistakes and arrived at the press conference with images of those moments. Diego Simeone, meanwhile, said his team controlled the game, its defensive structure and its collective effort; in public remarks, he called for respect to be maintained.

While the season's second defeat increased the pressure on Real Madrid, Atlético moved up to second place. Although the figures given for the points gap to Barcelona varied, the derby's weight in the title race and Mourinho's side's lack of attacking effectiveness stood out.

items.descriptionTR: PORT-AU-PRINCE, Sept 20 - A military plane whisked 18 suspects in the 2021 killing of Haitian President Jovenel Moise out of Haiti and flew them to the United States on Sunday, according to Jason Reding Quiñones, the US Attorney for the Southern District of Florida.
items.titleTR: Suspects in 2021 killing of Haitian president flown to US to face trial

slots.packetSpot:
Eighteen suspects detained in connection with the killing of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse in July 2021 were sent from Haiti to face federal court proceedings in the United States. Jason Reding Quiñones, the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida, described this as a new phase in the process of accountability, while Haiti’s Justice Ministry said it had handed over the suspects to ensure they were tried, and reported that proceedings in the country had faced difficulties.

The group is reported to include 17 Colombian soldiers and Joseph Badio, a former employee of Haiti’s Justice Ministry. While defence lawyers have alleged that Badio was the figure behind the plan, officials said some suspects had planned a coup rather than an assassination; the Colombian soldiers, meanwhile, said they had been beaten in Haiti, threatened with death and forced to sign documents in a language they did not understand.

Moïse was killed by 12 bullets at his private residence in Port-au-Prince; his wife was also injured in the attack. A total of 30 people are reported to have been charged in the case, with other defendants in the United States having been convicted or pleaded guilty; some suspects are reportedly still awaiting trial or remain at large. The process in Haiti was disrupted by gang violence, threats, judges’ resignations and a courthouse falling under gang control.
slots.packetTitle: A new phase in the Moïse case

items.descriptionTR:
The Green Bay Packers struggled throughout the course of their Week 2 matchup against the New York Jets. Winning on the road is never easy, but the team struggled in nearly every aspect for the majority of the game. Despite trailing by 10 points in the fourth quarter, the Packers were able to come back […] The post Tucker Kraft Sends Strong Message to Green Bay Packers After Jets Win appeared first on Gridiron Heroics.
The Green Bay Packers struggled throughout the course of their Week 2 matchup against the New York Jets. Winning on the road is never easy, but the team struggled in nearly every aspect for the majority of the game.
Despite trailing by 10 points in the fourth quarter, the Packers were able to come back to win. When the final whistle was blown, Green Bay led on the scoreboard 20-17.
Trey Smack, the rookie kicker, nailed a game-winning field goal to help the Packers move to 1-1 on the young season.
Following the win, Green Bay star tight end Tucker Kraft spoke out with a strong message to himself and his teammates.
￼
Kyle Terada-USA TODAY Sports
Green Bay Packers Tight End Tucker Kraft Sends Strong Message
Even though the Packers were able to win the game, Kraft made it clear that the team has a lot of work to do.
“We can’t let a win mask our problems. We have to get back to the chalk board, and we have to be aggressive,” Kraft said. “We have to look in the mirror and set a standard for ourselves as a team and each individual.”
At the end of the day, Green Bay has a lot of reasons to be concerned despite the win. For one, the Packers were penalized 14 times for 133 yards. That cannot continue happening if they want to be a legitimate Super Bowl contender.
Once again, the offensive line struggled to keep Jordan Love upright. The line also saw star tackle Zach Bako-Bewele go down with what Green Bay believes could be a season-ending injury. Matt LaFleur and company have to figure out how to give Love more time.
Defensively, the Packers played well. There is a lot of positive to take away from the win on the defensive side of the football.
All of that being said, Kraft’s message is excellent leadership. Even though it was ugly, a win is a win for Green Bay. But, if the Packers want to make their goal of being a Super Bowl contender come true, there’s a lot of work left to be done.

The Packers, meanwhile, won after coming back from 10 points down in the fourth quarter. Violence flared in the occupied West Bank on Sunday after a suspected Palestinian gunman shot dead an Israeli man, police said, while Israeli soldiers killed a Palestinian motorist who the military said had attempted to run them over.
The gunman opened fire from a vehicle at Israelis gathered at a spring near the settlement of Neve Tzuf, near Ramallah, according to the Israeli military and police.
Medics who arrived at the scene found a man in a car suffering from critical gunshot wounds. He was pronounced dead at a hospital, police said. The gunman was located several hours later at a hospital in Ramallah and arrested, police said.
Shortly after the shooting, the military said its forces had “eliminated” a Palestinian driver who had attempted a ramming attack on soldiers near the settlement of Ganim, further north in the West Bank. No soldiers were hurt, it said. It is not known if the two incidents, which occurred on the eve of the Jewish holy day of Yom Kippur, are connected.
Following the incidents, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had instructed security agencies to increase their presence and carry out arrests and offensive operations in the area. The Palestinian militant group Hamas praised the shooting but did not claim responsibility for it.
Violence has escalated in the West Bank since Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel and the ensuing Israeli military offensive in Gaza. The violence has included a sharp rise in attacks by militant settlers on Palestinians, as well as sweeping Israeli military raids and Palestinian attacks on Israelis.
items.titleTR: Israeli man shot dead in West Bank and Palestinian driver killed by soldiers

slots.packetSpot:
On the eve of Yom Kippur, an Israeli man and a Palestinian driver were killed in two separate incidents in the occupied West Bank. Israeli authorities reported that Israelis gathered by a spring near Neve Tzuf, close to Ramallah, came under fire from a vehicle, and that a seriously wounded man died in hospital. Police said the suspected Palestinian gunman was later found and detained at a hospital in Ramallah.

Near Ganim in the north, meanwhile, the Israeli army announced that a Palestinian driver whom it said had tried to run over soldiers was killed by the soldiers; no soldiers were injured. It remains unclear whether the two fatal incidents were connected.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had instructed that security forces be reinforced in the area and that detentions and offensive operations be carried out. Hamas praised the shooting but did not claim responsibility. Violence has been escalating in the West Bank since 7 October 2023, with settler attacks on Palestinians, large-scale Israeli army raids and Palestinian attacks on Israelis.

•	World No 294 lets victory slip in agonising fashion
	•	JJ Spaun triumphs by two shots at Wentworth
We will come to JJ Spaun and Jeremy Clarkson later. Only those without an ounce of compassion in their body could feel no sympathy for Manuel Elvira. The Spaniard, without a professional win to his name, stood on the 18th fairway at Wentworth’s West Course with one of golf’s most extraordinary stories in his grasp. Having just eagled the 71st hole and found the short grass on the friendly par five, the 30-year-old who began tournament week as the world’s 294th ranked player knew a birdie would seal the PGA Championship title. A par would force Spaun into a playoff.
What happened next was a form of sporting torture rather than the realisation of a fairytale. Elvira pulled his layup into a bunker, flew the green, fluffed a chip into another sand trap and missed a bogey putt from 4ft. He did exceptionally well not to burst into tears. The disastrous 18th meant Elvira finished in a four-way tie for second place. Even Spaun, a winner on his Wentworth debut, had to be bashful at the manner of success.
items.titleTR: Elvira’s fairytale crumbles at the last to hand Spaun PGA Championship title

slots.packetSpot:
American JJ Spaun won the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth at 17 under. Spain’s Manuel Elvira, meanwhile, finished the final hole of his bid for a first victory with a double bogey to remain at 15 under; Rory McIlroy, Adam Scott and Aaron Rai also finished on the same score.

The 2025 U.S. Open champion Spaun became the third American to win the BMW PGA Championship; Billy Horschel and Arnold Palmer had previously achieved the title. Spaun said not being selected for the U.S. Presidents Cup team gave him something he wanted to prove this week.
slots.packetTitle: The final hole turns at Wentworth

items.descriptionTR:
￼
Yemen's Houthi armed forces patrol the capital Sanaa on Sept. 12, 2026. Mohammed Huwaish/AFP via Getty Images
It took just a few days for Houthi forces to seize most of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, including the shores of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial Red Sea maritime choke point.
The offensive started on Sept. 3, 2026, with a push to cut the strategically important road linking the city of Taiz to the port of Mokha. By Sept. 11, Mokha, the town of Dhubab and the island of Mayyun, in the mouth of the strait, were under Houthi control.
The Yemeni rebel group seized some 2,100 square miles of territory, forcing more than 100,000 people to flee, according to the U.N., with many making the risky journey to nearby Djibouti by boats.
It is the largest shift in the front lines of Yemen’s civil war since a U.N.-brokered truce froze them in April 2022.
Most of the coverage has interpreted the offensive as a new lever for Iran – a key ally of the Houthis – in its ongoing war with the United States, or a fresh threat to Saudi Arabia and global shipping.
Such framing is not wrong, but it is incomplete. The more consequential question, I believe, is what the offensive means for Yemen itself, and where it leaves both a civil war that had quietly stalemated for years and the Houthis’ own unresolved problem of legitimacy.
Why advance now?
Years of Yemeni civil strife entered a new phase in 2014 when Houthis seized the capital Sanaa from the increasingly unpopular government of President Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi.
A decade of subsequent fighting between the rebel group and a Saudi-led coalition brought famine and destruction across the impoverished nation. But since 2022 the conflict has largely been stalled, with Houthis controlling much of the country’s northwest and the Saudi-backed forces remaining dominant in parts of the country’s south and east.

So why have the Houthis advanced now? The group’s military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said it was triggered by years of Saudi aggression and blockade.
Such grievances are not invented. U.N. agencies have documented real, sustained damage from coalition restrictions on Yemen’s ports and airspace over the course of the civil war.
The Houthis also trace the latest round of fighting to a July 13 strike on the Sanaa airport’s runway by Yemeni government forces with Saudi backing. That attack forced an Iranian aircraft carrying officers of Iran’s powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to turn back.
The Houthis declared their ceasefire with Saudi Arabia over that day, struck the airport of the Saudi city of Abha within hours and announced a naval blockade a week later. They then opened a missile campaign in early August, well before the ground offensive on Sept. 3.
But it is hard to read the Houthis’ sustained campaign and the landings on Bab el-Mandeb’s islands as simple payback for an airport strike. Rather, something more deliberate appears to have been in motion.
Another factor is Iran. Since Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz in March following the U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran, Saudi Arabia has routed crude oil through Bab el-Mandeb at roughly eight times the rate it did a year earlier.
Houthi control of that strait hands Iran a mirror-image choke point to the one it has over Hormuz. Indeed, Yemeni security sources say a senior Iranian commander, Abdul Reza Shahlai, was on the ground overseeing part of the latest operation in September.
There’s also a potential economic incentive for the Houthis. Since March, Tehran has been charging vessels up to US$2 million a ship for safe passage through Hormuz. The Houthis may likewise see economic leverage as a way to bolster a movement long battered by war.
Forcing Riyadh back to that table
Perhaps the most important factor, however, is that the Houthis reasoned conditions on the ground were increasingly favorable for an offensive. Their already fractured opposition has become even more divided in the country’s south, particularly after a Saudi rift with the United Arab Emirates in late 2025 led the latter to withdraw its support for anti-Houthi forces in the south altogether.
With the broader region engulfed in conflict and Saudi Arabia distracted, the Houthis made their move against a coastal Yemeni force that has been left exposed.
First and foremost, the Houthis are a Yemeni movement whose fight has always been about power inside Yemen. As such, Houthi officials have been careful to frame the Bab el-Mandeb operation as a national, sovereign act rather than one done for its Iranian ally; they are adamant that they are not a mere Iranian proxy.
As recently as 2023, Saudi Arabia and the Houthis had been negotiating a comprehensive nationwide ceasefire that would have, in part, ended Saudi restrictions and sanctions on Houthi governance. But the plan was never implemented following the Red Sea crisis of late 2023 and 2024, when the Houthis ramped up attacks on commercial shipping in response to the Israeli war in Gaza. Riyadh has shown little urgency to revive the diplomatic process since.
The Houthis may now be betting that escalating inside Yemen, where the cost to Saudi Arabia is high, is the surest way to force Riyadh back to that table. This time, they may believe they have leverage to receive the political recognition they have wanted all along, not just the economic terms Saudi Arabia was considering in 2023.
￼
A Houthi-provided image of vans carrying military supplies from Saudi Arabia on Sept. 7, 2026, in Hadramaut province, Yemen. Houthi Media Center via Getty Images
What the Strait operation cannot buy
The seizure of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the ongoing fighting in the country come with serious risks for the Houthis, however. The leverage the Houthis are gaining vis-a-vis Saudi Arabia and on the battlefield in Yemen could come at the cost of their broader standing in Yemen.
No government or entity has ever managed to hold both military and political supremacy over the entire territory of Yemen in modern history. While the Houthis have achieved military supremacy in the vast majority of the northwest, they have never pursued anything resembling a political bargain with the internationally backed government or even other parties. Their movement has always prized military dominance over political inclusion.
The latest coastal offensive is no exception.
According to Houthi-affiliated news sources, within days of taking Mokha the group had moved to reopen the port’s customs house, cut port fees and customs duties by as much as half and launched a drive to hand out 20,000 food baskets across Mokha and the neighboring coastal districts, while its authority in Sanaa offered a general amnesty to the fighters who had held the coast against it. A week later, its leader, Abdulmalik al-Houthi, told southerners directly that his forces were not targeting them, only the troops Saudi Arabia had brought in.
That is legitimacy performed through governance after a military conquest, more public relations than policy. It certainly isn’t the political bargain that could hold Yemen together for long. Moreover, a decade of Houthi rule in Sanaa suggests that they have no desire to work with others. Their modus operandi has been to rule by guns, not coalition.
More broadly, seizing the Arabian Peninsula’s other choke point and banning Saudi shipping through it makes the Houthis look, to much of the world and no small part of Yemen, like Tehran’s instrument – whatever their own objectives actually are.
And it invites the Houthis’ enemies to respond with force, potentially weakening the group’s capabilities.
Saudi Arabia is not a neutral party waiting patiently for good sense to prevail. It has prosecuted the war in Yemen for over a decade at enormous cost to the country’s civilians. Few in Yemen expect the Saudi-backed government to try retaking Sanaa by force, and a negotiated settlement will most likely be necessary eventually. But the Houthis have certainly now exposed themselves – and any Yemeni civilians caught up in escalation – to relentless airstrikes by Saudi Arabia and its allies.
For the Houthis, the gamble to advance now may backfire. It is one thing to take territory and quite another thing to hold it. Moreover, the Houthis may now find themselves controlling a strait the world wants reopened while still lacking the one thing that strait was never going to buy them: a whole country that actually consents to their rule.
￼
Mahad D. Darar does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
Seizure of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait complicates a widening conflict in the Persian Gulf. It also risks reigniting Yemen’s civil war.
items.titleTR: Houthi advance boosts Iran’s leverage over the US and Saudi Arabia – but may cost rebel group its legitimacy back in Yemen

items.descriptionTR:
An escalation of attacks on Saudi Arabia by the Houthi rebels in Yemen, and the group’s seizure of Yemen’s western coast, comes at a critical time in the region.
The rapid advance in a matter of days has given the group unprecedented access to the Bab Al Mandeb strait, a global maritime chokepoint, while displacing at least 125,000 civilians.
Meanwhile, the Strait of Hormuz, another critical route for international energy supplies, remains effectively closed because of the war between the US and Iran.
The violence in the two waterways has disrupted the flow of oil, goods and aid.
The fighting only intensified over the past week as the Iran-backed group attacked Saudi targets, including the holy city of Makkah, while the East-West pipeline was struck from Iraq.
In Yemen, pro-government forces have suffered major losses.
In this episode of Beyond the Headlines, host Nada AlTaher looks into how the Houthis' capacity to fight has grown enough for them to make such sweeping gains so quickly and whether the confrontation will escalate further before it dies down.
She speaks to Baraa Shiban, political analyst on Yemen at the Royal United Services Institute, and to Gulf expert Cinzia Bianco, visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations.
items.titleTR: How did the Houthis become so emboldened?

Rout raises questions about coordination and morale as some politicians claim billions of dollars were offered to persuade forces to abandon position
A bitter inquest is under way among Yemen’s anti-Houthi forces as to how what was being billed as a decisive assault on Sana’a, the Houthi-controlled capital, suddenly collapsed into a military rout.
More than 15 brigades were defeated as the country’s entire west coast fell into Houthi hands. Efforts are now being made to reorganise the anti-Houthi forces representing the UN-recognised Yemeni government in order to capture the Kahbob mountains, a strategic point from which to restrict Houthi forces moving closer to the crucial Bab al-Mandab strait.
items.titleTR: Yemen’s anti-Houthi forces launch inquest into sudden military collapse

slots.packetSpot:
The Houthi operation that began on 3 September rapidly changed the front along Yemen’s Red Sea coast. The Houthis are reported to have seized a broad stretch of coastline including Mokha, Dhubab and Mayyun near Bab al-Mandab, gaining around 2,100 square miles of territory. While the United Nations says more than 100,000 people have been displaced, another assessment puts the figure at at least 125,000. This development is described as the biggest change in the front lines since the UN-brokered truce of April 2022.

Access to Bab al-Mandab has tied Yemen’s balance of power more directly to maritime shipping and regional tensions. Houthi attacks are reported to have struck targets in Saudi Arabia, including Makkah, while the Strait of Hormuz is said to have remained effectively closed because of the US-Iran war. Violence in these two waterways is said to be disrupting flows of oil, goods and aid.

The retreat on the western coast by anti-Houthi forces representing Yemen’s UN-recognised government is also being assessed as a heavy defeat. More than 15 brigades are alleged to have been defeated, with up to 30,000 well-equipped fighters withdrawing. The National Resistance Forces said it had lost 500 soldiers before withdrawing to avoid encirclement. Coordination and morale problems, internal divisions, Houthi intelligence and military capabilities, and the claim that billions of dollars were offered in exchange for abandoning positions are among the leading explanations for this collapse.

Iran’s support for and influence over the Houthis remain at the centre of the debate. Yemeni security sources say Abdul Reza Shahlai, a senior commander in Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, directed part of the September operation on the ground. The Houthis, however, present the Bab al-Mandab operation not as one undertaken on Iran’s behalf but as a national and sovereign step, while Iranian officials argue that the group is not a simple proxy force. Whether the military gains on the coast will prove lasting and whether they will turn into a broader political settlement in Yemen remain uncertain.
slots.packetTitle: Yemen's war reaches the strait

items.descriptionTR: Iranian authorities on Sunday shut down the French Language Centre (CLF) in Tehran, alleging the French embassy-linked institute conducted "illegal acts that violated diplomatic conventions" and "abused its status as a language training facility". France has vowed to take "appropriate measures" in response.
items.titleTR: Iran closes French language centre in Tehran for ‘illegal acts’

items.descriptionTR: Iran accuses the French language centre of conducting 'illegal acts that violated diplomatic conventions'.
items.titleTR: France to summon Iran envoy after language centre closure in Tehran

slots.packetSpot:
Iranian authorities announced on September 20 that the French Language Centre (CLF), linked to the French Embassy in Tehran, had been closed. Iran’s judiciary alleged that the centre had engaged in illegal activities violating diplomatic norms, abused its status as a language education institution, failed to obtain the required licence despite warnings, and sought to facilitate the departure of qualified individuals from the country by building networks among Iran’s elites.

France’s Foreign Ministry described the closure as an unacceptable attack on France’s cultural presence in Iran. Paris announced that it would take appropriate measures and summon Iran’s ambassador at the request of Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot.

The closure became a new point of friction in already tense relations between the two countries. Diplomats report that disputes over allegations of attacks on embassy staff, reciprocal measures concerning diplomats, Iran’s nuclear programme, French nationals in detention, and French statements concerning Iran have strained relations in recent times. Jean-Noël Barrot and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi were expected to meet at the UN on September 22.

items.descriptionTR:
A new US law targeting major buyers of Russian oil could squeeze an increasingly important source of crude for India and China as Gulf supply disruption tightens the global market.
President Donald Trump on Friday signed into law the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, giving him authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 per cent on any of the five largest buyers of Russian crude or gas that “knowingly” book a new cargo. The House passed the legislation 262-159 on Wednesday after the Senate cleared it last month.
The tariffs could take effect 30 days after enactment.
The threat itself could prompt buyers to move faster. “Paradoxically, it could incentivise more purchases from Russia to get ahead of any future risks,” said Rachel Ziemba of Ziemba Insights. “Risks front-loading, buying more now.”
That could further entrench Russia’s role as a key alternative to Gulf supply for Asian buyers. “Russian crude has effectively become an important supply line and an important hedge against Middle Eastern supply disruption,” said Sumit Ritolia, lead analyst at Kpler. “Replacing Russian crude at current volumes would be challenging or impossible.”
If you keep buying cheap Russian oil to allow this war to continue, we're going to tear the hell out of you, and we're going to crush your economy, because what you're doing is blood money
Lindsey Graham, late Republican Senator from South Carolina
'Blood money'
Mr Graham, who died in July, spent more than a year arguing for that leverage in increasingly forceful terms. “If you keep buying cheap Russian oil to allow this war to continue, we're going to tear the hell out of you, and we're going to crush your economy, because what you're doing is blood money,” he said in a Fox News interview in July 2025, naming China, India and Brazil.
As Mr Trump’s additional 25 per cent duty on Indian goods took effect that August, Mr Graham wrote: “India is experiencing the cost of supporting [Russian President Vladimir] Putin.” His original bill carried a 500 per cent rate and remained stalled for 15 months.
Impact on India
Kpler data shows Russia's total exports were 6.79 million barrels per day in August, down from a peak of 8 million bpd in May. Russian crude accounted for 18.7 per cent of India’s imports in February, on par with Saudi Arabia and Iraq. By July, its share had reached nearly 50 per cent, or 2.96 million bpd, as India’s Middle East imports fell 63 per cent to 1.26 million bpd.
The US bought $58.9 billion of Indian goods in the first seven months of this year and sold India $30.4 billion worth, US Census Bureau data shows, leaving a $28.4 billion deficit. That was less than a third of the $91.2 billion gap with China over the same period.
A tariff aimed at Russian oil could also hit Indian exports with little connection to the trade it is trying to punish. Electrical machinery, including smartphones and electronic components assembled for American brands such as Apple, was India’s largest export category to the US in the first half of 2026.
China’s Russian crude imports have fallen 15 per cent since February to 1.89 million bpd, but their share of the country’s imports has risen to 22 per cent from 16 per cent as Gulf supplies declined. China also receives about 800,000 bpd of Russian crude by pipeline, under long-term contracts that would not be affected by tariffs on seaborne shipments.
The broader oil market is already tight, with Brent above $100 for seven straight sessions. The 10-day average for traffic through the Strait of Hormuz was 14 crossings on Friday, compared with nearly 100 before the war, while Saudi Arabia’s East West Pipeline was damaged in a drone strike last week and its alternative route through Bab Al Mandeb strait remains restricted by Houthi attacks.
New Delhi’s response on September 17 was firmer than its answers to Mr Graham’s earlier threats. The Ministry of External Affairs said India “remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people” and would take “all necessary measures to protect its trade and economic interests”.
Washington’s position has been more ambiguous. At the start of the Iran war, the administration briefly allowed India to lift Iranian crude for the first time in seven years to help keep oil flowing and prices down.
“The White House is likely to be cautious about imposing tariffs in the near term because doing so would tighten supplies further, push oil prices higher and place additional pressure on the global economy,” said Neil Quilliam, associate fellow at Chatham House.
“The high price at the pump in the US has already hit Trump’s popularity rating.”
China trade-off
China could also escape immediate tariffs. Bloomberg reported this week that planned duties will be held back until Mr Trump meets President Xi Jinping. Even tariffs of 20 per cent to 30 per cent “would end the truce, risk critical mineral shortages and additional export controls”, Ms Ziemba said.
Refiners are likely to seek ways around the measure rather than simply stop buying Russian crude. “China and India are the key pressure points as refiners will seek exemptions, reduce spot purchases and demand wider Russian discounts rather than stop buying altogether,” said Janiv Shah, vice president for oil at Rystad Energy.
The US tariffs could be “mildly bullish for oil prices as available volume theoretically tightens”.
items.titleTR: Trump tariff law targets Asian buyers of Russian oil as Gulf supply falls

slots.packetSpot:
The Lindsey O Graham Russia and Iran Sanctions Act, signed by Donald Trump on September 18, authorizes tariffs of up to 100% on any of the five largest buyers that knowingly make new cargo bookings for Russian oil or gas. The law is said to be intended to pressure Russia over the war in Ukraine; the tariffs may be imposed 30 days after it takes effect.

The measure, passed by the House of Representatives by 262 votes to 159 following Senate approval, is seen as a tool that could particularly target India and China. India’s dependence on Russian crude rose to nearly half of its imports in July, while China’s crude oil imports from Russia stand at 1.89 million barrels per day. China also receives around 800,000 barrels per day of Russian crude by pipeline under long-term contracts.

Declining Gulf supply and a tightening oil market make the use of this authority more complicated. Rachel Ziemba says the threat of tariffs could encourage buyers to make earlier and larger purchases from Russia as a precaution, while Sumit Ritolia states that replacing Russian crude at current volumes could be difficult or impossible. Neil Quilliam believes the White House may act cautiously in the near term because it could tighten supply further and raise prices. Janiv Shah assesses that, rather than halt purchases entirely, refiners may seek exemptions, reduce spot purchases and demand deeper Russian discounts.

India said it is determined to ensure the energy security of its 1.4 billion people and will take all necessary steps to protect its commercial and economic interests. According to Bloomberg, the planned tariffs on China may be postponed until Trump meets Xi Jinping.

President Trump was asked in the Oval Office whether it was appropriate that his son accepted the gift from Umar…
items.titleTR: Trump says son paid back Russian oligarch for wedding gift

items.descriptionTR:
The businessman, who accompanied Vladimir Putin on his recent trip to China, controls the country’s betting payment system and heads the opaque International Boxing Association, suspended by the IOC
The U.S. nonprofit journalism organization ProPublica has revealed that Umar Kremlev, a 43-year-old Russian businessman with close ties to the Kremlin, paid hundreds of thousands of dollars for Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding celebrations last May, and that another contractor for Russia’s Defense Ministry, Alexander Lagutin, was also invited to the event. Only one photo taken by a guest fleetingly shows Kremlev’s presence at the event, just days after both men accompanied Vladimir Putin on a trip to China.
Seguir leyendo
items.titleTR: Who is Umar Kremlev, the Russian magnate who paid for Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding festivities?

slots.packetSpot:
According to ProPublica, Russian businessman Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on part of the post-wedding celebrations in the Bahamas for Donald Trump Jr. and Bettina Trump. This included the rental of a private island, a fireworks display and other expenses. Bettina Trump described Kremlev as a friend and said he hosted the two-night celebrations; she stressed that the money did not finance the private wedding ceremony attended only by family members.

President Donald Trump said he understood that his son had paid Kremlev, but did not share details about it. The arrangement drew criticism from Senators John Curtis and Thom Tillis, while Senate Majority Leader John Thune said he needed more information.

Kremlev is a Russian businessman reported to have close ties to the Kremlin and serves as president of the International Boxing Association. Alexander Lagutin, who is said to work for Russia's Ministry of Defense, was also reportedly invited to the celebration; the two were reported to have accompanied Vladimir Putin on his trip to China shortly before the event.

items.descriptionTR:
Warren Buffett has stepped down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway and been named chairman emeritus with immediate effect, ending his more than six-decade tenure in the company’s top leadership role.
Mr Buffett, 96, is to remain on Berkshire’s board as a director and will continue to provide his “judgment and perspective”, the US company said on Friday.
His son, Howard, a Berkshire director since 1993, has been elected chairman of the board.
“Serving as your chairman has been the privilege of a lifetime, and I have never taken your trust for granted,” Mr Buffett said in a letter to shareholders. "Father Time always wins. He has, however, been generous with me. He has given me the opportunity to see Berkshire reach a point where I am more confident than ever about what lies ahead."
Greg Abel, who succeeded Mr Buffett as chief executive this year, will continue to run Berkshire’s operations, Berkshire said in a statement.
Mr Buffett joined Berkshire in 1965 and transformed the company from a struggling textile manufacturer into one of the world’s largest conglomerates, with businesses spanning insurance, energy, rail, manufacturing, services and retail.
In the letter to shareholders, Mr Buffett said the time was right to complete the leadership transition and praised Mr Abel for exceeding his expectations since taking over as chief executive.
“My son, Howard, will succeed me as chairman,” Mr Buffett said. “Greg runs the company; Howard will guard its culture and values – both worth more than anything on our balance sheet. Think of Howard as a policy the shareholders own and hope never to claim against.”
Howard Buffett has led the Howard G Buffett Foundation since 1999. Warren Buffett said he remained confident about Berkshire’s future and said the company was “in excellent hands”.
items.titleTR: Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire Hathaway chairman after six decades

Buffett will remain on the board as honorary chair; under the company’s succession plan, his son Howard Buffett will assume the role of board chair. Executive management is in the hands of Greg Abel, who became chief executive at the end of 2025. items.descriptionTR: Martin O'Neill says he will use the international break to reflect on his position after Celtic suffer three consecutive defeats in big games.
items.titleTR: 'It might be time to wrap it up' - O'Neill ponders Celtic future after defeat

items.descriptionTR:
If ever a stadium can be rocked by silence, this was the moment. With no visiting fans allowed at any of this season’s Glasgow derbies, Ryan Naderi’s winning goal was met with nothing but the banging of fists of the clear plastic of the Rangers bench, and the shouting of the broadcast commentators. A screaming void of apathy and atrophy, the sound of a beckoning abyss, of a title race blowing open and a team slowly breaking apart.
That Rangers were unable to celebrate this triumph with their fans in the stadium was, of course, a source of lament, as well as a measure of just how ugly this fixture has become over the years.
items.titleTR: Rangers and Ryan Naderi finish off Celtic’s horror week with Old Firm victory

slots.packetSpot:
Rangers’ Old Firm victory at Parkhead, secured by Ryan Naderi’s goal, handed Celtic their second derby defeat in a week. Alongside their home European defeat to Ferencvaros, Celtic have lost three matches in a row, though they remain top of the Premiership.

The 74-year-old Martin O’Neill said he would use the international break to consider whether he can still help the team and whether it is right for him to continue in the role. O’Neill, who said he would also speak with the board, has yet to have a decision made on his future.

Rangers, under Derek McInnes, stand out as a team recovering after a difficult spell at the start of the season. The result has also made the title race more open.
slots.packetTitle: Rangers win deepens Celtic doubts

items.descriptionTR:
Perhaps it is testament to the progress Leeds have made since returning to the Premier League just over a year ago that there was frustration at failing to move up to third after drawing with Crystal Palace. Instead, Daniel Farke’s team enter the prolonged international break in fifth and unbeaten, which is a fine achievement in itself.
Apart from Tyrick Mitchell’s disallowed goal, neither side gave much impression they would secure the points. For Palace, it was a first clean sheet of the season, having conceded at least twice in their opening four games, relieving pressure on Pierre Sage, while the hosts endured their first blank.
items.titleTR: ‘Mixed emotions’ for Farke as Leeds stay unbeaten with Crystal Palace stalemate

slots.packetSpot:
The goalless draw at Elland Road extended Leeds United's unbeaten start in the Premier League. According to the match report, Crystal Palace earned a point by keeping a clean sheet after conceding 11 goals in their first four league matches.

While Palace were reported to have looked more threatening in the second half, Tyrick Mitchell's goal was disallowed for offside. Daniel Farke said his team were not at their best in attack, but that extending the unbeaten run and not conceding were important; Pierre Sage stated that they wanted to build on the improvement in defence.

The draw was reported to have moved Palace one point above the relegation zone.
slots.packetTitle: A balance neither side could break at Elland Road

items.descriptionTR:
Germany's Carsten Breuer and Canada's Jennie Carignan are battling it out to become to next chair of NATO's military committee.
BRUSSELS — NATO’s most senior commanders elect a new leader on Saturday in a consequential vote that will help shape how the alliance prepares for a potential Russian incursion and navigates persisting transatlantic tensions.
The alliance’s 32 chiefs of defense staff will elect a new chair of NATO’s most senior military body, the military committee, in Copenhagen in a hush-hush ballot — and choose between two candidates: Germany’s Gen. Carsten Breuer and Canada’s Gen. Jennie Carignan.
“NATO is in a very decisive moment and in a demanding spot — there’s a large conventional war raging in Europe and NATO is transforming itself again into a more robust, more European NATO,” said Janne Kuusela, Permanent Secretary at the Finnish defense ministry. “That of course means … we need the best possible individuals to fill these positions.”
Although little-known, NATO’s military committee is the alliance’s most senior military authority, with the chair expected to give honest military advice to allies — helping assess the feasibility, financing and capabilities of operations. They oversee dozens of working groups of NATO military staff, and broker consensus on formulating military advice.
The position is a “highly complex role,” said Eleonora Russell, the spokesperson of former chair Adm. Rob Bauer, because it requires simultaneously gaining the trust of both the military and the political leadership across the alliance — and not taking sides. 
Such a role is particularly challenging today given enduring transatlantic tensions, she said, and important as sensitive talks on NATO’s next four-year war planning cycle will kick off in October. “The trick is you have to be … an extremely good listener,” Russell said, “but then you have to also have a very strong backbone.”
Germany’s Breuer, who Berlin announced as a candidate in February, is seen as the front-runner, according to one NATO diplomat and two European national security officials, who were granted anonymity to speak freely about the sensitive matter.
Berlin is now Europe’s leading defense spender, the officials said, and the U.S. has previously nudged Germany toward leadership roles in the alliance as it seeks to reduce its military engagement on the continent. Strained bilateral ties between Ottawa and Washington might also make Carignan’s case more difficult, the officials said.
That support was on display in Washington on Jul. 23, when Breuer briefed Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby on Germany’s new military strategy. Colby later called the strategy “historic” and “highly laudable” and said Germany was positioning itself as “a key leader of Europe’s conventional defense” in a post on X.
“Both candidates are exceptional military leaders,” said another military official, who nonetheless wondered whether it was more important today to have a European in charge given the alliance’s push for the continent to take charge of its own defense, dubbed NATO 3.0.
Breuer’s pitch for the job has included its leadership role on NATO 3.0, the officials said, as well as the four-star general’s strong existing relationships with his counterparts since he took over as Germany’s chief of defense in 2023.
Carignan, Ottawa’s top general since 2024, has focused her campaign on reinvigorating the role of the military committee, the officials said, and signaling enduring transatlantic unity inside NATO. That comes as the alliance has repeatedly been rocked by feuds with U.S. President Donald Trump since he retook office last year.
Germany’s defense ministry didn’t respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for Canada’s defense ministry said Carignan’s “candidacy reflects Canada’s enduring commitment to NATO and to strengthening collective defence and transatlantic security.”
Out of sight, out of mind
Yet the campaign is enigmatic and behind closed doors — all the way down to the blind vote.
That’s because “the whole point of this is for this to be a military group of professionals who trust each other,” Russell said, since “on the military level you need to have boundless loyalty, and if you know exactly who voted for you and who didn’t, then you lose that.”
To ensure that loyalty, the vote count will stop once a majority — or 17 votes — is reached, leaving the real result unknown, one NATO official said. Adding to the mystery, some chiefs of defense are under strict instructions by their ministries to vote for one candidate, the official said, while others can make up their own minds. 
Behind the scenes, the candidates have lobbied their counterparts through letters, face-to-face pitches with NATO ambassadors, at security summits and with phone calls to ministries, said the three officials. 
Since Berlin nominated Breuer, he has been a frequent visitor to NATO capitals. His recent stops have included Albania, North Macedonia, the U.S., Slovenia, Latvia and Estonia — all in the past two months. Breuer has used trips and meetings with fellow military leaders to make the case for Germany’s candidacy, said a person familiar with the effort.
The next military committee chair is expected to take over from Italy’s Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone next July, the same NATO official said.
items.titleTR: Inside the secret race to become NATO’s next top general

items.descriptionTR: Dallas took advantage of a depleted Washington to bounce back from a disappointing Week 1 loss.
items.titleTR: Cowboys find their offense, but one big question remains after win over Commanders

items.descriptionTR:
Jayden Daniels suffered a dislocated elbow in the Commanders' loss to the Cowboys, raising serious questions about his availability and Washington's season moving forward.
The NFL is a league where hindsight is often 20/20. Whether it’s the draft, decisions on the field, or coaching hires, every move comes under the microscope, especially when it leads to an unfortunate turn of events. The Washington Commanders might be wishing they had done things differently on Sunday.
Jayden Daniels might feel the same way to some degree. The Commanders have made some questionable play calls, approaches, and decisions through the first two weeks of the season. One decision late in the first half Sunday could have a major impact on their season.
Down 17-10, the Commanders had a few seconds left in the Dallas Cowboys’ red zone. They could have elected to kick a field goal and head into halftime with points from the drive. Instead, they took a risk that could alter the course of their season.
MORE: Latest Caleb Williams injury update is massive win for Chicago Bears
Daniels took the snap, was tripped by his offensive line, and dislocated his left elbow while trying to stay upright. It was an unnecessary play call with points seemingly in their back pocket. Of course, the consequences could extend far beyond the end of the first half.
￼
Sep 20, 2026; Arlington, Texas, USA; Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels (5) leaps to avoid a tackle by Dallas Cowboys safety Caleb Downs (13) while running with the ball during the second half at AT&T Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Kevin Jairaj-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)
Daniels’ Season in Jeopardy
It remains unclear whether Daniels’ season is over, but the early outlook is not encouraging. So far this season, multiple questionable decisions have contributed to the Commanders’ 0-2 start.
Daniels missed 10 games last year because of an elbow injury that was re-aggravated later in the season when he returned. Now, that same injury could force the Commanders to make another difficult decision about their franchise quarterback.
MORE: Jayden Daniels suffers devastating arm injury, leaves game on cart
If Daniels misses extended time, it will raise questions about his durability and whether the Commanders are doing enough to protect him. There’s no doubt he is a tough competitor and has the ability to become one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL.
￼
Sep 20, 2026; Arlington, Texas, USA; Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels (5) reacts as he leaves the game with an apparent injury to his left arm during the second half against the Washington Commanders at AT&T Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Kevin Jairaj-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)
However, his rookie season was two years ago, and if he misses the rest of this season, that would put another year between him and the start of his career. In the NFL, that can compound quickly and make future roster decisions more difficult, especially with the Commanders facing a decision on his fifth-year option in 2027.
For now, the Commanders and Daniels are in waiting mode as they await more information about the severity of his elbow injury.
