Ravens defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver unintentionally gave Saints quarterback Tyler Shough a new nickname last week.
Ravens defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver unintentionally gave Saints quarterback Tyler Shough a new nickname last week. Weaver called Shough a "poor man’s Josh Allen."
Weaver meant it as a compliment. Saints coaches, though, began referring to Shough as "Poor Man" the rest of the week.
"I loved it. I knew what [Weaver] meant by it, but yeah, obviously [Allen] is an elite player, but it fires me up," Shough said, via Katherine Terrell of ESPN.
Shough threw for two touchdowns against Weaver's Dolphins defense last season in the Saints' 21-17 loss. On Sunday, Shough ran for a touchdown and threw for a touchdown in a 24-17 victory over the Ravens.
Shough's quarterback sneak with 1:28 left proved the game-winner.
Since Week 10 of last season, Shough has 10 fourth-quarter passing and rushing touchdowns, per Terrell. Allen leads the league with 11 in that timespan.
"He's making a name for himself in his league and by the end of the year, I feel like he's going to be one of the top quarterbacks," wide receiver Chris Olave said of Shough.
items.titleTR: Tyler Shough "loved" Anthony Weaver calling him a "poor man's Josh Allen"

slots.packetSpot:
The New Orleans Saints won 24-17 after entering the fourth quarter trailing 17-9 against the Baltimore Ravens. According to reports, Tyler Shough produced one rushing and one passing touchdown; his quarterback sneak with 1 minute 28 seconds remaining was the game-winning play.

This comeback increased interest in Shough's rising profile as a quarterback. After Ravens defensive coordinator Anthony Weaver, as a compliment, called him “a poor man's Josh Allen,” Saints coaches called Shough “Poor Man” throughout the week. Shough said he liked the comparison.

According to a statistic reported by ESPN's Katherine Terrell, Shough has produced 10 touchdowns through passing and rushing in fourth quarters since Week 10 of last season; Josh Allen has 11 touchdowns over the same period. Chris Olave said he believes Shough could be one of the league's best quarterbacks by the end of the season. Whether Baltimore exposed problems for Jesse Minter's team in this game remains the question at hand.
slots.packetTitle: Tyler Shough's rising profile

items.descriptionTR:
•	World No 1 jeered in Amsterdam defeat to Jonny Clayton
	•	Ross Smith beats Price to win World Series of Darts Finals
Luke Littler has threatened to boycott tournaments in the Netherlands after being booed and whistled during the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam. Littler lost to Jonny Clayton in the quarter-finals, with Ross Smith going on to win the event.
The back-to-back world champion faced a hostile environment during his win against the home favourite Danny Noppert on Friday and it escalated on Saturday night as the referee had to intervene in the last-16 win against Nathan Aspinall.
items.titleTR: Luke Littler threatens to boycott Netherlands darts events after booing

slots.packetSpot:
World No. 1 and two-time consecutive world champion Luke Littler said that he may not take part in Euro Tour tournaments in the Netherlands if the booing and whistling he experienced during the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam continues. He reportedly faced a tense atmosphere in his match against home favourite Danny Noppert, while the referee intervened in the match in which he beat Nathan Aspinall in the last 16.

Littler lost 10-4 to Jonny Clayton in the quarter-finals. Ross Smith won the tournament, beating Gerwyn Price 11-5 in the final. Littler also said that he had previously not attended European Tour events because of crowd reactions in Germany, stating that he was "100 percent" ready to take a similar stance in the Netherlands.
slots.packetTitle: Littler's Dutch threshold

items.descriptionTR: Sweden's prime minister Ulf Kristersson has tendered his resignation as the vote count for Sweden's election was completed shortly after 1pm on Thursday, with the opposition parties retaining their 176-173 lead over the government bloc.
items.titleTR: Kristersson resigns as PM after Sweden's centre-left opposition wins election

slots.packetSpot:
With the count, including late and overseas votes, completed in 6,626 electoral districts in Sweden, the centre-left opposition retained its 176–173 advantage over the government bloc. After the result was confirmed, Ulf Kristersson applied to Speaker Andreas Norlén to step down as prime minister.

Magdalena Andersson, leader of the left bloc, called for “a new direction” after four years of right-wing rule. The Social Democrats invited the other three opposition parties to talks; the Centre Party has not yet confirmed whether it will take part.

Kristersson and Ebba Busch, leader of the Christian Democrats, indicated that lines drawn before the election could make forming a new government more difficult. As no party or bloc holds a parliamentary majority, the government-forming process facing Andersson depends on finding an arrangement that can secure support in parliament.
slots.packetTitle: The count ends, the bargaining begins

items.descriptionTR: Towering flames tore through a shopping centre in the south-eastern Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on Thursday after a Russian attack, according to officials. Footage released by the regional military administration showed the fire sweeping through the building. No casualties were reported
items.titleTR: Fire engulfs Zaporizhzhia mall in Ukraine after Russian attack – video

slots.packetSpot:
According to Ukrainian authorities, Russian drones struck the Amstor shopping centre on the right bank of Zaporizhzhia on the night of Thursday, 17 September. Footage from the Emergency Service shows crews tackling flames that engulfed the complex; the agency later described the building as “almost completely destroyed.”

Rescue operations were completed on Friday morning. Fire crews returned to the site and extinguished the blaze after repeatedly having to take shelter because of the risk of further Russian attacks. According to local media, children at a nearby outdoor skate park survived the explosion by sheltering in the concrete hollows of the skate bowls. Ukrainian officials reported that businesses, buses, bus stops and commercial facilities were also targeted or damaged.
slots.packetTitle: A shopping centre in flames in Zaporizhzhia

items.descriptionTR:
Constitutional Court rules that Shell and its partners failed to consult affected communities and did not properly consider environmental risks
The post South Africa’s top court blocks Shell’s offshore oil exploration right appeared first on Climate Home News.
After a five-year legal battle, the Constitutional Court of South Africa has blocked Shell and local partner Impact Africa’s permit to explore for oil and gas off the country’s East Coast, in a landmark victory for local communities and civil society.
“Today’s judgment makes me feel very happy and proud that the ocean is not for profit for mining companies,” said East Coast resident and environmental campaigner Siyabonga Ndovela. 
The verdict concludes a years-long process in which nonprofits Sustaining the Wild Coast, Natural Justice, Greenpeace Africa, and others took legal action against Shell, Impact Africa and the South African government for failing to consult affected communities – a legal requirement in the country.
South Africa’s offshore oil push meets grassroots resistance in court
The Constitutional Court ruled that Shell and Impact Africa had not complied with resource governance law, had failed to meaningfully conduct public consultation and had omitted to consider the impact on climate change, cultural rights, livelihoods and ecological harm. 
The ruling references last year’s landmark advisory opinion by the International Court of Justice, which states that countries have a legal duty to prevent and repair damage to the climate system. The South African judges argued that climate change “transcends borders” and states’ obligations “must be understood within the broader framework of international law”.
“This case must also be understood against the backdrop of well-documented struggles by coastal communities to protect their land, marine resources and ways of life in the face of extractive activities that they believe threaten their very existence,” wrote Justice Narandran Kollapen.     
￼
Protesters march to the Constitutional Court in 2025 (Photo: Ihsaan Haffejee/GroundUp)
The Constitutional Court found that the exploration right had been unlawfully granted by the Department of Mineral and Petroleum Resources. The ruling upholds a 2022 regional court decision against Shell and overturns a 2024 appeal that allowed the company to conduct fresh public consultations under the original exploration right. Friday’s decision means the right, initially granted in 2014, must be set aside.
Celebrating the ruling, Sherelee Odyar, oil and gas campaigner at Greenpeace Africa, told Climate Home News that the court confirmed “serious failures” in the awarding of exploration rights to Shell and Impact Africa, which “cannot simply be corrected later”.
The Wild Coast is a biodiversity hotspot that has been conserved over generations by coastal communities who rely on the ocean and land. “Our land and sea are central to our livelihoods and our way of life. Over generations we have conserved them, and they have conserved us,” reads the founding statement in the case. 
	•	￼   Aug 13, 2026  Nature   Will the world’s drying lands get relief from COP17 in Mongolia? Governments will discuss ways to combat drought and protect herders and their pastures from land degradation in a warming world  Read more    
	•	￼   Aug 12, 2026  News   “We’ve gone backwards” – new plastics treaty text dims hopes for production curbs During troubled talks, fossil fuel-producing nations have pushed for a global pact to tackle only plastic waste rather than reducing the size of the problem  Read more    
	•	
A Shell spokesperson said it noted the ruling, adding that “we are committed to responsible offshore exploration, meaningful stakeholder engagement and environmental stewardship.”
The Department of Mineral and Petroleum Resources had not responded to requests for comment at the time of publication.
“Renewed strength” for communities
The ruling adds to a series of legal challenges brought by civil society groups against oil companies and the government as South Africa has expanded oil and gas development since 2014 under Operation Phakisa, a plan aimed at “unlocking the economic potential of the oceans”.
On the West Coast, Walter Steenkamp, chairperson of Aukotowa Fisheries Cooperative, which is involved in a separate ongoing legal action against TotalEnergies, said that “today’s court case gave me renewed strength”.
The case could also set a precedent for future oil developments, said Alessandro Mazzi, legal governance researcher at the University of Wageningen. He added that the verdict “sends a strong signal to investors that where projects affect people’s land, livelihoods and environment, meaningful consultation and genuine ecological assessment are an integral part of responsible investment”.
Janet Solomon, coordinator of advocacy group Oceans not Oil, said that the court’s emphasis on democratic participation, culture, livelihoods and the health of future generations in handing down the verdict signals a shift in jurisprudence on environmental governance, saying that this focus “may prove to be the judgment’s most enduring legacy”.
items.titleTR: South Africa’s top court blocks Shell’s offshore oil exploration right

slots.packetSpot:
In the South African Constitutional Court’s 2026 ruling in Sustaining the Wild Coast NPC and Others v Minister of Mineral Resources and Energy and Others, Shell’s mineral rights over an approximately 250-kilometre stretch of the Wild Coast in the Eastern Cape were permanently set aside. The ruling ended Shell’s attempt to explore for oil offshore.

The court’s reported reasoning highlighted that notices in isiXhosa-speaking villages had been published only in English and Afrikaans, while consultations had been conducted through traditional leaders despite objections. According to the judgment written by Justice Narandran Kollapen, consultation is not merely a procedural step, but a matter of human dignity and equality that enables affected communities to participate as equals in decisions concerning their own land and seas.

Taking into account the sea’s connection to livelihood, identity and living cultural heritage for the Dwesa Cwebe, Amadiba and Sigidi communities, the court declined to refer the matter back for the process to be rerun, to allow the shortcomings to be remedied a second time, or to award compensation to Shell. Shell is said to have spent 1.1 billion rand on the venture by that point.
slots.packetTitle: A voice on the shore

items.descriptionTR:
The Trump administration has upended protections for hundreds of endangered species by redefining the words "take" and "harm."
The Endangered Species Act has stood as a pillar of conservation in the United States since 1973, bringing animals like bald eagles, manatees, and humpback whales back from the brink of extinction. 
But now, the Trump administration has taken its boldest step yet in an effort to strip legal protections for endangered species. Starting this week, the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service says that it now considers it legal to kill a federally protected animal, as long as it wasn’t on purpose.
The directive comes after another recent revision to these legal protections went into effect this week, saying that damaging an animal’s habitat is no longer considered “harming” it. The two changes in combination take the teeth out of the Endangered Species Act and pave the way for industries to log, mine, pollute, or travel through areas without regard for what lives there.
The fate of the country’s rarest creatures could come down to the meaning of two seemingly simple words: “harm” and “take.” In this case, “take” refers to killing an animal. 
“A vessel that inadvertently strikes a whale has not taken it, because the vessel’s course was not set against the whale,” said the memo, signed by Brian Nesvik, director of the Fish and Wildlife Service. “Felling a tree is not a take of the bats roosting in it unless the tree was felled for the purpose of killing or capturing them.”
Legal experts say this is an unprecedentedly narrow view of what these words mean in the Endangered Species Act, and that the moves are sure to be challenged in court. Almost two dozen states recently sued the Trump administration over changes to the law, and more lawsuits from environmental groups are expected to come. And if history is any indicator, the agency could soon find itself on the losing side of an old argument — one that’s been heard in courts before. 
“They are trying to disregard 50 years of the act, and how the agency — and everybody — has always interpreted this word,” said Ryan Shannon, an attorney at Defenders of Wildlife, a conservation nonprofit that has long spearheaded endangered species recovery efforts. “This is not a bunt — they are really swinging for the fences with this.”
That’s because the words “harm” and “take” are at the core of what makes the Endangered Species Act so effective. 
Efforts to protect the northern spotted owl are one such example. Decades of logging in the Pacific Northwest had eliminated much of its forest habitat. But after the species was listed under the act in 1990, cutting down those trees was considered to be harming the owl, and therefore illegally “taking” it.
The law has been a thorn in the side of industries for decades. Environmentalists have often sued companies that want to log, mine, or build in a particular area, using the Endangered Species Act to make their case.
Now, “the administration is telling every industry in America that killing endangered wildlife is fine as long as it wasn’t their primary goal,” said Andrew Wetzler, an executive at the Natural Resources Defense Council, in a statement. “But unintentional harm is exactly what is driving many species towards extinction.”
Read Next
￼
Gray whales are starving as the Arctic warms. Will the US protect them?
Sachi Kitajima Mulkey
The Supreme Court has considered these words and their meanings before. In a 1995 case, Babbitt v. Sweet Home, it ruled that modifying a creature’s habitat — such as logging the forest where spotted owls live — counts as harming it. In a dissenting opinion, the late Justice Antonin Scalia argued that “take” means to directly kill or injure wildlife. The Trump administration’s new memo uses Scalia’s interpretation — even though the majority of the court disagreed with Scalia back then. 
Earlier this summer, in a revision that changed which actions it considers to be “harming” an animal, the Trump administration argued that there’s a “traditional meaning” of the word “take,” meaning “to kill or capture a wild animal.” But the verb “take” is so notoriously difficult to define that it’s been tormenting dictionary editors for more than a century. In 2001, the lexicographer Kory Stamper spent weeks trying to capture all the senses of the word, and she reflected that the ordeal “unspooled” her sanity, leading to panic and despair.
In 2024, the Supreme Court ruled that courts — not agencies — have the power to interpret the law. That decision was generally seen as a blow to environmental efforts, but in this case, it might mean the Trump administration doesn’t have final say in how it interprets the Endangered Species Act.
All these factors make the Fish and Wildlife Service’s memo legally flimsy, if not illegal, according to Brett Hartl, director of government affairs at the Center of Biological Diversity, an environmental nonprofit. 
The memo is “essentially performative cruelty for the sake of it” and “barely worth the paper it’s printed on,” Hartl said. “They’re trying to turn it into an anti-poaching statute, but it’s actually supposed to be the strongest conservation law in the world.”
Ironically enough, the administration’s rewrite may leave companies in a tougher spot than before, Shannon said, because it blows up the settled rules they’d been following for decades. Corporate attorneys now have to choose between telling clients to take advantage of the agency’s new approach, or holding off in case a court or new administration puts the old protections back into place.
For companies that actually want long‑term regulatory certainty, like timber corporations and real estate developers, Shannon said that this deregulatory swing may be “more than they ever really would have asked for.”
If the courts do end up siding with the Trump administration, some species will suffer more than others. Those listed as endangered in more recent decades were given “critical habitat protections,” which provided an extra layer of scrutiny to activities that could harm animals and were made mandatory for all newly listed animals.
But many of the species listed during the Endangered Species Act’s early years — including the Florida panther and the California sea otter — never received those protections. Instead, they depend on broader language in the law, like “harm” and “take.” That means the animals America once wanted to protect the most could now be the most exposed.


This story was originally published by Grist with the headline The fate of the Endangered Species Act rests on 2 simple words on Sep 18, 2026.
items.titleTR: The fate of the Endangered Species Act rests on 2 simple words

slots.packetSpot:
The Trump administration is taking steps to interpret the concepts of “harm” and “take” more narrowly under the US Endangered Species Act. According to a memo signed by US Fish and Wildlife Service Director Brian Nesvik, damage to an animal’s habitat may no longer count as “harm” to it; the unintentional killing of a federally protected animal may also not be regarded as a “take.”

This interpretation could affect legal oversight of activities such as logging, mining, pollution and travel in areas inhabited by endangered species. Ryan Shannon of Defenders of Wildlife and Andrew Wetzler of the Natural Resources Defense Council argue that the changes could weaken the established approach to protecting species. Brett Hartl of the Center for Biological Diversity says the memo is legally unsound.

In the 1995 Babbitt v. Sweet Home decision, the Supreme Court ruled that altering habitat could also constitute harm. The administration’s new approach is based on an interpretation of Antonin Scalia’s dissent in that case. A 2024 Supreme Court ruling stated that the authority to interpret laws rests with courts, not agencies; about two dozen states have filed lawsuits over the changes, and environmental groups are also expected to prepare new legal challenges.
slots.packetTitle: The narrowing ground beneath two words

items.descriptionTR:
At least one person dead as stormy weather causes severe flooding in Barcelona and Valencia
Intense and slow-moving thunderstorms broke out on Wednesday afternoon across parts of eastern Spain, bringing some severe flooding and killing at least one person.
Storms first struck over the Castilla-La Mancha region during the afternoon before passing over Spain’s east coast, becoming very slow-moving and continuing overnight. Torrential rainfall, strong winds and large hail were reported in Valencia and Barcelona, causing widespread flooding in both cities. Weather stations west of Barcelona recorded some of the highest totals with more than 100mm (4in) of rain falling in the space of a few hours, and locally 70mm in just 30 minutes in the early hours of Thursday morning. Cars and roads were submerged, and flights were cancelled across the region.
items.titleTR: Weather tracker: Thunderstorms hit Spain as Japan braces for typhoon

slots.packetSpot:
Slow-moving severe thunderstorms in eastern Spain stretched from Castilla-La Mancha to the areas around Valencia and Barcelona. In flooding caused by heavy rain, strong winds and hail, vehicles and roads were submerged; flights were cancelled, and the Levante–Athletic Club match in Valencia was postponed.

It was reported that rainfall exceeding 100 millimetres was recorded within a few hours at some stations west of Barcelona, while in the early hours of Thursday as much as 70 millimetres was recorded in 30 minutes in some places. Near Olivella, it was reported that a man's body was found after his vehicle was swept away by floodwaters; at least one person was reported to have died in the storms.
slots.packetTitle: What the storm left behind in eastern Spain

items.descriptionTR:
The film, winner of the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival, reveals how the mass killing of innocents in Gaza was organized remotely from the heart of the Israeli city
Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor live in Jerusalem, but their families are from Tel Aviv, the city where they filmed NAZA at night. Their documentary, which has won the Special Jury Prize at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival, gathers the testimonies of 24 military personnel, officers and soldiers from Israel’s intelligence service who demonstrate the systems used for mass killing in Gaza, some based on surveillance and attack programs generated by artificial intelligence.
Seguir leyendo
items.titleTR: Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, directors of ‘NAZA’: ‘That life in Tel Aviv goes on as if nothing was happening is also an act of violence’

slots.packetSpot:
Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor’s documentary NAZA examines, through the testimony of 24 Israeli military and intelligence personnel, the systems it alleges organize mass killings in Gaza. Said to rely on surveillance and AI-generated attack programs, these systems are set alongside the continuation of everyday life in Tel Aviv.

In the final minutes of the production, which received the Special Jury Prize at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival, the camera enters Gaza. The Israeli army, meanwhile, denied the allegation that it uses AI programs, stating that it has made unprecedented efforts to reduce civilian harm.
slots.packetTitle: Gaza’s systems beneath Tel Aviv’s night

items.descriptionTR: After six years away from the stage due to illness, the singer is back with a 26-show residency in Paris and a dazzling wardrobe that has transformed her comeback into a statement of resilience
items.titleTR: Céline Dion: The looks that became her armor against illness and vulnerability

slots.packetSpot: Céline Dion is reported to have returned to live performances in Paris after being away from the stage for six years due to illness. Her 26-show residency in Paris accompanies this return, in which her stage outfits also stand out; fans' emotional reactions are also drawing attention. The return is presented as an expression of resilience.
slots.packetTitle: Céline Dion returns to the stage

items.descriptionTR:
The Argentine Football Association confirms the World Cup-winning captain will appear in a friendly against Benin on October 6
A story that had it all, from painful defeats to everlasting victories, will come to an end. It will happen on October 6, when Lionel Messi plays his final match with the Argentina national team. That day the Albiceleste will face Benin in Buenos Aires in a friendly. “The last tango of the world’s best player,” said the president of the Argentine Football Association (AFA), Claudio Tapia.
Seguir leyendo
items.titleTR: Lionel Messi to bid farewell to Argentina national team with a final match in Buenos Aires: ‘The last tango of the world’s best player’

slots.packetSpot:
According to a statement by Argentine Football Association President Claudio Tapia in a video published by the AFA, Lionel Messi is preparing to bid farewell to the Argentina national team in the friendly against Benin in Buenos Aires on 6 October. Tapia said Messi accepted the invitation following a meeting with head coach Lionel Scaloni.

Messi had announced his decision to leave the national team at the end of the month. Having made 207 appearances and scored 125 goals for Argentina over more than 20 years, Messi won one World Cup and two Copa América titles. According to the AFA, the Benin match will be the only game Messi will play during this international window; Argentina will face Bolivia in Córdoba on 30 September and Burkina Faso in Buenos Aires on 3 October.

Tapia said the players who won the 2022 World Cup with Messi would also be invited to the match with their families. Scaloni's contract expires in December, while it is not yet clear whether the head coach will remain in his post.
slots.packetTitle: Messi's last tango

items.descriptionTR: Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson tells Bloomberg that mediators are shuttling between Iran and US to revive talks.
items.titleTR: Qatar says it is working to revive Iran-US talks

slots.packetSpot: Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson Majed al-Ansari said the mediation team has been exchanging ideas for about two weeks on restarting talks between Iran and the United States. According to al-Ansari, Qatar is moving its mediators between different capitals in an initiative it is pursuing together with Pakistan; however, there is no confirmed development indicating that talks will resume or that an agreement will be reached.
slots.packetTitle: Qatar shuttles between Tehran and Washington

items.descriptionTR: Electricity availability faces severe deficit amid thermoelectric breakdowns and maintenance problems
items.titleTR: Cuba restores national power grid following major outage

items.descriptionTR: Widespread power outages have become increasingly common due to fuel shortages made worse by a US blockade.
items.titleTR: Millions without power as Cuba hit by latest major blackout

slots.packetSpot:
Cuba announced that its national electricity grid had been brought back online following the major outage. However, the deep gap between generation and demand, breakdowns at thermal power plants and units taken offline for maintenance mean that the return of electricity does not amount to a stable supply.

The outage was reported to have begun with a transmission failure and adverse weather conditions in central regions. Electricity was first supplied to priority areas around hospitals and water pumping stations; as the gradual recovery continues, it is stated that at least the sixth partial or total outage this year has occurred.

Havana cites US sanctions and the blockade, which it says have limited access to fuel, spare parts and investment, among the causes of the crisis. Washington, meanwhile, attributes the energy crisis to poor domestic management. Shortages of food, medicine, water and cooking gas, as well as disruptions at hospitals, schools and public institutions, are also reported; repeated outages have also led to rare protests.
slots.packetTitle: The grid returns, the darkness remains

items.descriptionTR:
Row at Athenian riviera resort turned violent after two elderly bathers reportedly argued over shortage of loungers
Greek police are investigating the death of an 82-year-old man after a brawl over a sunlounger at a beach on the Athenian riviera.
The man had arrived at the popular bathing spot of Vouliagmeni before 10am on Sunday hoping to secure a sunbed, but he soon began arguing with a fellow bather – described by authorities as a “76-year-old man unknown to him” – when it became clear loungers were in short supply.
items.titleTR: Man, 82, dies after brawl with 76-year-old over sunlounger on Greek beach

slots.packetSpot:
A fight reportedly sparked by a shortage of sun loungers in Vouliagmeni on the Athens Riviera ended with the death of an 82-year-old man. According to reports, the 82-year-old, who had been arguing with a 76-year-old man he did not know, may have suffered a heart attack during the scuffle, which others were also said to have joined. He was taken to Asklepieion Hospital in Voula and died at around 11 a.m.; an autopsy was requested.

Greek police detained the 76-year-old man; the 21-year-old woman who was with him was also initially detained. The manager of the beach facility was held for questioning. Authorities said those involved would appear before a magistrate; the investigation is ongoing.
slots.packetTitle: A death in the shadow of a sun-lounger fight

items.descriptionTR:
Four of Nurat Osman’s alleged abductors were killed during rescue after she was taken from outside her home last week
A British woman kidnapped in Malawi last week has been rescued by police after a shootout in which four of her alleged abductors were killed.
Nusrat Osman was abducted outside her home in the southern city of Blantyre on 11 September at about 12.30pm. Police had offered a reward of 30m Malawi kwacha (£12,950) for information leading to her rescue and the arrest of the perpetrators.
items.titleTR: British woman who was kidnapped in Malawi rescued by police after shootout

slots.packetSpot:
Police said that 47-year-old British national Nusrat Osman, from Leicester, was abducted by four unidentified people in Blantyre's Mount Pleasant neighbourhood on 11 September. Police reported that Osman's vehicle was blocked and that he was forced into another vehicle and taken away.

Osman was rescued in a police operation carried out on Thursday on the outskirts of Blantyre. According to the police statement, four suspects were shot in an armed clash with suspects said to have been carrying an AK-47 rifle and a handgun; the individuals taken to hospital died of their injuries. Assistant Inspector General of Police Noel Kayira, who took part in the operation, was also reported to have been injured and to be in a stable condition.

Reunited with his family, Osman was taken to hospital for treatment and physical and psychological assessment. Inspector General of Police Richard Luhanga said Osman was still experiencing trauma. The identities of the four suspects who died, how the group was found and the reason for the abduction were not disclosed; the investigation is continuing. It was also reported that there was no known ransom demand or communication with the abductors.

Authorities had offered a reward of 30 million Malawian kwacha ($17,000; £12,500) for information that would secure Osman's rescue and the arrest and conviction of those responsible. The UK Foreign Office said it was aware of the incident and was in contact with local authorities.
slots.packetTitle: Armed rescue in Malawi

items.descriptionTR: Tehran says it has learned the US may be planning a new round of strikes, warns of retaliation 'without limitations'.
items.titleTR: Iran war live: Tehran warns US against new strikes; fighting rages in Yemen

slots.packetSpot:
Iran, through its military central command speaking to state media, warned against a possible new large-scale attack by the United States and its allies. Iran said such a move would lead to sustained retaliation against US bases and interests, and that Washington's allies in the region would also be considered parties to the conflict; it did not share details of the intelligence it claimed to possess regarding attack preparations.

The US State Department called on Americans to exercise greater caution, drawing attention to the possibility of an unpredictable escalation in the Middle East. In Yemen, the Iran-backed Houthis claimed to have targeted Riyadh and a major oil facility in Yanbu. While Saudi Arabia did not comment on these claims, the Saudi-led coalition said it had thwarted other attacks against the kingdom.

Iran also reiterated that it would not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until conditions it interpreted as its own for the temporary ceasefire agreement in June were met. The agreement had collapsed in July because of disagreements over its terms.
slots.packetTitle: Tehran warns of a wider war

items.descriptionTR:
￼The "Great Mosaic" may be the largest in the Roman world.
Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article The Largest Roman Mosaic Ever Excavated Opens to the Public appeared first on Colossal.
￼
At 33 feet wide and 52.5 feet high, an ancient mosaic recently unveiled to the public may be the largest in the entire Roman world. It sits within the recently opened Museum of the Baths of Trajan in central Rome, which preserves a monumental, early 2nd-century bath complex built by Emperor Trajan covering about 15 acres.
To construct the baths on the Oppian Hill, builders repurposed elements of a previous structure, Emperor Nero’s Domus Aurea, or “Golden House,” originally erected between 64 and 68 C.E. It’s unclear if the mosaic originated in that building; archaeologists think it could have also been part of a lavish dwelling that was later incorporated into the compound. But many of the monumental composition’s tesserae are missing and may have been used in the construction of the baths.
￼
Dubbed the “Great Mosaic,” the work was discovered in 2011, and archaeologists have been meticulously revealing and conserving it since. The in situ artwork depicts architectural features that may represent a dual-level theatrical set, known as a scaenae frons, plus statues of the Muses and other figures and patterns that mimic the appearance of marble.
Within the same complex, a remarkable architectural fresco uncovered in the 1990s also goes on view for the first time. Known as the “Painted City,” it’s unclear whether the scenic backdrop for bathers depicts an actual port city or an imaginary place. According to CNN, the aerial perspective portrays some unusual details such as public squares and towers that weren’t a common feature of municipal design in the 1st century.
Archaeologists continue to excavate the “Great Mosaic,” particularly an area focusing on wine-making and grapes. Much of it can now be seen by visitors from an elevated walkway.

slots.packetSpot:
The “Painted City” fresco and the “Moses and the Philosopher” mosaic, uncovered in the 1990s in the underground gallery beneath Trajan’s Baths in Rome, have been opened to visitors for the first time. The works are thought to date to the first century, possibly to the Neronian or Flavian period before the baths opened in 109.

The fresco depicts a port city seen from above, with its walls and towers. The mosaic, 10 metres high and stretching 16 metres along the wall, brings together figures, architectural structures, statues and real people in a theatrical scene. Archaeologist Francesco Pacetti said they estimate that the mosaic may be the largest wall mosaic found in the Roman world.

Visits initially took place on weekends in groups of 15; from 2 October, they are planned to continue between Friday and Sunday. A museum focused on Trajan’s Baths also opened at the beginning of the month; the restoration was carried out under the €500 million EU-funded PNRR-Caput Mundi programme.
slots.packetTitle: A city beneath Trajan’s Baths

items.descriptionTR:
•	Inglis hits 103 to set up chase and 3-0 series win
	•	Madhevere drops Ellis in penultimate over
Josh Inglis scored his second one-day international century and Nathan Ellis his highest score in ⁠the format with an unbeaten 36 from 44 balls as Australia claimed a dramatic one-wicket victory over Zimbabwe with a ball ⁠to spare in Harare on Sunday.
When Ellis was joined at the crease by Australia’s No 11, Spencer Johnson, ⁠the tourists needed 27 runs for victory, something the pair managed at a run-a-ball to take their side to the win.
items.titleTR: Australia deny Zimbabwe a consolation win after Ellis pulls off last-over heist

slots.packetSpot:
The third ODI in Harare became a match in which Zimbabwe, with a total of 271/8, pushed Australia to the very end. Australia reached the target of 272 with nine wickets down and one ball remaining; with this result, they completed the series 3-0.

Josh Inglis's 103 runs from 102 balls, including 11 fours, kept Australia's chase alive. Nathan Ellis, meanwhile, made an unbeaten 36 from 44 balls after taking 3-50 in 10 overs. With Ellis and Spencer Johnson, who made 7 runs from 13 balls, together, Australia needed 27 runs to reach the target.

Zimbabwe captain Sikandar Raza made an unbeaten 81 from 72 balls; Craig Ervine made 59 and Innocent Kaia 55. Kaia left the field because of a hamstring injury. Brad Evans's 4-47 stood out in the home side's defence.

It was reported that Wessly Madhevere dismissed Ellis in the penultimate over and was unable to defend nine runs in the final over. Australia captain Mitchell Marsh said Zimbabwe probably deserved to win and that his team was lucky; Raza said he was proud of his team's fight.
slots.packetTitle: To the final ball in Harare

items.descriptionTR:
Former president of Chile drops out after support collapsed in security council straw poll, leaving seven candidates in contest
Michelle Bachelet, a former president of Chile, has withdrawn her candidacy to become the next secretary general of the ⁠UN, ending an attempt that had struggled to gain traction among security council members.
Bachelet, 74, announced ⁠her decision in a video posted on Instagram on Saturday, saying: “I will now continue, with the ⁠same determination as always, my international work.”
items.titleTR: Michelle Bachelet withdraws from race to become UN secretary general

slots.packetSpot:
Michelle Bachelet, Chile’s former president and former UN high commissioner for human rights, announced in a video posted on Instagram on 20 September that she was withdrawing her candidacy to become the next secretary-general of the United Nations. Her campaign had reportedly been struggling to find support among Security Council members; in the third informal poll on 19 September, her support was reported to have nearly collapsed, while Costa Rican Rebeca Grynspan had moved into the lead.

With Bachelet’s withdrawal, seven candidates remain in the race to succeed António Guterres, whose second five-year term will end on 31 December 2026; it is still possible for new candidates to enter. The Security Council will ultimately recommend a single candidate to the 193-member General Assembly; it is noted that, following consensus in the Council, General Assembly approval is generally regarded as a formality.
slots.packetTitle: Bachelet exits the UN race

items.descriptionTR:
Embattled Friedrich Merz faces nervous wait while far-right Alternative für Deutschland party targets further gains
Voters in two German states are going to the polls with the political future of the embattled chancellor, Friedrich Merz, hanging in the balance and an emboldened far right targeting further gains.
Coming two weeks after a seismic election in Saxony-Anhalt in which the anti-immigration, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) scored its highest ever result in a regional poll, the nativist party is expected to drain support again from Merz’s conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
items.titleTR: Future of German chancellor hangs in the balance as two states go to polls

slots.packetSpot:
Voters went to the polls in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin on 20 September. Coming after the 6 September elections in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD was reported to be nearing an absolute majority, these votes were seen as a test for Chancellor Friedrich Merz and as ground for further gains by the AfD.

Merz's approval rating was reported to have fallen as low as 14 percent in recent polls. Despite leadership debates within the CDU, senior figures in the party are standing behind Merz for now; in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, meanwhile, the CDU was said to be facing the risk of recording the worst result in its history and failing to clear the threshold required to enter the state parliament.

A poll dated 18 September put the SPD at 37 percent, the AfD at 36 percent, the Left Party at 9 percent and the Greens at 5 percent in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. In Berlin, the Left Party was leading with 22 percent; the CDU stood at 20 percent, the AfD at 18 percent, the Greens at 15 percent, the SPD at 12 percent and BSW at 4 percent. These figures were poll measurements, not vote counts.

Energy, housing and the general cost of living were among the prominent issues in the campaigns. On 18 September, Merz presented a consumer support package that also included tax cuts on gas and diesel. While the other major parties continued to refuse to form a coalition with the AfD, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern Minister-President Manuela Schwesig described the AfD as a dangerous party; Alice Weidel, the AfD's national party leader, argued that Merz could be removed from office in the election.
slots.packetTitle: The ballot box in Merz's shadow

items.descriptionTR:
The USPSTF sets insurance coverage for preventive services, like colonoscopies.
Anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced the names of eight new members of a 16-person federal task force intended to make scientifically independent, evidence-based recommendations on an array of preventive medicine services for Americans—from depression screening to statin use, colonoscopies, and mammograms.
Recommendations from the panel—the US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF)—don't simply provide guidance for Americans; they also determine access. The USPSTF is supposed to use a rigorous, transparent framework for evaluating evidence and sets graded recommendations on an A to D scale. Health insurance providers are required to cover, at no cost, all preventive services that are given recommendations of an A or B grade.
Kennedy has sidelined the USPSTF for more than a year, canceling its meetings and refusing to appoint new members as terms expired and members left. In May, Kennedy also fired two leaders, sparking outcry and exacerbating fears that he would corrupt the nonpartisan independent panel by stacking it with unqualified ideological allies—which he did with an influence vaccine advisory committee at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

items.descriptionTR:
President’s latest order expected to bring NIH funding under control of Trump administration to align with agenda
Donald Trump’s latest executive order is expected to establish a board responsible for approving National Institutes of Health grant funding, marking another attempt by the Trump administration to censor topics that do not align with the president’s agenda.
The executive order, reported by outlets including the Washington Post and Politico, was discussed in a meeting on Friday where senior administration officials accused the NIH of funding “woke” initiatives that went against Trump’s political priorities.
items.titleTR: Trump reportedly to form health funding board that could veto ‘woke’ initiatives

items.descriptionTR: Click in for more news from The Hill {beacon} Healthcare Healthcare   The Big Story  CDC director says RFK Jr. has final say In her first interview since taking leadership of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Erica Schwartz told Atlanta News First that she isn’t afraid to disagree with Health Secretary Robert F.…
items.titleTR: CDC director says RFK Jr. has final say

slots.packetSpot:
Who makes public health decisions in the United States, and by what criteria, is being debated anew. Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s announcement of eight new names for the task force affecting insurance coverage for preventive health services brings the personnel dimension of this debate to the fore.

The Trump administration is expected, according to the Washington Post and Politico, to establish an external board that could approve or veto NIH grants. The regulation, which is said not yet to have been published, is alleged to review research funding for alignment with Trump's goals; NIH Director Jay Bhattacharya, meanwhile, defended the existing grant process.

CDC Director Erica Schwartz also told Atlanta News First that she can have disagreements with Kennedy behind closed doors, but that final decisions belong to Kennedy in his capacity as HHS Secretary. The disagreement over whether four measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania should be included in the CDC count continues: while Schwartz describes it as a matter of technical definition, Pennsylvania officials say the criterion they use is based on the CDC's classification of deaths from other respiratory viruses.
slots.packetTitle: Redrawing the boundaries of authority in US public health

items.descriptionTR: HANOI, Vietnam (AP) — Heavy rain caused flooding across parts of northern Vietnam on Thursday, disrupting travel, inundating homes and pushing several rivers above dangerous levels, authorities and state media said. Rain has fallen across northern and north-central Vietnam this week, with some areas receiving more than 50 centimeters (19.7 inches), according to the disaster […] HANOI, Vietnam (AP) — Heavy rain caused flooding across parts of northern Vietnam on Thursday, disrupting travel, inundating homes and pushing several rivers above dangerous levels, authorities and state media said. Rain has fallen across northern and north-central Vietnam this week, with some areas receiving more than 50 centimeters (19.7 inches), according to the disaster prevention department. More than 2,000 homes have been submerged, many key transportation routes blocked and more than 1,000 households isolated. Ninh Binh and Thanh Hoa provinces, which include lowland and hilly areas south of the capital Hanoi, have been among the hardest hit. Vietnam is among the world’s most climate-vulnerable countries and prone to flooding. A series of severe storms last year spurred the country to find new ways to prepare for and manage floods. In Thanh Hoa province, authorities told students to stay home because flooding had made travel to school dangerous, state media said. Heavy rains and flooding have submerged or damaged about 10,014 hectares (24,745 acres) of rice and other crops, with the largest losses reported in Ninh Binh, Thanh Hoa and Nghe An provinces. Thousands of livestock and poultry also have been killed. “The flood happens every year,” Ninh Binh resident Tran Ngoc Tai told national broadcaster VTV, adding that people were prepared with fresh water and food. items.titleTR: Torrential rain and flooding slam Tunis, forcing schools to close

items.descriptionTR: Intense rainfall dumped up to 96 mm on Torrent, south‑west of Valencia, flooding roads, homes and the Parc Central tunnel, trapping cars and prompting emergency pumping operations.
items.titleTR: Valencia region deluge leaves streets covered in mud and vehicles unusable in Torrent

slots.packetSpot:
Heavy rainfall in northern Vietnam, Tunisia and Torrent in Spain’s Valencia region caused similar disruptions to urban life on different scales. In Vietnam, authorities and state media reported that homes were flooded, transport was disrupted, and schools in Hanoi were closed or switched to online learning.

In Tunisia, roads and pavements were flooded, leaving vehicles stranded; water entered some homes, power and internet outages occurred, and afternoon classes were suspended. In Torrent, alongside mud-covered streets and damaged vehicles, 15 people were rescued from a flooded fast-food restaurant.

A forecast of 30 to 50 millimetres of rainfall had been issued for a short period in Tunisia. In Torrent, some residents, recalling previous floods, criticised the absence of structural measures and the timing of the emergency warning; those criticisms were not presented as a definitive failure of the warning system.
slots.packetTitle: Rain’s imprint on city life

items.descriptionTR:
Wildfires currently burning large swathes of land in Indonesia are on track to produce emissions on a par with the…
The post El Niño: Indonesia fire emissions in 2026 ‘on track’ to match record for this century appeared first on Carbon Brief.
Print article Share
Wildfires currently burning large swathes of land in Indonesia are on track to produce emissions on a par with the country’s most-intense fire season this century, according to experts. 
Data from the Global Fire Emissions Database reveals that, as of 7 September, fires in Indonesia produced 76m tonnes of carbon (MtC) in 2026.
This puts 2026 on the same trajectory as 2015, when fires burned 2.6m hectares of land across the country and generated a total of 333MtC. 
Dr Guido van der Werf, a researcher at Wageningen University in the Netherlands, tells Carbon Brief that the fires in Indonesia are “more or less on track” to reach levels seen 11 years ago.
Parts of the country – including the eastern province of Papua – are “burning more than they’ve ever burned”, he says.
￼
Indonesia is no stranger to emissions-intensive fires. Research has estimated that the record 1997 fire season generated carbon emissions equivalent to 13-40% of all global fossil-fuel emissions that year. 
Meanwhile, a separate study that looked at carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions from the 2015 fires in south-east Asia – which primarily burned Indonesia – found they were greater than the total of the EU’s fossil-fuel emissions that year. The “severe haze” from the fires has been linked to more than 100,000 premature deaths across the region.
El Niño influence
As in 2015 and in 1997, this year’s Indonesian fires come during an El Niño year.
The naturally-occurring climate phenomenon, linked to ocean temperatures in the Pacific, periodically drives up temperatures and dries out land in Indonesia – creating the conditions for fires so immense that they imprint on global emissions. 
Scientists are projecting that this year’s El Niño – which started in June and is expected to last into 2027 – will be one of the most intense on record.

Dr Mark Parrington, a senior scientist from the Copernicus Climate Change Service explains: 
“From August until the end of October [to] November is the dry season in Indonesia. We do normally see fire around this time of year, but nowhere near the scale that we’ve seen this year, or indeed any of the previous El Niño years”.
Dr Nisa Novita, strategic lead for peatland at Indonesian environmental NGO Yayasan Konservasi Alam Nusantara, tells Carbon Brief that El Niño “does not directly cause most fires”, but acts as a “major amplifier by creating hotter and drier conditions, making fires easier to ignite, spread faster and much harder to control”. 
Studies have shown that fires in Indonesia often occur where there has been significant land clearance and peatland drainage for agriculture and palm oil plantations. These practices create a dry landscape that is highly flammable during times of drought.
￼
Pink bars show years in which an El Niño event was called by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. GFED fire emissions data for 1980-96 is from Field et al. (2009) and Van Marle et al. (2017); data for 1997-2022 is from Van der Werf et al. (2025); and data for 2022 onwards is from Chen et al. (2026).
Van der Werf says the scale of this year’s fires – and whether they will end up being more intense than 2015 – will depend on the length of this year’s El Niño event, as well as the effectiveness of recent peatland conservation efforts.
Novita explains that Indonesia’s fires are heavily emissions-intensive due to its large tropical peatland ecosystem: 
“When peatlands are degraded and drained due to canal development for agriculture, the water table drops, making the peat dry and highly flammable especially during dry seasons or El Niño events, like now.  “Unlike fires in dry ecosystems, peat fires can smolder underground, so the soil itself becomes readily available fuel.”
Extensive peatland restoration efforts in Indonesia in recent years have been credited with reducing the number of fires during the 2019 El Niño.
After the catastrophic fires in 1997-98, the Indonesian government introduced a range of measures designed to strengthen peatland protection and restoration through dedicated institutions and regulations. This included the introduction of a moratorium on licenses to convert forests and peatlands into plantations and logging areas. 
In the aftermath of the 2015 fires, it established an official peatland restoration agency, which was given an additional mandate for mangrove restoration in 2021. This agency was dissolved last year. Novita says:
“We have learned and improved…But the question is: is it enough? Or are we still underestimating the risk that degraded peatlands pose, especially when we face another El Niño?”
Van der Werf says it remains unclear from the 2026 fire data how great an impact recent efforts to restore peatland in Indonesia have had on reducing the impact and spread of the fires: 
“I had hoped that this year Indonesia would be relatively quiet, even though we have a big El Niño…You could argue if those regulations worked, then this wouldn’t be a big fire [season], even though it [has been] very dry. 
“This is maybe the case in Sumatra [which has seen a quiet fire season], but definitely not in other regions. Papua [a region of Indonesia] and [neighbouring country of] Papua New Guinea – those are the new frontiers. They are basically going through the same thing that Sumatra went through 20 years ago.”

items.descriptionTR: A very strong El Niño is likely to persist until February 2027, potentially bringing drier, hotter summers to South Africa and raising heatwave, crop and food security risks.
items.titleTR: COMING IN HOT: Very strong El Niño is a ‘stress test’ for SA’s food systems

slots.packetSpot:
A forest fire near Villa de Leyva in Colombia consumed 40 hectares of native forest, according to local authorities; aircraft, a military helicopter and firefighting crews were deployed to combat the blaze. Severe El Niño conditions are reported to be increasing heat and drought, raising the risk of fires.

In Indonesia, the Global Fire Emissions Database recorded carbon emissions from fires at 76 million tonnes as of 7 September. According to experts’ assessment, the year is following a course similar to the intense 2015 fire season; the final scale, however, depends on the duration of El Niño and the impact of peatland protection efforts. El Niño is not considered the direct cause of most fires; land clearing and the draining of peatlands are also among the factors that facilitate fires.

In South Africa, it is stated that the very strong El Niño expected to continue until February 2027 could bring hotter, drier summers and increase risks related to heatwaves, agricultural production and food security.
slots.packetTitle: El Niño’s trial by fire

items.descriptionTR: For 100 consecutive days between June 2 and Sept. 10, the global ocean outside of polar regions sustained record high average sea surface temperatures, according to data from the Climate Reanalyzer, a platform overseen by the University of Maine’s Climate Change Institute in the U.S. On each of the 100 days, sea surface temperatures exceeded […] For 100 consecutive days between June 2 and Sept. 10, the global ocean outside of polar regions sustained record high average sea surface temperatures, according to data from the Climate Reanalyzer, a platform overseen by the University of Maine’s Climate Change Institute in the U.S. On each of the 100 days, sea surface temperatures exceeded those on the same date in every other year on record since 1982. One of the highest readings occurred on Aug. 22, when global ocean sea surface temperatures reached 21.10° Celsius (69.98° Fahrenheit), according to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. The Climate Reanalyzer reported temperatures climbing even higher between Aug. 22 and 27, with average ocean sea surface temperatures hitting 21.18° C (70.12° F). The platform draws on global sea surface temperature data recorded by the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA). These record temperatures are likely to remain elevated in the near future “given the state of the intensifying El Niño,” said Zachary Labe, a climate scientist at the U.S.-based nonprofit Climate Central, which communicates climate change science. Graphic illustrating climbing sea surface temperatures. Image courtesy of Climate Central. In a Sept. 10 press briefing that discussed the Climate Reanalyzer data, Labe said this record ocean heat is part of a long-term trend driven by the human-induced climate crisis. items.descriptionTR: Roughly a decade ago, a marine heatwave in the northeastern Pacific Ocean caused a dramatic decline in populations of forage fish and krill, the base of the marine food chain. A recent study found that the Hawaiian humpback whale population, which feeds on krill and small fish, also declined sharply during the 2013-16 heatwave and […] Roughly a decade ago, a marine heatwave in the northeastern Pacific Ocean caused a dramatic decline in populations of forage fish and krill, the base of the marine food chain. A recent study found that the Hawaiian humpback whale population, which feeds on krill and small fish, also declined sharply during the 2013-16 heatwave and has not yet recovered. Humpback whales (Megaptera novaeangliae) in the North Pacific feed in cold Alaskan and Canadian waters during the summer months before traveling roughly 4,800 kilometers (3,000 miles) to Hawaii to breed and give birth over the winter. To understand the impact of the 2013-2016 marine heatwave, researchers analyzed more than 27,000 photos of whale sightings between 2002 and 2023 across the main Hawaiian islands. The photos came from Happywhale, a citizen science platform where anyone can upload images of whale flukes (tail fins) that scientists use to identify individuals. “Their flukes are a bit like a fingerprint for each individual humpback whale,” study co-author Shannon Barber-Meyer, formerly with Pacific Whale Foundation, told Mongabay in a video call. The researchers found the Hawaiian humpback whale population declined by 37% between the 2014-2015 breeding season and the 2021-2022 season. Adult survival rates also fell sharply. Before the heatwave, roughly 99% of adult whales survived year over year, but during the heatwave, adult survival was estimated at just 68%. “It’s a very precipitous drop, and that’s not something you normally see in adult survival of long-lived mammals,” Barber-Meyer said. During the heatwave, researchers documented an unusual mortality event…This article was originally published on Mongabay
items.titleTR: Marine heatwave likely caused sharp decline in Hawaiian humpback whales, study finds

items.descriptionTR:
Africa and the EU are leading a push for COP31 to deliver a roadmap that lays out measures to protect fast-warming oceans
The post As marine heat breaks records, countries seek ocean roadmap at COP31 appeared first on Climate Home News.
With record-breaking ocean temperatures weakening the world’s largest carbon sink, a group of countries is pushing for the UN COP31 summit to deliver meaningful commitments to protect marine ecosystems. Yet this effort could be hobbled by a shrinking pool of climate finance, experts warn.
While discussions on oceans at UN climate talks have so far been limited to annual informal dialogues on the sidelines, African countries, the European Union, some Latin American nations and small island states have launched a bid for COP31 to incorporate ocean protection measures into “negotiated decisions”.
COP31 co-presidents Türkiye and Australia have responded to this call and are working with interested countries on a voluntary ocean roadmap, described as a “concise action plan” and expected to include regional and international steps to integrate measures to safeguard the planet’s ocean and climate.
	•	￼   Aug 20, 2026  Clean Energy Frontier   China keeps Indonesia’s battery dream afloat but future less certain Chinese capital and technology turned Indonesia into the world’s top nickel supplier, but its dependence on China and the rise of nickel-free batteries could upset its battery ecosystem plans  Read more    
	•	￼   Aug 14, 2026  News   South Africa’s top court blocks Shell’s offshore oil exploration right Constitutional Court rules that Shell and its partners failed to consult affected communities and did not properly consider environmental risks  Read more    
	•	￼   Aug 17, 2026  Energy   “Dangerous consequences” – how AI’s climate framing lets Big Tech off the hook Former Microsoft manager Holly Alpine explains why AI’s climate danger isn’t just data centres but also its unchecked use across the fossil fuel industry  Read more    
	•	
At a meeting in Türkiye in September, which plans to convene more than 25 ministers from Asia-Pacific, Africa, Europe and Latin America, governments will consider how to incorporate the recommendations of the informal UN ocean dialogues into global climate policy, according to the Turkish co-presidency.
Whitney Berry, associate director of climate policy at the nonprofit Ocean Conservancy, said that even an informal “multi-year” plan, instead of a negotiated roadmap, could help guide the ocean dialogues series in the UN climate process towards more concrete results.
“If this plan informed the following dialogues and made sure they were aligned with the Paris [Agreement] ambition cycle, including opportunities like the Global Stocktake, we’d have such a strengthened opportunity for ocean integration,” she said.
The upcoming stocktake – an international assessment of countries’ climate policies that takes place every five years and will culminate at COP33 in 2028 – presents a “huge opportunity” to turn fragmented actions into a “globally recognised evidence base” that can inform the next round of climate plans, Berry added.
Addressing rocketing ocean temperatures
Influenced by this year’s projected “super El Niño” on top of climate heating, the world’s oceans have experienced the warmest July on record, according to both EU and US monitoring data. Scientists are warning of severe mass die-offs of key species like corals, sponges and macro-algae.
John Bruno, a marine ecologist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, told journalists in a briefing that some organisms like coral reefs can only tolerate an increase of about 1 degree Celsius before they start experiencing heath declines. In some seas like the Mediterranean, marine heatwaves have caused temperature increases of up to 6C.
￼
As climate pressure mounts on ocean systems, a group of more than 150 top scientists has called on the COP31 Turkish and Australian presidencies to urgently “integrate ocean priorities into negotiation texts on mitigation, adaptation, and finance”.
They also urged world leaders to issue a “clear political declaration and finance outcomes” on ocean-based climate solutions at the World Leaders Summit, a two-day event during COP where heads of states give speeches laying out their climate priorities.
Measures to protect marine ecosystems have gathered more attention in recent years, as 90% of national climate plans submitted last year included at least one ocean-based target, compared to 62% in 2015. But countries have faced challenges implementing these commitments due to finance and governance constraints, according to a paper published in June by the World Resources Institute (WRI).
Most of the current targets focus on protecting marine areas, but have so far lacked commitments to reduce emissions produced at sea, for example through offshore wind or cleaner maritime transport.
Will the world’s drying lands get relief from COP17 in Mongolia?
Rethinking ocean negotiations at COP
At COP26 in Glasgow in 2021, countries agreed to “integrate and strengthen ocean-based action” across climate negotiations, which led to the creation of a yearly informal Ocean and Climate Dialogue. This dialogue does not produce a negotiated agreement like other parts of the COP.
The dialogue’s informal nature is both an advantage and a challenge, said Jonathan Baines, ocean programme manager at WRI. It provides a more flexible space than formal negotiations and has helped raise the ambition of countries’ climate plans, but COP presidencies have not fully incorporated its outcomes into the official climate talks, he said.
After five years of holding this dialogue at the mid-year climate negotiations in Bonn, countries called for more tangible outcomes in their submissions to this year’s Ocean and Climate Change Dialogue in June. Some proposed the creation of a roadmap to guide discussions on specific topics and feed them into the formal COP negotiations.
In their submission, the African Group of Negotiators called for a “structured, multi-year roadmap” aligned with the next Global Stocktake. The EU also backed this roadmap proposal, while Pacific islands and some Latin American countries supported incorporating the dialogue outcomes into the negotiations without specifically endorsing the roadmap initiative.
As part of a preparatory event before COP31 focused on oceans, Türkiye has confirmed to Climate Home News plans for a Blue COP31 roadmap, which will be discussed by the ministers attending the gathering in September.
“In essence, this programme is designed to ensure that the ocean is no longer the missing link in climate action, but rather the driving force behind a more resilient, sustainable, and prosperous future for all coastal communities,” Türkiye’s COP31 presidency said in a written comment.
￼
Co-facilitators of the Ocean and Climate Change dialogue Ulrik Lenaerts from Belgium and Sivendra Michael from Fiji. (Photo: IISD/ENB/Maja Schmidt-Thomé)
Opposition emerges to “additional burdens”
Some regional groups have already started presenting their priorities publicly, with small island nations calling for more finance, ocean-based renewable energy and bolstering regional research institutes.
African diplomats said “the core problem remains translating these paper commitments into real-world, on-the-ground implementation” and noted that while countries in the region have strengthened their climate plans, “the support required to implement these commitments has not kept pace”.
“The truth is that ambition without implementation is an illusion,” the African submission reads, adding that nearly half of all ocean-related commitments in national climate plans are “strictly conditional on external support”.
This year’s Ocean and Climate Dialogue, chaired by Fiji and Belgium, urged countries to discuss ways of “transitioning away from fossil fuels”, which generated pushback from big fossil fuel-producing and consuming countries who said they would not accept this as a negotiated agreement.
Both the group of Arab nations and India, meanwhile, warned against “imposing additional burdens” on developing countries and rejected a dialogue with “prescriptive expectations”.
The Arab group submission said its members oppose “any report that explicitly or implicitly targets specific energy sources, advocates sectoral restrictions, or fails to adequately reflect different national circumstances, development priorities, and energy security considerations”. This is a thinly veiled reference to singling out fossil fuels within the discussions.
New coal mine openings slow as East Asian demand plateaus
Climate finance constraints
While developing countries are already seeking more funding to implement ocean-based conservation, carbon storage and clean energy measures, experts said this will be a “difficult discussion” at COP31, as developed countries will arrive in Antalya with shrinking aid budgets.
Historically, ocean-related finance has accounted for only a small share of overseas development assistance (ODA), fluctuating between 0.8% and 1.4% of the total, according to data from the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
Berry of the Ocean Conservancy said one opportunity to “grow the pie” of available climate funds will come at a meeting of the UN climate convention’s Standing Committee on Finance, which this year will be held in September in Sydney and will concentrate on financing water systems and the ocean.
“We haven’t had a focused conversation on ocean climate finance before from the UN climate process,” she said. “If they can clarify those financing pathways specific to ocean climate action and help provide the necessary support for countries to translate commitments into projects, that will be a real benefit.”
items.titleTR: As marine heat breaks records, countries seek ocean roadmap at COP31

slots.packetSpot:
In the global ocean outside the polar regions, the highest average sea surface temperatures recorded for the same dates were seen for 100 days between 2 June and 10 September. According to data from Climate Reanalyzer, overseen by the University of Maine’s Climate Change Institute and drawing on NOAA observations, this continuity had not previously been seen in records kept since 1982. Copernicus measured 21.10°C on 22 August, while Climate Reanalyzer reported that the average rose to 21.18°C between 22 and 27 August.

Zachary Labe of Climate Central said the warmth is part of the long-term trend of human-caused climate change, while the strengthening El Niño could intensify the warming. Effects on marine ecosystems, weather events, fisheries, tourism and the lives of coastal communities stand out, while the decline of Hawaii’s humpback whales linked to the 2013–16 marine heatwave in the Northeast Pacific emerges as one concrete example of this vulnerability.

Research based on more than 27,000 photographs from Happywhale found that Hawaii’s humpback whale population declined by 37% between the 2014–15 breeding season and the 2021–22 period. Researchers say the heatwave’s effects on krill and small fish may have played a role in this decline, while the possibility that some whales may have migrated to other regions remains. The estimated adult survival rate fell from about 99% before the heatwave to 68% during this period; the final estimate points to roughly 5,000 fewer humpback whales.

Under this pressure, African countries, the European Union, some Latin American countries and small island states want ocean-protection measures to be included in decisions negotiated at COP31. COP31 co-chairs Türkiye and Australia are working with the relevant countries on a voluntary ocean roadmap. But implementation and financing remain contentious: according to OECD data, ocean-related funding has historically accounted for only 0.8%–1.4% of overseas development assistance.

The race to study the North Water between Canada and Greenland before it changes has led to a bold plan for an Inuit-run protected area
Electric-blue meltwater sprays up under Terry Noah’s snowmobile as he races across sea ice extending out from Canada’s northernmost public community: Grise Fiord in Nunavut, a hamlet of 144 people closer to Murmansk in Russia than the Canadian city of Toronto. The bay’s cliffs loom higher and higher like stone icebergs as he approaches his destination across the bay.
Noah pulls his sled carefully over a seal’s breathing hole, about the circumference of a basketball. Using a custom-made winch, he lowers a submersible instrument into the sea below the ice.
items.titleTR: The place that never freezes: the Arctic habitat where global heating threatens more ice, not less

slots.packetSpot:
Warming is not changing ice-shaped environments in the same way. In Sweden, Kebnekaise's ice-covered southern peak fell by 10 centimetres in one year, according to official measurements; it has lost about 30 metres since 1951. By contrast, the ice-free northern peak, measured at 2,096.8 metres above sea level, remained Sweden's highest point for the eighth consecutive year, while the southern peak was measured at 2,088.3 metres.

In East Africa, climate assessments are reported to project that the equatorial glaciers on Mount Kenya, Kilimanjaro and the Rwenzori Mountains will disappear entirely within three to five years. The ice cover on Mount Kenya is reported to have declined by 96 percent over 115 years, while the region's total glacier area is said to have shrunk by 40 to 60 percent over the past decade. Climate scientist Rainer Prinz explains the main cause of the retreat as a decline in annual snowfall, altered by Indian Ocean sea-surface patterns linked to global warming.

In North Water between Canada and Greenland, however, the risk may be not less but more sea ice. The frequent failure of an ice arch to form in Nares Strait can allow sea ice from the Arctic Ocean to cover the polynya that remains open year-round. Scientist David Harning says the loss of the ice bridge could lead to a sharp decline in the polynya's productivity. Canada has designated the Sarvarjuaq marine protected area on its side; a proposal for a protected area under Inuit governance, to be jointly managed by Canada and Greenland, remains under consideration. Terry Noah and researchers are collecting data to monitor the changing waters.

Conservationists say the agency’s new priorities are the latest signal from an administration intent on deregulating and defunding the agency. They warn that deregulation will open the door to overfishing and do lasting harm to ecosystems that support ocean health and sustain fisheries. “If we are reducing regulations and overfishing some really valuable fisheries this year or next year, it may take years for those fisheries to get back on track to healthy [stock] levels,” Reggie Paros, senior director of public affairs at the New York-based NGO Environmental Defense Fund, told Mongabay by phone. “The outcomes we would see on the water would be particularly damaging.” A pile of young Atlantic sea scallops (Placopecten magellanicus) on the deck of the New Bedford, Massachusetts-based fishing vessel Selje, collected during a NOAA survey to help track scallop abundance, distribution, ages, lengths, weights, sex, maturity and disease presence.
