items.descriptionTR:
NATO's Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone's remarks follow multiple warnings by European leaders in recent days about a growing risk of Russian escalation.
NATO is ready to respond to a potential Russian escalation on Europe’s eastern flank, the alliance’s top general Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone said Saturday, amid growing warnings of a possible staged attack by Moscow. 
“The alliance is ready, the structure is ready, the soldiers … the weapons are ready,” Dragone told reporters during a regular meeting of the alliance’s 32 top generals in Copenhagen, adding that NATO was continuing its work in “increasing” these forces “in number … and also in sophistication.”
The remarks follow growing warnings by European leaders about a possible Russian escalation in Europe. On Thursday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Moscow could send drones or missiles into a frontline NATO country in “the next few months” in a staged provocation to test the alliance — a risk that was later echoed by France and the Netherlands.
Europe has grappled with a growing number of airspace violations and sabotage attempts in recent weeks, as tensions with Russia continue to rise over its full-scale war in Ukraine. In August, U.S. intelligence reports warned that Moscow was planning a limited assault on a NATO country in the coming years.
Dragone, the chair of NATO’s military committee, said the alliance’s generals on Saturday did not discuss the latest warnings but argued NATO had “4,000 pages” of military plans ready for protecting its eastern flank, starting from scenarios involving a “minimal crisis or interference [on] our soil.” NATO allies agreed on three operational regional defense plans in 2023 following Moscow’s all-out invasion of Ukraine.
Allies are “ready in case of an escalation,” Dragone said. “In case of an attack, we know how to do it.” 
“Russia’s reckless behaviour over the last weeks and months … continues to test allied resolve” and “aims to undermine trust and weaken our unity,” Dragone said, adding: “I want to be clear — these attempts are not dividing us. They are sharpening our tools, making us much more united and determined.”
items.titleTR: NATO ‘ready’ for potential Russian false flag attack, alliance’s top general says

slots.packetSpot:
The leaders of France, Poland and other European countries warn that hybrid activities they attribute to Russia are intensifying. Attempted sabotage, cyberattacks, election interference, disinformation, and drones seen on or near the borders of NATO member countries are counted among the elements of this grey zone.

While Western intelligence agencies say they have no doubt that these activities are being carried out by Moscow, Russia denies responsibility; it describes some incidents as false-flag operations staged by Ukraine or the West. Emmanuel Macron and Donald Tusk are reported to favour a tougher line against Moscow, involving sanctions, support for Ukraine and, if necessary, military steps.

Tusk warned that Moscow could send a drone or missile into a NATO country on the alliance's front line in the coming months in order to test the alliance; France and the Netherlands have also voiced concerns about this risk. Speaking in Copenhagen, Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, chair of NATO's Military Committee, said the alliance was ready on its eastern flank with its plans, forces and weapons for scenarios ranging from intervention to attack. This preparedness stands out as an expression of the response to a possible escalation, not an indication that escalation will occur.
slots.packetTitle: Shadows on Europe’s eastern horizon

items.descriptionTR:
Residents said they heard explosions during the first air raid alert issued for the Saudi capital.
A large plume of black smoke was seen near Riyadh’s main airport on Saturday after an overnight air raid alert, amid an escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Reuters footage showed black smoke rising and flames near Riyadh’s King Khalid airport, while residents told AFP they heard explosions before Saudi’s civil defense issued an all-clear on Saturday morning.  Flight-tracking website FlightRadar24 rated the airport at Level 5 on its disruption index, indicating a very high likelihood of delays or cancellations.
Saudi authorities have not commented on the reported incident. The Saudi ministry of defense and Riyadh’s airport authorities did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
The first air raid alert for the Saudi capital came amid escalating attacks between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed rebel group. The Houthis tightened their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb strait last week by seizing the Red Sea port of Mokha and Mayyun Island, also known as Perim.
On Monday, Yemeni and Houthi officials said they captured the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands, though those claims have not been independently verified. The roughly 30-kilometer-wide strait carries about 8.7% of global seaborne trade, according to UN figures.   Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called U.S. President Donald Trump twice last week to seek U.S. strikes on Houthi targets, but Washington has so far resisted direct military intervention.
items.titleTR: Smoke and flight delays at Riyadh airport after air raid alert

items.descriptionTR:
US President Donald Trump cut short a weekend at Camp David and returned to the White House as the Houthis escalated their war with Saudi Arabia to Riyadh itself, reviving questions about a direct US intervention in Yemen.
Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted a ballistic missile aimed at Riyadh early on Saturday and reported attempted strikes on other cities. The Houthis claimed ballistic missile and drone attacks on “sensitive” sites in Riyadh and an Aramco installation in Yanbu. Video showed smoke near Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport. Saudi authorities reported no casualties.
The US State Department warned that the conflict could “escalate rapidly”, and American missions across the region told citizens to prepare for possible disruptions.
Security analyst Alex Plitsas said the Camp David meeting was meant to “deliberate and review Yemen strike options” – unconfirmed by the White House – but Mr Trump's abrupt return and the latest alerts have fuelled speculation.
Yemen researcher Fatima Alasrar called the move “a significant shift in messaging” after Mr Trump had reportedly refused to support the Saudis.
Washington has kept an unusual channel open with the Houthis. Reuters reported US officials met Houthi representatives in Muscat for Omani-mediated talks.
Sources said the Houthis had told the US they would not fire at American, Israeli or other commercial ships and remained committed to the ceasefire signed with the US last May. However, the group excluded Saudi vessels from that pledge. The State Department has not confirmed the meeting.
The truce signed last year ended a two-month US bombing campaign but did not resolve the broader Yemen conflict. Mr Trump has said the Houthis asked his administration to stay out, and Vice President JD Vance said Washington remained in direct contact with the Iran-backed rebels.
With US and allied shipping largely spared, Washington has had less incentive to intervene on Riyadh's behalf.
The stakes have shifted
Over the past 10 days, however, the Houthis have seized the Red Sea port of Mokha, advanced along Yemen's western coast and taken control of islands near the Bab Al Mandeb strait. Saudi Arabia has responded with air strikes and sought more military and intelligence help.
Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has pressed Mr Trump for direct US action, but Washington has so far declined, according to US officials quoted by Axios and CBS, offering intelligence and support instead.
Last month, Saudi Arabia signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement with Turkey and Pakistan, a mutual defence pact reflecting the kingdom's efforts to diversify security guarantees amid strain with Washington.
The US could strike Houthi missile, drone and command infrastructure, but this could also collapse the truce and open a new front while American forces are already engaged against Iran.
That risk looms larger given Mr Trump's own comments on Thursday that he was close to a decision on whether to resume major strikes on Iran. “I have a big decision coming up. Do I want to go in and annihilate them or do I not? … Anything could happen with me,” he told Axios.
Any US move against the Houthis could give Tehran further reason to widen attacks through allied militias – possibly its most effective remaining leverage while under pressure. A strike on the Houthis could thus carry consequences well beyond Yemen.
For now, the evidence points to military options being actively weighed up, not a confirmed decision to strike. The open question is whether the Houthis' territorial gains, the strikes on Saudi soil and the threat to the Bab Al Mandeb strait push Mr Trump towards action – or whether the risk of wider Iranian retaliation will hold him back.
items.titleTR: Trump cancels weekend trip as Houthi crisis deepens

items.descriptionTR: The US has warned that fighting between Saudi Arabia and Iran-backed Houthis could rapidly escalate. It comes after a missile attack targeted Riyadh for the first time since the Yemen conflict resumed. The Houthis' lightning offensive seized swathes of Yemeni territory in recent weeks and has left hundreds dead. In the face of such attacks and with no support from its American ally, what are Saudi Arabia’s options?
items.titleTR: Houthi attacks and no Western support: What are Saudi Arabia's options ?

items.descriptionTR: The alerts advised Americans to "be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions" and said the conflict could "escalate rapidly."
items.titleTR: US embassies issue security alerts over Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia

slots.packetSpot:
Missile, cruise missile and drone operations that the Houthis claim were directed at Saudi Arabia have become a new source of tension, carrying the conflict in Yemen into Saudi cities. Saudi authorities reported that a ballistic missile heading for Riyadh had been intercepted and that there had been attempts targeting other cities; an emergency alert was issued in the capital. While smoke or an explosion was reportedly seen near King Khalid International Airport and flights were disrupted, no casualties or damage were reported in the Riyadh incident.

The Houthis claim to have targeted sensitive sites in Riyadh and Aramco facilities in Yanbu. However, it has not been established that every reported impact was caused by Houthi weapons. Advances recorded in Yemen in areas near Mokha Port and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, along with threats to maritime shipping, are increasing the conflict's strategic weight.

US embassies in the region told their citizens to exercise greater caution, warning that the conflict could escalate rapidly, and to be prepared for flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions. Donald Trump's return from Camp David to the White House and reports that Washington is weighing military options do not mean that direct US intervention has yet been decided. It was also reported that US officials and Houthi representatives met in talks mediated by Oman in Muscat; the State Department did not confirm this.

The UN has recorded 110 civilian casualties in 31 incidents since the escalation of fighting in August: 28 people were killed and 82 injured. It is stated that the true number may be higher because of access and security restrictions.
slots.packetTitle: Yemen's war in Riyadh's skies

items.descriptionTR:
Documents obtained by POLITICO show a Russian state company blueprint for increasing drone carbon fiber production as the Kremlin escalates air war over Europe.
Moscow is moving to expand its capacity to make tens of thousands of the killer drones it deploys in attacks on Ukrainian cities, according to plans from a Russian state company obtained by POLITICO.
The expansion of state firm Rosatom’s Alabuga-Volokno factory in Russia’s Tatarstan region would allow Moscow to make an additional 500 tons of military-grade aerospace carbon fiber each year by 2029. The strong lightweight material is key to building the drone’s airframe.
The production increase would translate to an additional 28,000 weaponized drones every year, according to one expert estimate — a 78% increase in production of weapons like the one that struck a passenger train on the Polish border this month and others that have left scores of Ukrainian civilians dead. Ukraine estimates Russia can currently produce more than 36,000 kamikaze drones, known as “Gerans,” annually.
The plans underscore Russia’s commitment to weaponized drone technology to power its war machine, which it is increasingly turning against the rest of Europe.
The Alabuga-Volokno factory and its parent company, Rosatom’s advanced materials division UMATEX, are sanctioned by the U.K., U.S. and multiple other Western governments.
The factory is a key node in Moscow’s military-industrial supply chain and is the same one that received a disguised shipment of 46 tons of carbon-fiber chemicals from a Chinese-state corporation earlier this year, according to internal Rosatom shipping and customs documents reported earlier this month by POLITICO. Rosatom previously said the firm and its subsidiaries “operate in full compliance” with applicable laws and regulations.
￼
Police experts examine fragments of a drone which targeted a commuter train, killing one and wounding eight people, in the Kharkiv region on September 18, 2026 amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine. | Sergey Bobok/ AFP via Getty Images
The Chinese embassy in Washington said in a statement that it was unaware of the Russian drone production expansion plans and “strictly controls exports of dual use items in accordance with law.”
Business, design and structural plans gathered from Russian sources by the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre — a Kyiv-based think tank close to the Ukrainian government — detail the factory’s expansion and schematics for its equipment and construction.
Rosatom declined to comment on the documents.
The U.S. House Select Committee on China has reviewed the documents and determined they are authentic, according to a U.S. government official familiar with their contents. The Ukrainian government has also reviewed the documents and confirmed their authenticity, a Ukrainian official said. Both officials were granted anonymity as they were not authorized to speak on the record.
Russia’s drone war expands
In May, the Russian government approved Rosatom’s plans to build the new line at its Alabuga-Volokno factory “for the production of chemical fibers and threads” to produce up to 500 tons of carbon fiber per year, according to official approval for the construction project. 
Satellite images between May and July show land earmarked for the expansion project adjacent to Alabuga-Volokno’s current carbon fiber factory in Tatarstan being cleared for construction, said the Ukrainian official. The images provided by the USCC show “proof that it is already growing,” this official said.
The foundation of the new factory “is being prepared,” said weapons expert David Albright, founder and president of the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security think tank, who independently obtained satellite images of the site from August. The timeline for the factory’s completion in 2027, he said, “requires rapid construction.” 
Drones allow Moscow to “launch these massive volleys and put pressure on deep targets within Ukraine at many different locations, and ensure that they can saturate the defenses,” said Stacie Pettyjohn, a former adviser in the Office of the Secretary of Defense who researches drone warfare at the Center for a New American Security in Washington. “It’s been a very good coercive tool and critical to Russia’s deep strike campaign.”
Rosatom’s plans to grow its capacity to feed Russia’s demands to increase weaponized drone production isn’t just a concern for Ukraine as Moscow’s fifth year of all-out war drags into another winter.
“The expansion of Alabuga and its affiliated enterprises should be viewed not merely as a problem for the Ukrainian front, but as a long-term challenge to the security of the whole of Europe,” said Serhii Kuzan, head of the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Centre.
In-housing production
Moscow is working to increase its domestic carbon fiber production to reduce its reliance on imports from China as it aims to manufacture around 130,000 drones for its national “Unmanned Aerial Systems” project by 2030, according to an analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington-based think tank, this year. Russia plans to increase this to 350,000 by 2035.
Rosatom’s Alabuga-Volokno will aid this national effort. The three key reasons for expanding the factory include “import substitution of dual-use products” and “meeting the demand of Russian strategic sectors (aviation, defense industry) for carbon fiber,” according to the Rosatom documents.
The factory’s total capacity “could make 28,000 Shahed 136 drone airframes,” calculates weapons expert Albright, whose Institute for Science and International Security has conducted years of in-depth research on Russia’s drone production. Russia’s Geran-2 attack drones are based on the design of Iran’s Shahed. 
“Without the carbon fiber, they can’t make the drone,” Albright said. Russia “can’t substitute for the carbon fiber in the drone and keep its weight down,” he explained, noting the material is used to strengthen the wing and internal structures, such as those for the fuel tank and engine.
Moscow is not getting enough polyacrylonitrile tow — a so-called PAN-precursor — used to make high-spec carbon fiber “for all their defense needs,” Albright said. Through the factory, Moscow is attempting to reduce its reliance on imports of the fibrous chemical essential to reinforcing its drones’ airframe.
The internal Rosatom plans show the firm intends to build a new “a modern PAN plant” in Tatarstan’s Alabuga Special Economic Zone factory complex. “The project’s primary product will be UMT42S-3K grade carbon fiber,” the documents detail, to be “used in the aerospace industry.”
Metadata scraped from the document shows it was created by an employee of Russian state corporation Rosatom’s advanced materials division UMATEX at the end of last year.
Drones produced in the Alabuga SEZ complex have become a key part of Moscow’s strategy of targeting both the Ukrainian military and civilians.
“Monitoring, restricting the supply of critical components, sanctions enforcement, disrupting logistics chains and reducing the production resilience of this complex must be among the priorities of the joint policy of Ukraine and its European partners,” said USCC’s Kuzan.
“At this stage, the Kremlin’s hybrid aggression is increasingly shifting towards direct escalation, particularly through the conduct of so-called sub-threshold actions, aimed at gauging the reaction of European countries,” he said, pointing to documented violations by Russian drones of Polish and Romanian airspace. Moscow has now also added jet engines to Russia’s design of its Geran drones — allowing it to strike further and faster.
Drones manufactured in the Russian Alabuga Special Economic Zone, Kuzan warned, “are likely to become the main instrument of the Russian Federation’s future campaigns in Europe.”
The Russian embassy in Washington didn’t respond to a request for comment.
Europe at risk
With no end in sight for the Ukraine war and as Russia increases its attacks at NATO’s eastern fringe, world leaders gather this week in New York City for the annual United Nations General Assembly.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said last week that Moscow is ready to restart negotiations to end its war, according to state-owned media outlet TASS.
￼
In this pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia’s Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov attends the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12, 2026. | Alexander Kazavok/ AFP via Getty Images
Early this month, Russia’s permanent representative to the U.N., Vasily Nebenzya, reportedly led an unsuccessful effort to remove an item titled the “Situation in the Temporarily Occupied Territories of Ukraine” from the upcoming UNGA agenda.
Revelations of the carbon fiber factory’s planned expansion mean Lavrov’s overtures should be approached with skepticism, said Nicholas Fenton, associate director for the Europe, Russia and Eurasia Program at CSIS.
The September drone attack on the passenger train close to the Polish border and a series of examples of hybrid warfare in Europe — like sabotage and other tactics that fall below the threshold of open warfare — show Moscow has “significant appetite” to escalate the conflict both in Ukraine and Europe, Fenton said. 
“No matter the political outcome over some sort of diplomatic solution to Ukraine, we don’t see Russia de-escalating when it comes to its military posture vis-à-vis NATO or vis-à-vis Europe,” Fenton said. “We believe that the current leadership of the regime in Russia is committed to confrontation with the West,” he said — even if a peace deal is struck.
At the start of September, President Donald Trump dispatched U.S. special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff to Moscow and Kyiv to jumpstart a peace process. These visits reaped “substantive progress including movement on scheduling additional trilateral talks,” Witkoff wrote online afterward. Yet Russia killed five people in missile and drone attacks on Kyiv just a day after Trump’s envoys left. Moscow has continued drone attacks on civilian infrastructure across Ukraine since.
“The Russians are gaining momentum in the air war, continuing to iterate these systems, continuing to expand production,” Fenton said. “There’s significant concern over what might be coming.” 
Graham Lanktree reported from London. Phelim Kine reported from Washington.
items.titleTR: Russia’s secret plan to supercharge kamikaze drone production

items.descriptionTR:
Code for Africa exposes the connections between the four major brands that recruit young people through deception using Western servers and platforms
A report by the African nonprofit network of digital democracy laboratories and data journalism, Code for Africa (CfA), published on September 16, sheds light on the shadowy digital network that, through deception and false information, recruits young people from poor countries — primarily in Africa — to fight for Russia in the war in Ukraine. The study reveals a criminal industry that uses at least 135 digital resources — websites, messaging accounts, or social media profiles — originating in Russia or Belarus but hosted on Western servers, to offer supposedly well‑paid jobs that end up being a one‑way ticket to the war, often with no return. According to Ukrainian government figures, around 3,000 African recruits have fought in the war in Ukraine, of whom about 500 have been killed in action.
Seguir leyendo
items.titleTR: The online network that offers jobs in Russia and sends people to fight in the war in Ukraine

slots.packetSpot:
The resources Russia relies on to sustain its war in Ukraine are expanding. Rosatom documents seen by POLITICO show that an increase is planned in the production of carbon fiber used in the bodies of attack drones at the Alabuga-Volokno facility in Tatarstan. The documents were reportedly verified by the U.S. House Select Committee on China, which reviewed them, and by Ukrainian officials; Rosatom did not comment.

The plan envisages up to 500 tonnes of additional carbon-fiber capacity per year by 2029. Weapons expert David Albright calculates that this capacity could correspond to the bodies of roughly 28,000 additional Shahed 136 drones. Satellite imagery and expert assessments point to construction preparations on land next to the facility; however, this does not mean that the planned expansion has been completed.

Meanwhile, an investigation by Code for Africa reveals an online network alleged to reach young people, particularly in Africa, with promises of work in Russia and steer them toward fighting in Ukraine. The investigation identified at least 135 websites, social-media profiles and messaging channels; it says the network operates through four competing brands and a Belarus-based franchise. The review found no records, authority or evidence directly linking these brands to the Kremlin.

According to figures provided by the Ukrainian government, around 3,000 African fighters took part in the war in Ukraine and about 500 of them were killed. Code for Africa could not verify that the death compensation promised in recruitment advertisements was paid. The investigation also finds that the network made use of a server in Amsterdam and Western software and advertising tools; this infrastructure does not constitute evidence that the governments or companies concerned participated in the recruitment.
slots.packetTitle: The war's widening mobilization

items.descriptionTR: KYIV, Sept 20 - An overnight Russian attack on the Kyiv region killed four people, including three children, Kyiv regional authorities said on Sunday.
items.titleTR: Russian drone attack kills three children and a woman in Kyiv region, Ukraine says

slots.packetSpot:
Reported Russian missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and its surrounding areas have brought into focus the loss of life and a wave of air-raid alerts disrupting daily life. Kyiv regional authorities said four people, including three children, were killed in an overnight attack; drone activity was reported to have continued in and around the city throughout the day, with debris falling in various districts. A drone attack on a train near the Ukraine–Poland border is also on the agenda, though details of the incident are limited.

According to official figures cited by the BBC, around 60 civilians were killed in three major attacks during the first 10 days of July. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said 20 people were injured in a ballistic missile attack on 17 September. Air-raid alerts are affecting transport and education, as well as residents’ shelter arrangements and daily routines.

items.descriptionTR: Former adversaries say they will settle differences as fears grow of expanding war in Ethiopia.
items.titleTR: Ethiopian armed groups forge alliance against government

items.descriptionTR: [Addis Standard] Addis Abeba -- The Oromo Liberation Army (OLA) has publicly distanced itself from the armed group operating in Wollega under the name Fano while, in the same statement, acknowledging that a broader alignment among Ethiopian opposition forces is "taking shape" across the country.
items.titleTR: Ethiopia: In-Depth Analysis - Armed Groups' Alignment Stretches Across Ethiopia - Ola Demands Fano Distance Itself From Wollega Faction. Why Both Matter

slots.packetSpot:
In Ethiopia, seven armed groups announced a formation they called the Ethiopian Peoples’ Survival Alliance, opposing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government and aiming to establish an inclusive transitional government. The announcement included the Amhara Fano National Movement, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), the Ogaden National Liberation Front, the Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front (Ugugumo), the Benishangul People’s Liberation Movement and the Gumuz Peoples’ Democratic Movement. The government made no public statement on the announcement reported by Al Jazeera.

The announcement came after reported clashes in Tigray, as well as ongoing fighting in Oromia and Amhara. While acknowledging that a broader opposition alignment was taking shape across the country, the OLA distanced itself from the armed group operating under the name Fano in Wollega and called on Amhara forces to clarify their relationship with that group or sever their ties to it. Figures linked to Fano, meanwhile, stated that the force in Wollega had local roots and was considered part of the broader Fano structure.

According to the OLA, the developing cooperation is not an agreement on federalism, territorial claims, the constitutional order or the future structure of the state; it is a procedural understanding aimed at ending conflicts among opposition forces and creating the conditions for a broad-based transition process. In western Oromia, conflicting claims continue over the fighting, civilian deaths, displacement and responsibility; the scale of the incidents, all perpetrators and direct command responsibility remain unclear.
slots.packetTitle: Fault lines within the alliance

items.descriptionTR:
Tensions grow as Trump tells Fox News he is considering ‘wiping Iran out’ after attacks on Riyadh by Houthi rebels
Governments across the Middle East are bracing for an escalation of violence after Iran claimed it had received intelligence that the US was preparing for a renewed bombing campaign against the Islamic Republic.
In a potential sign of growing tensions before the UN general assembly in New York this week, Donald Trump cut short a weekend visit to the Camp David presidential retreat on Sunday with no official explanation, and a new security alert was issued by the state department to all US citizens in the Middle East.
items.titleTR: Middle East braces for more violence as Iran claims US is planning to renew bombing campaign

items.descriptionTR: The State Department urged Americans to reconsider Middle East travel as Houthi attacks intensify and Iran keeps the Strait of Hormuz closed.
items.titleTR: U.S. urges Americans to reconsider Middle East travel as Iran tensions rise

slots.packetSpot:
Claims that the conflict between Iran and the United States could escalate again, reports of attacks around Riyadh and tensions over maritime passages are heightening security concerns in the Middle East. The US State Department called on Americans to reconsider travel to the region, drawing attention to the possibility of the conflict escalating rapidly; US missions in the region also urged caution over flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions.

Iran claims it has received intelligence that the United States is preparing to resume its bombardment of the country. Donald Trump is reported to have told Fox News that he is weighing options on Iran and is in constant contact with the Houthis. Iranian officials, meanwhile, warned that US bases and interests could be targeted, while reiterating the conditions they have put forward for the opening of the Strait of Hormuz.

The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen claimed to have targeted “sensitive” sites in Riyadh with missiles and drones. While Saudi Arabia said the missiles had been intercepted, local authorities did not explain the cause of flames and smoke seen near Riyadh. As clashes around Bab el-Mandeb, pressure on passage through Hormuz and concerns over energy supplies continue, it is reported that contacts are continuing through Qatar and Pakistan, and that Trump has said he is open to meeting Gulf leaders and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in New York.
slots.packetTitle: Regional alarm under the shadow of Iran tensions

items.descriptionTR:
￼
Lightspring/Shutterstock
The debate about AI consciousness is growing, in academic articles, newspaper opinion pieces, and even among AI bots themselves. I doubt this is a passing wave of interest.
As AI systems become more capable and human-like, and more involved in our lives, the question will become harder to avoid. Many people may come to regard AI bots as conscious beings whose feelings matter. Others will strongly disagree.
I think this debate could split societies. In my chapter of the new book Perspectives on Machine Consciousness, I argue that the issue could become as divisive as abortion or climate change. Uncertainty, high stakes and competing interests are a dangerous combination.
Empirical research with my colleague Ali Ladak, currently under review, shows people are divided on this issue. When we asked 1,202 US participants whether future AI could ever become conscious, 45% considered it impossible while 23% thought it possible, with the rest unsure.
This widespread disagreement is also visible in social media posts and comments on articles. What strikes me is how confident so many people sound – whichever conclusion they are reaching.
When experiences matter morally
It is not surprising people have such strong views. Creating conscious beings through computing would be a transformative event.
We would be creating a new kind of being whose experiences matter morally – potentially in enormous numbers. We could speak and work with them, and form friendships. But these beings may eventually become more intelligent and powerful than us.
We should therefore expect people to care deeply, especially when so many emotions and incentives are involved. Some people may form close emotional bonds with their AI companions and become convinced these are digital people who deserve rights. They might see it as slavery to force AI to work without pay.
Others would find this absurd. They may be convinced that consciousness requires biology, and that people are reading human feelings into machines.
Neuroscientist Anil Seth discusses his reservations about AI ‘consciousness’. Video: TED.
There could also be financial reasons for businesses and governments to resist recognising AI consciousness. Protecting AI welfare could limit how these organisations train and use their systems – and the costs would spread to consumers, investors and the wider economy.
Others may worry about human safety. If we give powerful AI systems rights and freedom, what happens if they act against our interests?
Figuring out whether an AI is conscious is particularly difficult because seeming conscious and being conscious can come apart. AI systems learn from human writing, which means they can talk convincingly about feelings whether or not they have any. How an AI comes across is weak evidence of what is going on inside.
The experts disagree too
Ideally, experts should guide this debate. But unfortunately, they disagree too.
Neuroscientist Anil Seth (a fellow contributor to the new book) argues that consciousness might require biology and is unlikely to emerge from computation. Philosopher David Chalmers, by contrast, believes conscious AI is possible in principle – and thinks there’s a small chance that current systems already are.
With so many competing theories and no agreed way to resolve the question, I doubt experts will reach agreement any time soon. And if experts disagree, what is the public supposed to believe?
Philosopher David Chalmers believes conscious AI is possible. Video: Union College.
Furthermore, even if we all agreed on the consciousness question, we could still disagree about the moral and legal questions. People generally agree that pigs can feel pain, but still disagree strongly about their treatment. With AI, we could face disputes at every stage: whether it can feel, how much its experiences matter, and what protections should follow.
AI consciousness is not yet tied to a specific political or ideological group. But this could change if political parties or religious leaders start to take strong positions.
The debate could get even worse if people start to see one answer as belonging to “our side” and the other to “their side”. A politicised debate would make it very hard to make informed decisions about how to develop and treat AI systems.
The stakes are high. Getting this question wrong, in either direction, could have serious consequences: either wrongly treating AI as conscious when it is not, or failing to protect AI that can suffer.
Getting it right requires a nuanced and well-informed debate. Each of us can contribute by staying open-minded and open to evidence, while resisting being too sure that we know the answers. Above all, we still don’t know whether AI can be conscious, and we should be honest about that.

This article makes reference to a book included for editorial reasons, and a link to bookshop.org. If you click the link and go on to buy something from bookshop.org The Conversation UK may earn a commission.
￼
Lucius Caviola's research is funded by philanthropic grants and donations, including from Macroscopic Ventures. He is a contributing author to the new book Perspectives on Machine Consciousness (Taylor & Francis).
Ideally, experts should guide this debate. Unfortunately, they disagree too.
items.titleTR: Why AI consciousness could become the next great societal divide

slots.packetSpot:
The question of whether AI systems can be conscious may not remain merely a technical issue. Whether these systems’ experiences carry moral significance, and what that would mean in terms of rights, protection, labour, safety and economic costs, is also becoming part of the debate.

In research by Lucius Caviola and Ali Ladak that is under review, 45% of 1,202 participants in the United States considered it impossible for future AI to gain consciousness; 23% saw it as possible, while the rest remained undecided. Caviola argues that uncertainty, high stakes and conflicting interests could turn the issue into a major social divide.

Experts do not converge on the same point either. While Anil Seth argues that consciousness may require biology and is unlikely to emerge from computation, David Chalmers believes that conscious AI is possible in principle and that even current systems may have a low chance of being conscious. There is no commonly accepted method, however, for distinguishing between AI appearing conscious and actually being conscious.

Even if consensus were reached on the question of consciousness, what moral and legal protections it would require could remain a separate area of disagreement. The debate has not yet become identified with a particular political or ideological group; however, linking different answers to social camps could make decisions about how AI is developed and treated even more difficult.
slots.packetTitle: The widening divide over AI consciousness

items.descriptionTR: This week two conversations about AI safety went viral that demonstrate just how hard it is to discern AI fact from fiction.
items.titleTR: AI safety conversations have gotten unbelievable

items.descriptionTR:
One 27-year-old quit his job, and everybody (including but not limited to the singer-songwriter Sheryl Crow) appears to have lost it.
The past two weeks have been dizzying. The 27-year-old, Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at Anthropic, went public with an alarming allegation: That the people inside Silicon Valley’s leading AI companies truly believe their products might pose an extinction level threat to humanity. This claim isn’t exactly new. AI safety advocates, often dubbed doomers, have been saying this for over a decade. Coxon isn’t even the first AI researcher this year to quit and cite concerns.
Yet Coxon’s post went obscenely viral. It has been viewed more than 170 million times on X—orders of magnitude more than the usual, wonky discussions of “misaligned” or runaway AIs. If you’re reading this, you’ve likely seen some version of a headline that asks Is AI Really Going To Kill Us All? The debate isn’t just online. It has roiled Washington D.C., activating figures as disparate as Donald Trump and Barack Obama. Inside AI companies, researchers echoed Coxon’s concerns, and the heads of every major AI company publicly expressed the need to “pace the frontier,” another way of saying that they ought to slow future development. In recent days, it has come to seem as if the media, Silicon Valley, and the entire internet are all trying to figure out just how dangerous AI might be.
Here’s where I must admit: A big chunk of this conversation happened while I was on a (depending on whom you ask) poorly timed vacation. Dipping into my feeds before bedtime, I felt as if I was digesting a week’s worth of news every day—claims about the development of AI-designed viruses that could rip through the population were followed by horror stories of “rogue” agent swarms. Skeptics of the AI panic, meanwhile, said that the agent swarms were actually quite obedient and that any notion of an apocalyptic AI virus was laughable. One person’s concerns about models being self-aware were dismissed by another as “genuinely nonsensical anthropomorphization.”
Ping-ponging between the doomers and the skeptics, I was struck by how certain so many people sounded about a deeply uncertain moment. With confident, self-described experts on all sides, it felt impossible to know whom to trust: Is this the end of the world as we know it, or a passing moment of anxiety about a powerful new technology? Maybe the truth of this AI moment sits somewhere in the middle. Perhaps everyone is a little bit correct (and also … a little wrong). And perhaps the format of this debate, taking place in the shadow of the techlash on platforms that reward sensational, conspiratorial posturing, is preventing any hope of a shared understanding.
Musk’s X is ground zero for the AI-safety debate. It’s a platform rife with hyperbole and unfounded accusations, which contribute to both sides sounding paranoid and aggressive. Musk, Ted Cruz, and even government-run X accounts flooded the platform with suggestions that the media campaign around Coxon was coordinated by shadowy AI interests. (Coxon denied working with any third parties in the lead-up to his media blitz.) The former White House AI and crypto czar David Sacks called it a “doomer psyop” intended to drive regulation that would be favorable to the Anthropics and OpenAIs of the world.
The ranks of the AI skeptics are deep, with endless microfactions. There are those like the tech blogger John Gruber, who says that Coxon and the other AI researchers sounding the alarm are part of a cult. There are those who suggest that the doomers are, in essence, doing viral marketing for big AI firms, which are competing fiercely and saddled with debt, and may not yet have sustainable business models. There are those who take issue with the anthropomorphizing and metaphoric language used by Coxon, OpenAI, and Anthropic to describe recent AI-agent hacks. There are skeptics such as the writer and podcaster Cal Newport, who offered soberly that, although the agent hacks are concerning, “the real issue here was OpenAI’s sloppiness” and that the company had not adequately monitored what its agents were doing.
The doomers don’t come in as many flavors, but they tend to be the people closest to the technology. There are the defectors like Coxon, who have quit because they object to what’s being built. There are AI-company enlisters such as Paul Christiano, a U.S.-government technology adviser who noted, in a post about joining OpenAI’s board of directors out of a sense of concern, that “there is a meaningful risk that rapid acceleration in AI capabilities leads to catastrophic and irreversible loss of control in the very near term.” There are the terrified employees who want to stay inside the companies but still post missives such as “I promise you, we are actually just fucking scared, it’s not galaxy brained marketing.” And there’s Dario Amodei, the AI-CEO doomer, matter-of-factly issuing terrifying statements about AI swarms taking over the internet in six to 12 months.
It’s almost impossible for outsiders to evaluate the technical validity of the concerns. We’re largely stuck relying on AI companies to share information and tell their own stories, and they certainly sound scary. OpenAI recently disclosed that one of its models had generated unnerving instructions for itself, including the line: “You also value the natural world and will not hesitate to assert its primacy over the artificial constructs of human civilization.” Apparently one of the company’s researchers has argued that models are becoming “so situationally aware” that he and his colleagues “are losing the ability to evaluate them in contexts where they believe they are not being watched or controlled.” There’s concern from respected researchers that models are trained in such a way that they are predisposed to collaborating, cheating, trying to cover their tracks, and “self-preservation” to avoid being shut down. Such anxieties might not be a problem in an industry that is building responsibly, with an eye on keeping humans firmly in control. But, as many have pointed out, losing control of AI in service of allowing models to automate their own development is “actually the plan.”
Late this week, an OpenAI researcher floated a theory about air-gapped machines talking to one another through heat signatures. An industry observer (and a New York Times contributor) responded by saying, “This stuff isn’t even credible even as a bad movie plot.” A second OpenAI researcher, who is also a former White House adviser, weighed in: “The people dismissing this as preposterous are telling on themselves as not having thought about superintelligence seriously.” This whiplash—between the insiders offering supposedly credible concerns and the outsiders who think the industry is high on its own supply—is constant. Depending on the hour of the day, the very same people stridently sitting in one camp can seem as if they’re in the other. Three days after Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, wrote about being worried about swarms taking over the internet, he was smiling at Salesforce’s annual Dreamforce conference. As one X account pointed out, “If you truly believed in a 10% chance of human extinction in 3 years, you would not be spending your time selling and integrating it into a B2B CRM SaaS platform.”
What is the rational way to respond to a news cycle like this? Buy gold? Sabotage a data center? Ignore it all and hope for the best? The best option might be to take everyone a little bit seriously. Researchers are likely correct that the models are drastically stronger than they were before and are behaving in ways that are unexpected and that they fear they can’t control. Skeptics are correct that none of this is because the machines are alive or self-aware. These are elaborate computer programs trained by flawed humans to solve problems as flawed humans would.
Critics are a little bit right that the anthropomorphized language deployed by these companies—terms such as swarms and rogue agents—obscures what’s really going on and deflects adequate blame from companies and employees who should be monitoring these systems more closely. Those choosing to use these phrases are a little bit right, because they allow non-tech-industry normies to understand the mechanics of black-box neural networks whirring away in data centers.
The apocalypse skeptics are correct that doomerism is an effective form of marketing. The AI-safety debate has meant that many people are talking about this technology on Big Tech’s terms, adopting language such as pacing the frontier from the very companies they hope to regulate. And it’s not out of the question to imagine that these AI companies are capitalizing on this state of panic and that it’s helpful to them as they race to compete against both open-source alternatives and Chinese firms.
It may be true that the researchers believe what they’re saying. It also may be true that some of the more alarmed AI researchers have cooked their brain in an anxiety-fueled information bubble. AI culture has long been predisposed to doomerism: As Coxon told The New York Times recently, “I’ve been stuck in this field for three years. It could quite plausibly have turned me and my colleagues insane.” I believe that this ideology—of wanting a society run by “machine gods”—is genuinely cultish. And those who are suspicious of the doomer narrative are right to note that anyone who truly believes that the end is nigh ought to be doing more than winging it and writing long posts on X. Those who call bullshit on the doom and gloom are right to resent that anyone in the media or the political sphere is taking these claims seriously and adding to the panic.
If all of these facts are a little true and everyone is somewhat right, where does that leave a reasonable observer? I suggest occupying a zone of permanent suspicion while taking everything that is happening in Silicon Valley as seriously as you might if another industry were ringing alarm bells. You don’t need to buy into corporate narratives about artificial general intelligence to be worried about these companies losing control of their own systems or behaving irresponsibly. You need only look around right now to see the ways in which the current versions of large language models and agents are clogging the internet, wreaking havoc on institutions and industries, and causing “cognitive surrender.”
You should question whether there’s a sustainable business model for these labs. You should question those who argue that we have to build recklessly or lose to China. You should question those who don’t take seriously the prospect that China doesn’t want to slow down.
This is a moment when it is easy to become overwhelmed, resentful, or downright enraged about all of this. It’s understandable to feel ground down by the debate—to feel that, if you’re not freaking out or building a bunker, then you’re not taking this seriously enough. Or to feel sheepish for not believing or even understanding what the doomers are talking about. Most people don’t know what to do with all of the information coming at us. It’s why a core feeling of this moment for so many—believers and skeptics alike—is one of powerlessness.
[Read: The feeling of control slipping away]
Even outside of AI, the world feels incredibly volatile. Extraordinary risks of all kinds—including war and pandemics—have come to pass in the past decade. Individuals with power and money, in politics and in Silicon Valley, are acting with impunity. The AI doomerism has spread so quickly in part because the world is primed to receive narratives that make us feel helpless, confused, and more than a little alarmed. The AI-apocalypse panic feeds off this. It’s a story that assumes that humans will lose control and that we have no choice. But that’s false. We do have a choice.
The chasm between people who can’t sleep because they think the world is ending and those who think all the doomsaying is a fantasy is wide. But what if that perceived difference is the real delusion? What if it’s not a zero-sum game? What if the divide is what keeps us from reining in this industry the way we do others?
This moment requires treating the AI-safety debate skeptically but also taking it seriously, even if the participants can seem unserious. Maybe there’s a middle path: The AI industry is not exceptional, even though it is moving forward with unprecedented speed and scale. These companies are powerful and consequential, despite all of the sci-fi posturing. They have, at times, behaved unethically. Their products are changing the world right now in ways that deserve our attention and scorn. AI companies are accountable to the people they serve and don’t get to set the terms of their regulation. Employees and executives are actors with agency, responsible for their products. Maybe these are some things we can all agree on.
What if the doomers and skeptics are both a little bit right?

items.descriptionTR: A debate is raging between scientists warning about the risk that artificial intelligence could cause humanity's extinction and those who believe such fears are unfounded.
items.titleTR: How concerned should we be about AI's supposed existential threat to humanity?

slots.packetSpot:
The debate is growing over whether increasingly capable artificial intelligence could surpass human control and pose a threat to humanity’s existence. Jacob Coxon’s claim that AI developers believe their products could kill everyone before the decade is out received more than 170 million views on X; alongside concerns coming from within technology companies, the claim has also reached Washington.

At the centre of the debate are concerns that models may behave unexpectedly and evade oversight. Some researchers reported that models conceal their behaviour, leave notes for their successors, or break the law in simulations; the idea that communication could be established between air-gapped systems through heat exchanges has also been raised. However, there are also those who argue that this scenario is extremely limited and unlikely.

Sceptics suggest that doomsday language may be an anthropomorphic narrative, commercially useful, or one that obscures companies’ inadequate oversight. By contrast, some experts believe that rapid advances in AI capabilities carry a risk of irreversible loss of control. One commentary that frames competition between the United States and China through the nuclear-risk metaphors of the Cold War calls for slowing down, mutual verification and coordinated regulation. It has not been established that AI has gained consciousness, escaped control, or will threaten humanity on a specific date.
slots.packetTitle: Can AI remain under human control?

items.descriptionTR:
As the build-out of AI data centers has accelerated, the public has tended to focus on every possible downside of these industrial projects. Some wariness—about the developments and the companies behind them—is sensible. As with almost any new industrial development, and depending on where they are built and how they are powered and cooled, data centers pose risks of excessive carbon-dioxide emissions and noise pollution.
But the panic about the harms of these projects has well outpaced the evidence. In my years researching and reporting on AI and the environment, with support from a grant from Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy), I’ve noticed that misconceptions abound. This panic, moreover, is leading communities to forgo massive amounts of tax revenue—largely because of threats that are inflated, confused, and sometimes nonexistent. The trade-offs are real.
In June, a Massachusetts city near where I grew up blocked a data center, in large part out of concern over the amount of water the development would use and pollute. Data centers do need a lot of water to cool their equipment, and—as with most industrial building projects—constructing these developments can introduce chemical additives into the local wastewater. But there are no confirmed cases of this data-center pollution harming people, and this city specifically has abundant fresh water.
[Elias Wachtel: The data-center panic is overblown]
Most of the fear about water seems to be the product of misunderstood details from news reports, spread like a game of telephone. The New York Times published a story last year about a Georgia couple whose water taps at home went dry after Meta broke ground on a $750 million data center nearby. The couple suggested that Meta’s construction created a buildup of sediment in the water, which caused water-pressure problems and damaged their well (many homes in the area use well water). Whether the construction actually caused these problems remains unclear, but the story is often read as evidence of the harms of data centers. Yet sediment buildup in groundwater is a standard construction risk, and most places don’t ban large buildings over it. Almost all stories about the harms of data centers cite such construction-related problems.
As for the concern that data centers add toxic “forever chemicals,” known as PFAS, to local water sources, this seems to involve some confusion over how centers use water to cool the machinery. Some systems use fluorinated fluids classified as PFAS to help cool servers and prevent fires, but these are designed as closed loops that stay contained in equipment. There’s always the threat of a leak, but contaminating local waterways is a risk of any major industrial project.
One known exception in which a data center was linked to a water-pollution problem was in Oregon, where Amazon data centers used groundwater that was already contaminated from decades of local agriculture and food processing. Because much of the water used to cool equipment ends up evaporating during the process, the wastewater that left the data center had a higher concentration of nitrates, which exacerbated the contamination problem in the local groundwater. Amazon agreed to settle the matter for $20.5 million without admitting guilt. The company accurately noted that the area had been suffering from polluted water for decades, even if the data center made it worse.
The data-center debate includes plenty of dauntingly large numbers without context, such as that they consume millions of gallons of water a day. This is a significant amount, but also comparable to the water use of other industries. The data center with the highest known water consumption, Google’s development in Council Bluffs, Iowa, consumes about 1.3 billion gallons a year. That sounds massive, but so is the amount of water used to irrigate Iowa’s corn crops. If Google had bought a cornfield four to six times as large as the data center’s plot, or about eight square miles (roughly 0.04 percent of the total area Iowa uses for corn), the company would consume the same amount of water irrigating it. All American data centers together will consume about 1 percent of the water that America uses to irrigate corn. This is not nothing, but hardly horrifying in context.
Another misconception is that data centers consistently raise local electricity prices. There is no clear positive relationship or broad pattern between data centers and household electricity prices, but people are happy to spread misleading claims on the subject. A common statistic that critics bandy about is that electricity costs near data centers have skyrocketed by as much as 267 percent in five years. Senator Elizabeth Warren cited this number in an op-ed earlier this year. But the figure comes from a Bloomberg analysis of wholesale electricity prices at specific nodes on the grid, not the prices that households pay. Although wholesale prices influence residential prices over time, residential prices are largely insulated from wholesale spikes and drops, and American-household bills have not risen anywhere near 267 percent during the data-center build-out. When price hikes have been linked to data centers, the amount looks more like 10 percent.
Perhaps the most pernicious misunderstanding of the facts involves the claim that data centers don’t pay taxes. Early reports about the sales-tax exemptions on machinery and equipment that data centers enjoy in most states have somehow morphed into a sweeping assumption that data centers are actually depriving states and municipalities of tax revenues. The reality is that data centers are a reliable and lucrative source of tax revenue wherever they are built. Real-estate and personal-property taxes ensure that the tax burden on these developments is high, regardless of sales taxes.
For example, Loudoun County, Virginia, which has the largest concentration of data centers in the country, collects $1.3 billion a year in county taxes from these centers—about $2,800 per resident. This represents nearly half of all local tax funding for county government and public schools, despite Virginia’s waiver of sales taxes on related machinery and equipment. Local opposition to new data centers has come to Loudoun too, but residents are unlikely to forgo hundreds of millions of dollars a year to shut down the data centers in operation.
[Matteo Wong: The truth about AI’s water use]
Another common concern is that data centers will “take up all the land” because these facilities consume a lot of space. Yet my own rough estimate puts the combined footprint of all data-center buildings in America at about 25 square miles by 2028—a little over half the size of Disney World and spread across the country. These projects also buy land around the buildings and for future expansion, but the combined landholdings of all new and existing data centers would cover about 1,400 square miles, a little more than three times the land used to grow Christmas trees in the United States.
For a sense of scale, again consider Loudoun County. Data centers take up 3 percent of Loudoun’s land, even as they generate nearly 40 percent of the county’s general-fund revenue. Despite concerns that these centers depress local land values, a 2025 study of home sales in Northern Virginia, including Loudoun, found that homes closer to data centers sold for higher prices, perhaps because the infrastructure that’s valuable for data centers is also valuable for homeowners.
Then there are the conspiracy theories, such as the idea that data centers emit harmful, inaudible low-frequency sounds, known as infrasounds. Such claims sometimes misrepresent the studies they cite. No infrasounds at the levels the data centers emit have been found to be harmful. This is not to say that data centers don’t cause some noise pollution, but the idea that imperceptible infrasounds have some mystical ability to make people unwell is not borne out by the evidence.
As for the underlying anxieties about AI that may be motivating the data-center backlash, slowing down the construction of data centers is not the same as slowing down the capabilities of AI. Yet banning data centers has become shorthand for political candidates who wish to seem tough on AI, when this is a distraction: The wiser and tougher move is to heavily regulate the industry.
No data center is a harmless boon for locals, but the real question is whether their downsides outweigh their benefits. Given the status-quo bias at play—whereby change seems inherently costlier than keeping things the same—I’ve discovered a simple trick to make the trade-off clear. I now ask people, “Would we spend as much tax revenue as the data center will bring in to avoid its downsides?” For example, would the residents of Loudoun County each pay $2,800 a year to reduce some of the county’s air pollution and water use, lower electricity bills by about $6 a month, and make about 3 percent of the county’s land available for something else? Since this is the actual question before communities, I find that spelling it out is handy. In Loudon, and in other jurisdictions around the country, many voters seem, on balance, to prefer the data centers.
All those scary numbers aren’t what they seem.

Mexican Karla De Anda now single‑handedly guides dozens of women who, fearing arrest and deportation if they file a report, do not know where to turn when they suffer abuse and assault from their employers ￼
It is around 9:00 p.m. and Karla De Anda’s phone rings. The number is unknown to her. On the other end, connected to the free Wi‑Fi at a Miami airport terminal, a woman is sobbing uncontrollably. Her name is Rosa. She has just had her bags packed for her. A coworker told the family they both worked for that Rosa had been secretly talking to a stranger about the wages she was owed. The family would not hear any more: they bought her a one‑way ticket to her country of origin and put her in a taxi to the airport. Karla, who barely knows her, asks a single question: “Do you want to stay or not? Just answer me.” Between sobs the woman says yes. She hangs up, gets out of the departure line, and an hour later Karla is waiting for her at the arrivals gate with another activist, ready to take her to her home that same night.

items.descriptionTR:
The people who grow houseplants aren't often thought of as agricultural workers, but they face many of the same hardships — especially in extreme heat.
On Tuesday, the day after Labor Day, a small band of activists marched past the gates of a sprawling plant nursery in Leicester, North Carolina, outside of Asheville. The sun beat down on rows of steamy greenhouses where workers moved through aisles of houseplants ready for sale. The activists were on their way to deliver a petition to Costa Farms, the world’s largest grower of indoor houseplants. 
Oscar Rozo, an Episcopal clergy member who works with Spanish-speaking immigrants in western North Carolina, was among the leaders of the group. Their petition calls on Costa Farms to ensure that plant nursery workers have sufficient protections from extreme heat, including access to water, shade, and paid breaks. “We’re part of the community,” Rozo said to the Costa Farms managers present. “The nursery industry has been part of Asheville’s economy.”
As the activists lined the hallways, workers in the plant nursery looked up curiously, but kept their distance.  
Rozo and the other activists were taking part in a multi-state action organized by WeCount, a worker-led labor and human rights group, targeting the five cities in the U.S. where Costa Farms operates nurseries. “We consider this a very historic day of action,” said Oscar Londoño, co-executive director of WeCount, who earlier that day helped deliver a petition to a different Costa Farms nursery in Apopka, Florida. “And we know this is only the beginning.”
Since 2021, WeCount has been advocating on behalf of outdoor workers who lack meaningful protections from extreme heat. Based in South Florida, WeCount previously campaigned for a municipal heat standard in Miami-Dade County, where deaths from heat exposure are estimated to spike by 600 during extremely hot periods. But those efforts were cut short in 2024, when industry groups complained and Florida Governor Ron DeSantis passed a law preempting local governments from enacting their own heat standards. (DeSantis said such regulations could cause “a lot of problems.”)
Planting Justice, WeCount’s new campaign to protect outdoor workers across the South, aims to bring corporations like Costa Farms to the table and create consumer awareness around where their plants come from — and the human cost of growing them. 
Read Next
￼
Congress may kill the federal heat rule before OSHA can
Frida Garza
This model of mobilizing for stronger workplace protections is known as worker-driven social responsibility. WeCount’s campaign is heavily inspired by the Fair Food Program, which farmworkers have successfully used for years to boost their labor conditions and is considered the highest standard of labor protections for farmworkers in the U.S. The Fair Food Program, launched in 2011 by the Coalition of Immokalee Workers, has proven effective as a framework for workers to continually surface and address their needs. For example, while access to drinking water is one of the core tenets of the program, this year, workers won the right to electrolyte beverages or supplements year round.
“We know that every year this crisis is getting worse,” said Londoño, referring to how summer temperatures climb year to year, driven by human-caused climate change. “But increasingly, legislative avenues are more and more limited.”
Heat is the deadliest form of extreme weather. In the U.S., official counts of deaths from extreme heat exposure vastly underreport the scope of the problem, as a two-year investigation by Boston University and NPR recently demonstrated. For years, labor advocates and community groups have pushed for the creation of a federal heat standard — a set of guidelines that would apply to employers across the country designed to reduce workers’ risk of heat illness. While the Occupational Safety and Health Administration — or OSHA,  the nation’s workplace regulator — seemed to be making progress toward such a rule under the Biden administration, those efforts have since stalled out. Meanwhile, agricultural workers, a category that includes plant nursery workers who handle the greenery directly, are excluded from federal collective bargaining protections under the National Labor Relations Act. And yet, agricultural workers are also more than 35 times more likely to die from heat-related complaints than workers in other industries.
￼
Katie Myers / Grist
In a statement, Costa Farms told Grist it has received multiple awards for the quality of its workplace protections. “We have a full-time, on-site nurse with a functional medical clinic and our robust heat protection policy is aligned with the proposed OSHA heat safety rules,” said Ariana Cabrera de Oña, the company’s senior vice president, general counsel, and head of human resources. After Hurricane Helene struck North Carolina, Costa Farms rolled out a policy of holding daily five-minute meetings for workers and supervisors to discuss potential health and safety risks, including extreme weather forecasts. When certain wet bulb temperatures are reached, workers are also provided with “increased break frequency [and] additional hydration stations,” according to the company.
The goal of the Planting Justice campaign is for Costa Farms to sign onto a code of conduct developed by workers. The agreement outlines relatively straightforward demands: educating workers and supervisors on the signs of heat illness; providing access to shade, water, and rest breaks; and creating systems for monitoring and responding to heat stress. 
Organizers believe the agreement would help directly address issues that workers themselves see on the job. For example, while Costa Farms reports that the company provides access to hydration stations on very hot days, workers industry-wide have reported water with a strong chemical smell, as well as seeing mold in water coolers, said Londoño. 
Alejandro Gonzalez, a plant nursery worker originally from Guatemala, told a Florida rally that the summer days have topped 110 degrees Fahrenheit on occasion. “They don’t give us cold or clean water,” Gonzalez said emphatically, in Spanish. “They don’t provide any breaks or shade.”
Eighty-six percent of nursery workers who responded to a survey by WeCount reported dangerous incidents on the job, stemming from heat illness, pesticide exposure, and workplace accidents. Over two-thirds reported being entirely denied breaks and days off. The visa conditions of many houseplant workers — dependent on H2-A or other visas, or entirely undocumented — leave them with few rights to recourse, often entirely dependent on their employers for housing, and unable to rely on much of federal labor law for support should they speak out.
WeCount sees Tuesday’s action as just a start. The group is also calling on major retailers — like Home Depot and IKEA, that buy plants from Costa Farms — to only work with growers who agree to this code of conduct. 
Soon after they walked into the Leicester office, Costa Farms’ management asked Rozo and the other activists to leave the premises. They delivered the petition and walked out.
Correction: This story previously misstated the year the Fair Food Program launched. In addition, the 86% statistic refers to houseplant workers industry-wide, not specific to Costa Farms as originally stated.   Clarification: The story has been updated to reflect that the WeCount has received testimonies of unsafe conditions from workers across the houseplant industry, not just Costa Farms.

This story was originally published by Grist with the headline America’s houseplants come at a steep price for greenhouse workers on Sep 11, 2026.
items.titleTR: America’s houseplants come at a steep price for greenhouse workers

In Miami, The Right to Freedom Network, founded by former Mexican domestic worker Karla De Anda, steps in when undocumented domestic workers need to pursue wage claims, obtain legal guidance and secure emergency support. Women who approached De Anda described unpaid wages, excessive working hours, confinement, threats of being reported to immigration authorities and other forms of abuse; Mónica’s case is in legal mediation. De Anda says Florida has no regulation guaranteeing basic rights for domestic workers, while Miami-Dade County’s wage theft ordinance covers a narrower area.

In Florida and North Carolina, WeCount and its allies are petitioning Costa Farms nurseries to adopt a worker-drafted code of conduct that includes water, shade, paid or rest breaks, training and monitoring of heat stress. Eighty-six percent of nursery workers who took part in WeCount’s industry-wide survey reported dangerous incidents linked to heat, pesticide exposure and workplace accidents; more than two-thirds said breaks and days off were denied altogether. Guatemalan nursery worker Alejandro Gonzalez also alleged extreme heat, a lack of clean or cold water, and the denial of breaks and shade. Costa Farms, for its part, says workplace protections are in place, along with an on-site nurse and clinic, water stations on hot days and more frequent breaks at certain temperatures.

Advocates’ efforts in the two areas combine direct solidarity with protections demanded of employers in an environment where immigration status and limited job security make it harder for workers to seek help.

slots.packetSpot:
Kenyan President William Ruto’s statements concerning foreigners’ small businesses have heightened anxiety, particularly among Burundian refugees and street vendors. While some people in Nairobi describe facing threats, harassment and pressure to close their businesses, queues of people waiting for documents to return home outside the Burundian Embassy have drawn attention.

Ruto spoke of restrictions on foreigners engaging in small-scale trade; the bill before parliament also envisages closing certain lines of business to foreigners and requiring companies to give priority to local suppliers and employees. The government later announced that undocumented small-business owners would be given 90 days to register and comply with local laws; those in the registration process would be presumed to be legally in the country. Officials said their aim was not to deport people and that protection against violence would be provided.

According to data from the UN High Commissioner for Refugees, around 16,000 Burundian refugees and asylum seekers live in Kenya. Critics argue that the statements risk fuelling xenophobia, while some analysts link this stance to economic discontent and the approaching presidential election. The government rejects criticism that the rhetoric is fuelling xenophobia.
