New Zealander plans to add ‘a bit of cricket sense in key moments’ to Bazball template and make England the world’s best Test team
“Flemball? That’s a medical condition.” Stephen Fleming’s first press conference as England Test coach was exactly what you would expect from a man appointed to bring calm to a team that had started to career off course.
While the Manchester rain did its worst outside, Fleming was the handsome sea captain on top of his ship, even if that ship had to float without him during the Test series against Pakistan. England won 3-0 while Fleming saw to family and commercial commitments. But the wait has given him thinking time to work out what he wants to achieve.
items.titleTR: ‘I can’t wait for the Ashes’: new England Test coach Fleming targets No 1 spot

slots.packetSpot:
Stephen Fleming has taken over as head coach of England’s Test team, replacing Brendon McCullum. In his first remarks, he said he wanted to build a more planned, disciplined and competitive identity without entirely abandoning the team’s positive and flamboyant style of play.

According to Fleming, events off the field can distract from the main goal; he stressed that standards, as well as runs and wickets, should matter in selections. Fleming, who said he had begun working with Joe Root on belonging and team identity, described his own approach as more measured than McCullum’s.

Fleming, who argued that England should aim for number one in the Test rankings and compete for major trophies including the World Test Championship, will begin with a series against South Africa in December. Tests in Bangladesh, a one-off anniversary Test in Melbourne and next summer’s Ashes are then on the schedule. Fleming also said he respected the decision of Ben Stokes, who has retired from Test cricket.
slots.packetTitle: Fleming’s blueprint for England

items.descriptionTR:
With help from government incentives, Ukrainian businesses and households are increasingly investing in solar.
On a spring day earlier this year, 10 men stood on the rooftop of a door manufacturing facility in the central Ukrainian town of Bila Tserkva, surveying the rows of solar panels that surrounded them. Since Russia invaded in 2022, the town has endured repeated attacks, triggering mass power outages. For the factory, which supplies doors to homes and businesses, keeping production going had become extremely challenging. The outages were particularly brutal in the winter, when limited power supplies led to rolling blackouts across the country.
Some days, the employees burned discarded wood in a fireplace to keep the warehouse warm. The facility has backup generators, but they were expensive to run. Tired of relying on a grid that was being routinely bombarded by Russian missiles, Yaroslav, the facility’s owner, decided to switch to solar earlier this year.
Switching to solar energy will enable them to “further expand our capacity and be a bit more independent from the general grid,” he said. “It will be cheaper, more economical, and more ecological.” (Yaroslav requested that Grist use only his first name and withhold details about the facility for fear of Russian retaliation.)
In the spring, he contacted Yasno, a private Ukrainian electricity and gas supplier, to install solar panels on his rooftop. Yasno’s clients pay for the panels to be installed, often with the help of a government program that covers some of the installation expenses. Ukraine created incentives to encourage businesses to switch to renewable energy, like the “Affordable Loans 5-7-9” program, which offers loans to purchase solar panels and other equipment. The preferential loans have interest rates of 5, 7, or 9 percent, depending on the type of business, and can cover up to 80 percent of the installation costs.
Yasno will ultimately decide where to station hundreds of solar panels on the warehouse rooftop and install them. The project is one of dozens that the company has undertaken across the country. In the past two years, it has installed solar panels at 117 sites with a combined capacity of 23 megawatts. The company paused its work for the first two years of the war, but resumed operations in the summer of 2024.
￼
Workers install solar panels on the roof of a door manufacturing facility in Bila Tserkva, Ukraine, in 2026.
Anna Conkling
Volodymyr Hershtun, a service maintenance manager with Yasno who led the project in Bila Tserkva, said that Ukraine is rapidly developing its renewable energy portfolio in part because the country needs to be resilient as it continues to face a barrage of Russian attacks.
“The enemy is trying to destroy energy infrastructure, and we are building what is very easy to restore,” he said. “And those same systems can store electric energy.”
Before Russia’s invasion, Ukraine relied on a highly centralized electricity system dominated by nuclear power. More than half of the country’s electricity came from four nuclear power plants, while natural gas and coal generated roughly a quarter of the energy mix.
￼
A damaged solar panel remains on a roof of a residential house after a Russian drone strike in August 2026 in Mykolaiv, Ukraine. Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images
Renewables made up a small share of the energy portfolio, though the country had been rapidly expanding its solar generation in the years leading up to the war. The surge was driven by the country’s “green tariff” program, which encouraged households and businesses to produce solar and wind power through guaranteed above-market payments for electricity. Ukrainian law guarantees the tariff until 2030, and lawmakers have described the program as a step toward integrating the country into the European Union’s energy market.
Those government incentives led Ukrainian businesses to install about 8 gigawatts of solar by 2022. But Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure over the past few years have upended that model. Since the invasion, missiles and drones have repeatedly struck power plants, substations, and transmission lines, leaving millions without electricity during the coldest months.
Roughly 30 percent of the installed solar capacity and most of the country’s 36 wind farms in the south were either destroyed, fell under Russian occupation, or are unaccounted for. The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in southeastern Ukraine has also been shut down and under Russian control since the invasion began. Given the legacy of Chernobyl, many Ukrainians live with the fear of another nuclear disaster.
The repeated attacks on the grid have caused prolonged power outages. Parts of Kyiv continue to ration electricity with scheduled power outages that can last for hours. Ukraine’s National Bank has said that Russia’s energy infrastructure attacks this year have worsened the electricity deficit assumptions, raising them from 3 percent to 6 percent.
With the vulnerabilities of relying on large, centralized power stations exposed, Ukraine has begun accelerating its shift toward smaller, distributed sources of electricity that are harder to knock offline. In 2025, the Solar Energy Association of Ukraine estimated that 1.5 GW of new solar capacity was built — almost double the prior year’s total — and it expects 2026 installations to at least match that pace.
“Renewables have become the very obvious choice for Ukraine when the full-scale invasion started and when Russia started deliberately and heavily attacking the energy infrastructure, especially the centralized generation facilities,” said Anastasia Vereshchynska, the director of the European-Ukrainian Energy Agency, a nonprofit that works with energy efficiency and renewable resources in Ukraine.
The investments are likely to help Ukrainians weather brutal winters. Last year, as temperatures dropped to -1 degree Fahrenheit, Russia’s bombardments caused widespread electricity and heating outages. Kyiv, Ukraine’s capital, had just half the electricity supply it needed to weather the winter, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy declared a state of emergency.
Volodymyr, a taxi driver in Kyiv who asked that his last name be withheld for safety reasons, told Grist in May that during last winter’s attacks, his apartment building lost power, leaving him and his family without heating and hot water. Fortunately, he said, his apartment faced south and received sunlight most of the day, keeping it relatively warm.
In an attempt to minimize the effects of outages, the building’s management company has since decided to install solar panels on the roof to help keep the boiler turned on and operate the elevators. The installation is part of the 5-7-9 program.
“It’s a cool thing that the government covers at least part of the cost,” said Volodymyr. “In emergency cases, during power outages, you could turn to the solar panels. There is no harm to the planet. It’s a good thing.”
￼
A photovoltaic power station at the industrial site of the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in 2025. Volodymyr Tarasov / Ukrinform / NurPhoto via Getty Images
The need for renewable energy is especially critical in communities closest to the war’s frontlines. As Russian forces advance, towns and villages are increasingly cut off from the energy grid as attacks destroy power lines, and the threat to maintenance workers makes repairs difficult or impossible. Some villages in particular have become so dangerous that repairs cannot be conducted, leaving residents without electricity and access to the outside world.
In those communities, volunteers and nongovernmental organizations have stepped in to install solar panels and battery systems that can power homes and businesses. Denny Ugorchuk, the founder of Kosmo Tabir, an NGO that works to help villages access solar energy, said that much of the funding for large projects comes from the help of international partners in the West, while local donations from Ukrainians help fund smaller projects. In one village, solar panels installed at a private residence gave a 50-year-old woman access to online university classes.
In Ukraine, solar panels are a “basic human right,” said Ugorchuk. “People should have access to communicate with one another — you can call a doctor, the police, and it helps you feel safe.”
This story was originally published by Grist with the headline As Russia attacks Ukraine’s grid, solar offers a path to resilience on Sep 16, 2026.
items.titleTR: As Russia attacks Ukraine’s grid, solar offers a path to resilience

Solar power generation in the UK reached a new record over the summer of 2026, as temperatures across the nation…
The post Analysis: UK solar power hits record high over summer 2026 appeared first on Carbon Brief.
Print article Share
Solar power generation in the UK reached a new record over the summer of 2026, as temperatures across the nation soared, according to new analysis by Carbon Brief. 
Collectively over June, July and August, solar farms and rooftops generated 8.8 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity in the UK*, as shown in the chart below. 
￼
Speaking to Carbon Brief, Chris Hewett, chief executive of trade association Solar Energy UK welcomed the new record, adding that it was driven by “clear skies and continued growth in deployment”. 
This surge in generation took place amid the hottest summer on record in the UK, with five heatwaves between May and August.
Summer 2026 was the sixth sunniest on record, with more than 620 hours of sunshine, according to the Met Office. England and Wales – which experienced the most extreme heat – saw their second-sunniest summers on record. 
June 2026 was the hottest June in England since records began in 1884, according to Met Office data, while Wales and the UK as a whole experienced their second-warmest June. 
It was the driest July for England and Wales since records began in 1836, with some parts of London seeing no rain at all in the month, while Wisley in Surrey had no rain for 62 days. 
In England, temperatures peaked at 38.1C at Kew Gardens in London on 13 August. 
According to the Met Office, this summer’s record mean temperature was made 130 times more likely by climate change.  
Amid these hot and sunny months, solar power generation increased 23% from the same period in 2025. This is double the level of solar generation over the summer of 2021, according to Carbon Brief analysis. 
While solar panels can be affected by periods of extreme heat, the longer hours of daylight and higher levels of irradiation over the summer more than offset any efficiency losses. 
June, July and August all saw solar set new monthly records for solar generation – July saw the highest solar generation in a calendar month ever, with 3.3TWh meeting 15% of overall electricity demand for the month. 
As of the end of August, the total UK solar generation in 2026 stood at 17TWh – 13% higher than the same point in 2025. 
The number of solar farms and rooftop installations has grown substantially in recent years, helping to boost generation. Domestic rooftop solar accounts for around 29% of total capacity.
In 2025, the UK’s solar capacity reached 21 gigawatts (GW) by the third quarter of the year, according to UK government figures. This is a jump of 3GW, or 18%, year-on-year, as Carbon Brief reported in January. 
(Capacity is the maximum output possible from an electricity generation, whereas generation is what was produced over a certain time period, such as a day, month or year.)
According to the University of Sheffield, the installed solar capacity is now nearly 24GW. 
This includes nearly 172,000 solar installations that have been fitted across the UK since the start of 2026, according to recent government figures. In July alone, more than 19,800 rooftop solar panels were installed – the equivalent of one installation every two minutes. 
In total, nearly 1.7m households in the UK now have solar panels installed. 
Over 26 heatwave days this summer – periods of at least three days when temperatures exceed the Met Office’s county-level heatwave temperature threshold – UK households with rooftop solar panels avoided an estimated £86.7m in electricity costs, according to analysis by Utility Bidder.
Talking about the surge in solar generation this summer, Hewett says: 
“[It] not only kept bills down for people with solar and batteries in their homes, but helped keep overall power prices much lower than they would have been if Britain had been relying on more gas generation during the day”.
Despite the record generation, no new half-hourly solar power output record was set in the summer of 2026. This still stands at 15.2 megawatts (MW) on 23 April 2026.
* This article refers to the UK throughout, but strictly relates to the island of Great Britain, made up of England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland is part of the separate, all-Ireland electricity system.

superPackets.body: U.S. President Donald Trump announced that he had banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House “immediately,” citing the claim that these outlets publish “fake news” and deliberately negative coverage. While MercoPress wrote that no implementation step had been seen by the end of the day on which the announcement was made and that reporters from the three outlets continued to work in the complex, subsequent reports recorded that journalists were denied entry and that their building passes were taken; the reports used the terms “ban,” “exclusion” and “denial of entry.” In Guinea, meanwhile, according to a CPJ statement carried by AllAfrica, authorities banned France 24’s broadcasts after one of its presenters called President Mamadi Doumbouya a “coup president,” and withdrew the accreditation of Diawo Barry, Jeune Afrique’s Guinea correspondent; CPJ called for both decisions to be reversed. In the first incident, the president’s announcement targeted the three outlets’ access to the White House; in the second, two separate administrative measures targeted a channel’s broadcasts and the accreditation of a named reporter. The Atlantic argued that Trump cannot tolerate negative coverage; an opinion piece in The Hill also described visa policy concerning foreign journalists as a tool for punishing unfavorable reporting, but these assessments of possible motives were not the reasons stated by the authorities. The sources did not record coordination or a common process between the two decisions; nor did they specify the duration of the restrictions, the manner of implementation, the avenue for appeal, or their effect on journalists other than those named.

superPackets.body: Following their talks in Saint-Pierre and Miquelon, Emmanuel Macron and Mark Carney committed to strengthening France-Canada ties in the face of geopolitical tensions, climate change and the erosion of democratic values; outlets presented the choice of the archipelago, visited by a Canadian prime minister for the first time, as a symbolic message amid tensions with the United States. Le Monde described the visit as a sign of Canada’s intention to move away from the United States under the Donald Trump administration, while other outlets noted Ottawa’s pursuit of stronger relations with Europe; they did not provide details on the binding nature, timetable or implementation limits of the commitments announced. Separately, Carney announced that he was seeking a “unique alliance” and a new form of associate membership with the European Union; European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen opened the door to the idea, while Trump called the proposal “ridiculous” and threatened to impose heavy tariffs on the EU if he perceived bad faith. The Conversation writer Stewart Prest interpreted this orientation as a search for security in the face of American intervention and Trump’s hostility, but also wrote that unanswered questions remained regarding the content of associate membership, decision-sharing, trade consequences and how existing ties with the United States would be affected. None of the sources recorded that the commitments made with France were legally or institutionally linked to the EU associate-membership proposal, that Canada had broken away from the United States, or that a completed new strategy had entered into force.

superPackets.body:
Volodymyr Zelensky, confirming that Ukraine had carried out attacks on infrastructure facilities in and around Moscow on the night of 20 September, said that a major oil facility and a logistics facility had been hit. Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin claimed that more than 1,600 drones had been downed, 450 of them headed for the capital, and that the attack was intended to disrupt parliamentary elections; Moscow Region Governor Andrey Vorobyov reported that at least two people had been killed, a refinery had been damaged, and 400 people had been evacuated from an apartment building. Separate reports said that Ukraine had stated it had targeted Wildberries- and Ozon-linked warehouses and logistics centres in Russia in recent weeks on the grounds that they supplied goods to soldiers at the front; the reported commercial losses and the military use of the targets were not independently verified.

In Ukraine, Deutsche Welle and CBC wrote that Russia had stepped up drone attacks in recent weeks on trains and infrastructure across the country’s roughly 20,000-kilometre railway network. The BBC reported that a drone had struck a train near the Ukraine-Poland border and that no casualties had been reported; Kyiv regional authorities said that three children and a woman had been killed in a separate overnight attack in the Kyiv region. It was reported that the Ukrainian government was preparing plans to protect tracks, trains and passengers, and had requested assistance for new locomotives to replace those destroyed. Sources did not record details of these measures or their measured effectiveness, the civilian or military character of each railway target, or the existence of a chain of retaliation between the attacks around Moscow and the railway attacks.

superPackets.axis: Husi ilerleyişi ve saldırıları üzerinden Yemen savaşı ile Suudi ve bölgesel güvenliğin haberleştirilmesi ← Husi ilerleyişi ve saldırılarının Yemen savaşını tırmandırarak Suudi Arabistan’ı ve daha geniş bölgesel güvenliği etkilemesi
superPackets.body:
Reports on the Houthi advance wrote that the process, which began with a move against the Taiz-Mokha road on 3 September, had by 11 September extended to the capture of Mokha, Dhubab and Mayyun Island; UN-attributed displacement figures varied between more than 100,000, at least 110,000 and at least 125,000. The Guardian reported that more than 15 brigades had been defeated and that the entire western coast had come under Houthi control, while Yemeni and Houthi officials later said that the Greater and Lesser Hanish islands had also been taken; POLITICO noted that these latter claims had not been independently verified. The Japan Times reported that the advance had led to the deaths of hundreds of people, but the packages did not provide a breakdown of the deaths by side or between civilians and combatants.

Separately from the coastal movement, the Houthis said they had carried out ballistic missile and drone attacks on “sensitive” sites in Riyadh and an Aramco facility in Yanbu. Saudi Arabia reported that a ballistic missile headed for Riyadh had been intercepted and that there had been attempted attacks on other cities, while smoke and flames were seen near King Khalid Airport after the first air-raid alarm in the capital; Saudi authorities did not announce any casualties and did not comment on the incident around the airport. US diplomatic missions issued warnings over possible flight cancellations, airspace closures and travel disruptions; the US State Department said the conflict could “escalate rapidly.”

The National wrote that Saudi Arabia was seeking support for air defence, intelligence and against Houthi targets, and that a small number of British and other Western personnel were in the country discussing assistance options. Downing Street said it would continue working with partners for regional stability and gave no operational details; International Institute for Strategic Studies analyst Sascha Bruchmann and other experts assessed that Europe and the United States lacked either the capacity or political will for a major intervention. According to reports attributed to Axios and CBS, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman requested direct strikes from the United States, while Washington has so far refused, providing intelligence and support instead; no confirmation was published that the White House had decided on strikes.

ABC News reported that a senior Houthi official warned other countries not to join the Yemen war alongside Saudi Arabia. In a separate account attributed to Reuters, the Houthis were reported to have told the United States during Oman-mediated talks that they would not fire on American, Israeli or other commercial ships, but had excluded Saudi vessels from that commitment; the US State Department did not confirm the meeting. Statements that the Houthi advance gave Iran leverage, reignited the Yemen war or affected regional security appeared as assessments by publications and quoted analysts; the reports did not confirm that Iran was directing the operation. The packages did not record the civilian effects of the reported attacks, the full scope of reciprocal ceasefire arrangements, or the specific mechanism by which control of the coast affected regional trade or security.

superPackets.axis: İran-ABD çatışması çevresindeki askerî tırmanma söylemi, güvenlik yansımaları ve paralel diplomatik temaslar ← İran-ABD savaşı çevresindeki askeri tırmanma tehditleri, güvenlik yansımaları ve paralel İran-ABD/bölgesel diplomatik temaslar
superPackets.body:
The Hill and UPI reported that Donald Trump said, while assessing the next steps in the war, that he questioned when he would destroy all of Iran; these records did not state that a new U.S. attack had taken place. Tehran, meanwhile, claimed to have received intelligence that the United States was planning new attacks and warned that new attacks by the United States or its allies would be met with “unlimited” and sustained retaliation targeting U.S. bases and interests; the reported intelligence was not independently verified. The U.S. State Department called on Americans to reconsider travel to the Middle East amid an intensification of Houthi attacks and Iran’s continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz; South Korean President Lee Jae Myung also stated that there would be no military deployment that would bring his country into the war.

In the same period, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry said its mediators were shuttling between Iran and the United States in an effort to revive talks; this was not recorded as direct bilateral talks. Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi met with CIA Director John Ratcliffe; The National’s sources said Cairo was conducting separate contacts with Washington, Tehran and the Arab countries that had been attacked, and was carrying messages between the parties. While U.S. presidential adviser Massad Boulos said Trump was working to end the war soon, Qatar’s prime minister called for a framework of mutual non-threat in the Gulf that included Iran; UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said that rebuilding trust with Iran after the Gulf attacks would take years. Sources did not record a common plan between the military rhetoric and these mediated and regional contacts; nor did they report an announced negotiating agenda or an agreed outcome for the Qatari and Egyptian initiatives.

superPackets.axis: Artan dizel ve yakıt fiyatlarının ekonomik etkileri ile hükümet ve siyasi tepkiler ← Yükselen dizel ve yakıt fiyatlarının tüketiciler ile işletmeler üzerindeki ekonomik baskısı ve buna yönelik hükümet ya da siyasi müdahaleler
superPackets.body:
The national average for diesel in the United States rose to $5.98 per gallon on 10 September and, in another measurement that same week, to a record $6.31; Grist reported that $5.98 was $2.31 higher than at the end of February and that the price in California had reached $7.91. According to the International Energy Agency, barrel-based diesel prices in the United States and Europe rose by about 95 percent from before the war to more than $220; in The National’s litre comparison for the same week, the United States was at $1.66, the Philippines at $1.363, China at $1.187 and Hong Kong at $4.695. These measurements relate to different dates, units, tax structures and markets; the sources did not derive a single global pump-price trend from them.

The Brown University tracker estimated that the rise in diesel prices in the United States had imposed an additional total cost of $46 billion on consumers, or about $350 per household; a Moody’s analysis estimated that, in less than eight months, the increase in all energy spending amounted to $121 billion and that the total cost of the war per household was $1,760. CNBC wrote that tariffs, fuel prices and interest rates were particularly squeezing manufacturers, automotive suppliers, retailers and transport companies; experts said costs would be reflected more heavily in store prices as freight contracts were renewed and fuel surcharges took effect. The Hill reported that winter bills could rise in the northeastern United States because of diesel-linked heating oil, while MarketWatch wrote that persistently high diesel prices could create upward pressure on inflation; these were statements of expectation and risk separate from measurements of household costs already incurred.

Sources identified the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the halt in exports from Russia, attacks by the Houthis in Yemen, the closure of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline, low inventories and high refinery margins alongside the increase. The U.S. Energy Information Administration raised its 2027 average retail diesel forecast by 8.2 percent to $4.40 per gallon and its 2026 forecast by 4.4 percent to $5.07; the latter forecast had been prepared before the weekly record spike.

Germany, which announced the tax-cut and price-cap plan last week, said it would bring into force next month a 17-cent-per-litre reduction for petrol and diesel and that the package would cost €2.5 billion; the temporary price cap remained a plan targeted for 1 January 2027. Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil called on the European Commission to propose an EU-wide windfall-profits tax on oil companies by the end of October; Economy and Energy Minister Katherina Reiche objected, subject to the condition that it would be meaningful only in cases of abused price increases. In the United States, Senator Chuck Grassley called for an embargo on diesel exports; sources did not record that this had been adopted or entered into force.

The sources did not state the starting price for the tax cut in Germany, how long it would last, or how the €2.5 billion cost would be shared between federal and state budgets; nor did they state the duration of the planned cap or its distribution among different consumer groups. No source recorded the duration or cost of the embargo proposed by Grassley, or how its burden would be distributed between domestic prices and exporters.
